[00033]	Figure 1 exemplarily illustrates a control system (100) comprising access module (102) for controlling one or more secondary devices, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. 
[00034]	The control system (100) as per the present subject matter comprises of a primary device (104), one or more secondary devices (106) and an access module (102). The system (100) as described here is provided to utilize an access module (102) to be in communication with the primary device (104). The access module (102) as per an embodiment may be utilized for a controlling one or more environments associated with a user of the access module. The one or more environments may include a vehicle environment, a home environment and an office environment. The environment may comprise one or more electrical and/or electronic components and a security access control system. The electrical and/or electronic components may include lighting units, horns, door access controls, thermal regulators, etc.
[00035]	In an aspect, the control system (100) comprises: an access module (102) configured to control one or more secondary devices (106) disposed in a threshold range of the access module (102) via a second communication channel; and a primary device (104). The primary device (104) is communicatively coupled to the access module (102) via a first communication channel. The access module (102) is configured to: identify the one or more secondary devices (106) disposed in the threshold range of the access module (102); detect one or more user inputs, each of the one or more user inputs being associated with an operation of the one or more secondary devices (106); and transmit one or more control signals corresponding to the one or more user inputs associated with the operation of the one or more secondary devices (106).
[00036]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter the access module (102) may be a key fob. The access module (102) may be configured to communicate with a primary device (104). The access module (102) may comprise one or more keys, with each key being associated with a user desired function of the one or more secondary devices (106). The access module (102) additionally comprises a memory unit and a processing unit. The access module (102) serves as an interface between the user and the target secondary device which is to be operated for a user desired function. In an embodiment, the access module (106) comprises a combination of one or more keys with a digital display. 
[00037]	In an embodiment the primary device (104) may be a digital device such as a mobile phone, a personal digital assistant, a tablet and a wearable digital device. The primary device (104) serves as an authentication platform for the access module (102). The authentication process permits safe interaction/communication between the secondary devices (106) and the access module (102).
[00038]	As per an aspect of the present subject matter, the access module (102) comprises: one or more keys, the one or more keys being configured to receive one or more user inputs; a memory unit and a processing unit. The memory unit is configured to store a unique id associated with each of one or more secondary devices. The unique id being received from a primary device (104) upon authentication. The processing unit is configured to: receive the one or more user inputs, identify at least one secondary device of the one or more secondary devices (106) with which the received one or more user inputs are associated, and transmit one or more control signals to the at least one identified secondary device for operation of the at least one identified secondary device.
[00039]	As per another aspect of the present subject matter the access module comprises of a communication interface (102a), a battery (102b), an input device (102c) and a microcontroller (102d). The communication interface (102a) associated with the access module is provided primarily for establishing communication with external devices such as the primary device, the vehicle or a remote server (108). The communication interface (102a) may utilize various protocols, including GSM, RFID, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi, ensuring that the access module (102) may communicate reliably and securely under different conditions.  The battery (102b) supplies sufficient electrical energy required to operate the internal components of the access module (102). As per the present subject matter a user interaction with the access module (102) may be facilitated by an input device (102c), which could be a button, touchpad, or any other mechanism that allows the user to send commands to the access module (102). The input device (102c) may alternately refer to the one or more keys of the access module (102). The microcontroller (102d) associated with the access module (102) process inputs from both the user and the communication interface (102a), execute commands, and manage the overall operation of the access module (102). In an aspect the microcontroller (102d) may be responsible for input processing. It receives inputs from the user via the input device (102c) and from one or more external devices through the communication interface (102a). It interprets the inputs to determine the appropriate actions. 
[00040]	In an exemplary scenario, when a user presses a button on the access module (102), the microcontroller (102d) processes this input to initiate a command, such as unlocking the vehicle. The microcontroller (102d) after processing the inputs, it executes the corresponding commands which may involve sending a signal to the vehicle's locking mechanism to unlock the doors or communicating with the primary device (104) to update the access status. Furthermore, the microcontroller (102d) coordinates the various components of the access module (102), such as the communication interface (102a), battery (102b), and input device (102c). The microcontroller (102d) ensures that these components work together seamlessly to provide a cohesive and efficient functioning of the access control. The microcontroller (102d) may also maintain the system's (100) integrity and performance and also handles complex tasks with precision and speed, ensuring that the access module (102) operates reliably under various conditions. 
[00041]	In an aspect of the present subject matter the microcontroller (102d) encrypts communication between the access module (102) and the primary device (104) to protect against unauthorized access. The communication channel between the access module (102) and the primary device (104) is referred to as a first communication channel. This encryption ensures that sensitive data, such as access codes, are transmitted securely, preventing potential breaches. Additionally, the microcontroller (102d) can facilitate firmware updates, allowing the system (100) to receive improvements and new features over time. This capability ensures that the access module (102) remains up-to-date with the latest security measures and technological advancements, enhancing its longevity and adaptability. 
[00042]	As per an aspect of the present subject matter, the access module (102) being communicatively coupled to the one or more secondary devices (106) upon authentication by the primary device (104). The authentication of the access module (102) comprises: transmitting, by the access module (102), a code associated with the access module (102) to the primary device (104) via the first communication channel; comparing, by the primary device (104), the received code with one or more credentials stored in the primary device (104); and enabling, by the primary device (104), the second communication channel between the access module (102) and the one or more secondary devices (106) based on comparing the received code with the one or more credentials.
[00043]	The primary device (104) as per the present subject matter may serve as a primary authentication device. The primary device (104) comprises of a communication interface (104a), a battery (104b), and a microcontroller (104c). These components work together to ensure that the authenticated access module (102) can communicate with the one or more secondary devices (106) securely and efficiently for operation of the one or more secondary devices (106) as per user inputs. The communication interface (104a) of the primary device (104) is responsible for establishing and maintaining communication with the access module (102) and other external systems. This communication interface (104a) can utilize various communication protocols, such as GSM, RFID, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi, to facilitate reliable and secure data exchange. The communication interface (104a) ensures that the primary device (104) can send and receive signals to and from the access module (102), enabling the necessary interactions for access control. The microcontroller (104c) associated with the primary device (104) acts as the central processing unit, managing the device's overall operation. It processes inputs from the communication interface (104a) and executes commands to authenticate the access module (102). The microcontroller (104c) ensures that the primary device (104) can verify the credentials of the access module (102) and authorize its operations. This involves complex processing tasks, such as encryption and decryption of data, to maintain security and integrity. The primary device (104) and the access module (102) interact to ensure that all operations associated with the access module (102) are authorized by the user. This interaction involves the primary device (104) sending authentication requests to the access module (102) and receiving responses that confirm the module's identity and authorization status. The microcontroller (104c) in the primary device (104) processes these responses to grant or deny access based on the received credentials. 
[00044]	In one embodiment of the system, the access module (102) may be registered directly on the primary device (104). This registration process involves storing the credentials of the access module (102) in the memory of the primary device (104). The microcontroller (104c) manages this registration process, ensuring that the credentials are securely stored and can be retrieved for future authentication. In an alternate embodiment of the present subject matter, the access module (102) may be registered through the primary device (104), with its credentials stored on a remote server (108). In this scenario, the primary device (104) communicates with the remote server (108) to verify the credentials of the access module (102). The communication interface (104a) facilitates this interaction, ensuring that the data exchange between the primary device (104) and the remote server (108) is secure and reliable. The microcontroller (104c) processes the responses from the remote server (108) to authenticate the access module (102) and authorize its operations. 
[00045]	As per an aspect of the present subject matter, the one or more secondary devices (106) is at least one of: an access control module of one or more environments of a user associated with the access module (102) and the primary device (104); and a controller of an electronic component disposed in the one or more environments of the user. The one or more operations comprising one of: locking and unlocking the access control module; and regulating operational parameters of the electronic component. For instance, the electronic component being an air conditioner, the same may be regulated remotely via the access module (102). 
[00046]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the access module (102) is designed to detect user inputs from one or more secondary devices (106). The secondary devices (106) as described here may include access control devices, illumination units, and smart home devices. The access module (102) interacts with a broader ecosystem of devices, enhancing its functionality and integration within a smart environment. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the input device (102c) of the access module (102) may be configured to function as one or more keys that are associated with the operation of these secondary devices (106). Each of the one or more keys may corresponds to a specific function or command for a secondary device (106). For example, a key might be programmed to turn on a light (illumination unit) or unlock a door (access control device). In an embodiment when the user interacts with the access module (102), it detects the input and processes it to determine the corresponding action for the secondary device (106). The access module (102) then transmits control signals that correspond to the user inputs. These control signals are sent to the secondary devices (106) to execute the desired operations. For instance, if a user presses a key to unlock a door, the access module (102) will send a signal to the access control device to perform the unlocking action.
[00047]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the primary device (104) and the one or more secondary devices (106) are interlinked through a remote server (108). The remote server (108) is configured to operate as a computing interface, facilitating communication and coordination between the primary device (104) and the secondary devices (106). The remote server (108) monitor and process data exchanged between the devices (102, 104, 106), ensuring that commands and responses are transmitted securely and efficiently. In an embodiment the remote server (108) executes tasks such as authentication, data encryption, and command execution, providing a centralized platform for managing the interactions between the primary device (104) and the secondary devices (106). In an embodiment of the present subject matter the remote server (108) serves as a computing interface. The system (100) ensures seamless integration and control of various smart devices within a user's proximity. By centralizing the control through the access module (102), users can manage multiple devices efficiently. 
[00048]	In an embodiment, the access module (102) comprises a full button, a part and perimeter button, a disarm button, a home automation ON/OFF button and a panic alarm button. The full button enables communication with all the secondary devices (106) irrespective of the threshold range. The part and perimeter button is configured to enable the access module (102) to identify the secondary devices (106) in a threshold range or perimeter of the access module (102). The disarm button is configured to disable the communication channel between the access module (102) and the secondary devices (106). The home automation ON/OFF button enables and disables respectively the communication between the access module (102) and the secondary devices (106) identified to be in the location coordinates corresponding to “home” environment. The panic alarm button is configured to trigger an alert on to the primary device (104). The primary device (104) may thereon transmit the emergency or panic state onto emergency contacts listed in the primary device (104).
[00049]	Figure 2 exemplarily illustrates a method for controlling one or more secondary devices by an access module, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. 
[00050]	The process begins at step 202. At step 202, the primary device (104) authenticates the access module (102). The primary device (104) is configured to communicatively couple with the access module (102) via a first communication channel. In a preferred embodiment, the access module (102) and the primary device (104) are within a communication range. The proximity of the access module (102) and the primary device (104) allows the devices to establish a connection and initiate the authentication process. The method proceeds to 204, after the primary device (104) authenticates the access module (102). 
[00051]	At step 204, the access module (102) identifies one or more secondary devices (106) disposed in a threshold range of the access module (102). The threshold range ensures that only devices in the specific environment are in communication with the access module (102). For instance, if the access module (102) is situated in a home environment, then only electronic and/or electrical devices in the specific home environment are identified and communicatively coupled to the access module (102) via a second communication channel. The identification of the one or more secondary devices (106) may be executed via geolocation mapping of the secondary devices with reference to the access module (102). The method 200 then proceeds to step 206.
[00052]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the primary device (104) is configured to store one or more credentials necessary for authentication. These credentials consist of specific codes that correspond to the access module (102). The primary device (104) uses the stored credentials to verify the identity of the access module (102). The authentication process is crucial for maintaining the security and integrity of the system. By authenticating the access module (102) before allowing any operations, the primary device (104) ensures that unauthorized devices cannot gain access or control. This step helps protect the system from potential security breaches and unauthorized use. 
[00053]	In an aspect, the authentication of the access module (102) comprises: transmitting, by the access module (102), a code associated with the access module (102) to the primary device (104) via the first communication channel; comparing, by the primary device (104), the received code with one or more credentials stored in the primary device (104); and enabling, by the primary device (104), the second communication channel between the access module (102) and the one or more secondary devices (106) based on comparing the received code with the one or more credentials. The primary device (104) being configured to store a unique id associated with each one or more secondary devices (106) and transmitting the stored unique id to the access module (102).
[00054]	In an aspect, the one or more secondary devices (106) are verified by the access module (102) for communicatively coupling of the access module (102) with the one or more secondary devices (106). The verification comprises: transmitting, by the access module (102) a challenge signal to the one or more secondary devices (106), the challenge signal being associated with the unique id of the one or more secondary devices (106); receiving, by the access module (102) a response signal from the one or more secondary devices (106), wherein the response signal is generated based on the challenge signal and the unique id; mapping, by the access module (102), the response signal with a solution dataset generated based on the challenge signal; and communicating, by the access module (102), with the one or more secondary devices (106) based on the mapping of the response signal with the solution dataset. The challenge signal being generated by an encryption algorithm comprising the unique id. The solution dataset being generated and stored by the access module (102) based on a decryption logic applied on the challenge signal.
[00055]	The method proceeds to 206, where the access module (102) detects one or more inputs from the secondary devices (106). In the present embodiment, each user input may be associated with a specific operation of the secondary devices (106). For example, a user input might correspond to turning on a light, unlocking a door, or adjusting the thermostat. Upon detecting the user inputs, the access module (102) processes them to determine the appropriate control signals. The method 200 then proceeds to step 208.
[00056]	At step 208 access module (102) transmits control signals to the corresponding secondary devices (106) to execute the desired operations. This step ensures that the user's commands are accurately interpreted and carried out by the secondary devices (106), providing a seamless and integrated control experience. The one or more secondary devices (106) are at least one of: an access control module of one or more environments of a user associated with the access module (102) and the primary device (104); and a controller of an electronic component disposed in the one or more environments of the user. The one or more operations comprising one of: locking and unlocking the access control module; and regulating operational parameters of the electronic component. The process then proceeds to step 210 and stops.
[00057]	Figure 3 exemplarily illustrates a flow chart of verifying the one or more secondary devices by the access module (102) in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. 
[00058]	The process initiates at step 301. The process 300 proceeds to 302 where the access module (102) transmits a challenge signal to the one or more secondary devices (106). The challenge signal is a unique code or request generated by the access module (102). The purpose of the challenge signal is to prompt the secondary devices (106) to respond in a way that proves their authenticity. The challenge signal can be a random number, a cryptographic nonce, or any other form of data that requires a specific response from the secondary devices (106). This step ensures that the secondary devices (106) are actively participating in the verification process and are capable of generating a valid response. The process 300 then proceeds to step 304. 
[00059]	At step 304, the one or more secondary devices (106) upon receiving the challenge signal, generates a response. This response signal is typically created using a predefined algorithm or cryptographic method that ensures its validity and security. The one or more secondary devices (106) process the challenge signal and produce a response signal that may be unique to the challenge signal. The response signal is then transmitted back to the access module (102). The use of cryptographic methods ensures that the response cannot be easily forged or replicated by unauthorized devices, adding an extra layer of security to the verification process. 
[00060]	At step 306 upon receiving the response signal from the secondary devices (106), the access module (102) proceeds to verify its authenticity. The authenticity of the response signal  is done by comparing the received response signal with a solution dataset stored within the access module (102). The solution dataset contains the expected responses for valid secondary devices (106) based on the challenge signals. The access module (102) uses this dataset to determine whether the received response signal matches the expected response. If the response signal matches the expected response in the solution dataset, the secondary devices (106) are considered authenticated and authorized to interact with the system. This step ensures that only legitimate one or more secondary devices (106) may communicate with the access module (102), preventing unauthorized access and potential security breaches.
[00061]	The challenge-response authentication method used in this verification process is a secure way to confirm the legitimacy of the secondary devices (106). By requiring the secondary devices (106) to generate a specific response to a unique challenge, the system can effectively prevent unauthorized devices from gaining access. This method also ensures that the verification process is dynamic and adaptable, as the challenge signals can be varied to prevent predictable patterns.
[00062]	A person with ordinary skills in the art will appreciate that the systems, modules, and sub-modules have been illustrated and explained to serve as examples and should not be considered limiting in any manner. It will be further appreciated that the variants of the above disclosed system elements, modules, and other features and functions, or alternatives thereof, may be combined to create other different systems or applications.
[00063]	One of the primary advantages of the described system is its enhanced security. The use of a challenge-response mechanism ensures that only authorized devices can interact with the access module. By requiring secondary devices to generate specific responses to unique challenges, the system effectively prevents unauthorized access. This robust authentication process protects against potential security breaches and ensures that only legitimate users can control the connected devices.
[00064]	The system allows for seamless integration of various smart devices within a user's environment. By centralizing control through the access module, users can manage multiple devices, such as smart door locks and lights, from a single interface. This integration simplifies the user experience, making it easier to control and automate different aspects of a smart home. The ability to interact with multiple devices through a single access module enhances convenience and efficiency.
[00065]	The system's design offers significant flexibility and scalability. The access module can communicate with a wide range of secondary devices using various communication protocols, such as GSM, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi. This flexibility allows the system to adapt to different technological environments and user preferences. Additionally, the use of a remote server as a computing interface enables the system to scale easily, accommodating more devices and users without compromising performance or security.
[00066]	By integrating with various smart home devices, the system provides enhanced control and automation capabilities. Users can program the access module (102) to perform specific actions based on user inputs, such as unlocking doors or turning on lights. This automation can be tailored to individual preferences, creating a personalized and responsive smart home environment. The ability to automate routine tasks enhances convenience and improves the overall user experience.
[00067]	The use of a remote server as a computing interface allows for centralized management of the system. This centralization simplifies the process of updating and maintaining the system, as updates can be deployed remotely to all connected devices. It also enables advanced features, such as remote monitoring and control, providing users with greater flexibility and oversight of their smart home environment. The present subject matter eliminates the need for traditional keys, providing keyless access to devices such as vehicles, homes, and smart locks. Through wireless communication between the key fob, digital device, and electrical devices, users can easily unlock doors, start vehicles, or control smart systems without the hassle of physically searching for or handling keys. The integration with smartphones and smartwatches means users can operate their devices with a simple touch or proximity detection, making the entire process faster and more efficient.

title: MODULAR CONFIGURATION OF AN INSTRUMENT CLUSTER OF A VEHICLE
abstract: The present subject matter discloses an instrument cluster (102) of a vehicle (100), which comprises of a first base board (104) configured to receive at least one computing unit (104a), a second base board (106) electrically connected to the first base board (104), and a third base board (108) electrically connected to at least one of the first base board (104) and the second base board (106). In an embodiment, the third base board (108) being configured to receive a plurality of indicators (108a). In an embodiment, the second base board (106) being configured to receive at least one communication module (106a). In the present embodiment the instrument cluster further comprises of a display unit (110). In the present embodiment, the computing unit (104a) may dynamically adjust a user interface displayed on the display unit (110) based on the presence and type of the selectively coupled one or more electronic components.

DESC:TECHNICAL FIELD
[0001]	The present subject matter generally relates to automotive industry. More particularly, but not exclusively to, a configuration of an instrument cluster for modularity.
BACKGROUND
[0002]	In existing solutions, a smart integrated module provides different capabilities, such as wireless capabilities, keyless entry capabilities, power management capabilities, data processing and rendering capabilities, etc., to the instrument cluster. However, the existing integrated module may not be an automotive grade component to be deployed in a high-performance vehicle where vibrations and temperatures experienced may be high.
[0003]	Further, if the same integrated module were to be manufactured in the automotive grade, it will be very expensive for the OEMs to deploy every vehicle and the cost of using such an integrated module may be transferred to the customer subsequently. Also, different variants of the vehicle will demand capabilities and may not require the same integrated module. Providing different versions of the software to activate and deactivate the capabilities offered by the integrated module will be tedious for the developers in the OEM. 
[0004]	Thus, there is a need for a modular configuration of the instrument cluster offering different capabilities as on demand, based on the vehicle variant, which addresses at least the aforementioned problems and other problems of known art.
SUMMARY OF THE DISCLOSURE
[0005]	According to embodiments illustrated herein, the present disclosure relates to an instrument cluster of a vehicle. In an embodiment, the instrument cluster as described here comprises of a first base board, a second base board, and a third base board. The first base board is configured to receive at least one computing unit. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, each of the at least one computing unit is a microprocessor and a micro controller unit. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the first base board is configured to receive a power management module and a memory module.
[0006]	The second base board is electrically connected to the first base board, additionally the second base board is configured to receive at least one communication module. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, at least one communication module comprises Wi-Fi, BLE, BT, GSM, 4G, autonomous BLE, etc. Furthermore, the power management module includes a PMIC. The memory module mentioned here is an eMMC or a LPDDR. In a further embodiment of the present subject matter, the second base board is configured to receive a photosensitive module. 
[0007]	The third base board electrically connects to at least one of the first base board and the second base board. The third base board is configured to receive a plurality of indicators. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the third base board is configured to receive a audio module.
[0008]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, each of the first base board, the second base board, and the third base board is configured with a conductive substrate to electrically connect a plurality of electronic components on respective base board. The plurality of electronic components comprises the at least one computing unit, at least one communication module, the first power management module, the memory module. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, each of the first base board, the second base board, the third base board and the plurality of electronic components is automotive grade compliant. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the first base board, the second base board and the third base board is electrically and communicatively connected with each other using a plurality of connectors. 
[0009]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, further comprises a display unit, wherein the computing unit dynamically adjusts a user interface displayed on the display unit based on the presence and type of the selectively coupled one or more electronic components.
[00010]	According to embodiments illustrated herein, the present disclosure relates to a modular configuration of an instrument cluster of a vehicle. The modular configuration comprises of at least one computing unit, at least one communication module, at least one power management module, at least one memory module, and at least one photosensitive module. The at least one communication module is electrically and communicatively connected to the at least one computing unit. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, at least one communication module comprises Wi-fi, BLE, BT, GSM, 4G, autonomous BLE. Furthermore, power management modules includes PMIC. The memory module mentioned here includes eMMC, LPDDR. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, each of the at least one computing unit comprises a microprocessor and a MCU.
[00011]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the modular configuration is achieved by placing a plurality of electronic components on at least one base board and is electrically connected to one another by a conductive substrate and a plurality of connectors.
[00012]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, comprises a display unit, wherein the computing unit dynamically adjusts a user interface displayed on the display unit based on the presence and type of the selectively coupled one or more electronic components.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION

[00025]	Figure 1 exemplarily illustrates a schematic diagram of a modular configuration of an instrument cluster (102) in accordance with the present subject matter. As per the present subject matter a vehicle (100) is described which comprises an instrument cluster (102). As per the present subject matter, the vehicle as described here may include a single track or multi track vehicle propelled by a prime mover (not shown). The prime mover may operate either as an internal combustion engine or an electric motor or a combination of both. The vehicle as described here further utilizes the instrument cluster (102) to display vehicle related parameters to a user of the vehicle (100). The instrument cluster (102) may be configured to render vehicle related information into user readable information and render it to the user. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the vehicle related information may be real-time information or pre-determined information. 
[00026]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter the instrument cluster (102) as described here comprises a first base board (104), a second base board (106), and a third base board (108). In an embodiment, the first base board (104), the second base board (106), and the third base board (108) are specifically provided to accommodate at least one of a plurality of electronic components. The plurality of electrical components may be secured onto the base boards (104,106,108) through certain provisions provided on the base boards (104,106,108) such as conductor pin securing openings.
[00027]	 In an embodiment, each of the first base board (104), the second base board (106), and the third base board (108) may be configured to accommodate the plurality of electrical components that may cater to a specific functionality thereby forming individual modules. In yet another embodiment, each of the first base board (104), the second base board (106), and the third base board (108) performing distinct functionalities may be interconnected to each other through one or more electrical coupling techniques. 
[00028]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the instrument cluster (102) is provided with a first base board (104) which accommodates a computing unit (104a). The computing unit (104a) as described here is configured to function as the primary logical and analytical core of the instrument cluster (102), responsible for processing, managing, and displaying all vehicle-related data and graphical information to the user. The computing unit (104a) further comprises a microprocessor and a microcontroller unit (MCU), which may be configured to function in a cooperative, dual-processor architecture to ensure both high-performance graphics rendering and real-time operational safety.
[00029]	The microprocessor may be designated as the high-level application processor, principally tasked with running an operating system (e.g., Linux, QNX, or Android Automotive). It handles computationally intensive tasks such as rendering the graphical user interface (GUI) on a primary display, processing multimedia data, managing connectivity protocols (e.g., Bluetooth, Wi-Fi), and executing user-facing applications like navigation and infotainment. The microprocessor is optimized for performance and is responsible for creating an interactive user experience.
[00030]	In an embodiment the microcontroller unit (MCU) may interface directly with the vehicle's Controller Area Network (CAN) bus to receive, process, and validate critical, time-sensitive data. This may include, but is not limited to, vehicle speed, engine RPM, tell-tale warnings (e.g., check engine, oil pressure, airbag status), fuel level, and gear position. The MCU operates independently or in a supervisory capacity to the main microprocessor, ensuring that the most vital driver information is processed with deterministic timing and displayed without interruption. The MCU may also manage the instrument cluster’s (102) boot-up sequence, power management states, and drive basic tell-tale indicators as a fail-safe mechanism, guaranteeing the operational integrity of the instrument cluster (102) under all conditions. This distributed processing architecture segregates non-critical, high-complexity functions from safety-critical, real-time operations to enhance system robustness and reliability.
[00031]	In an embodiment, the first base board (104) may also comprise a memory module (104b), communicatively coupled with the computing unit (104a). The memory module (104b) is configured to serve as the comprehensive data repository for the instrument cluster (102). In an embodiment, the memory module (104b) may be configured to store system-specific files, such as bootloaders, kernel images, device drivers, and graphical assets, which are essential for the microprocessor to initialize the operating system and render the user interface. Furthermore, the memory module (104b) may be configured for storing one or more data sets associated with the vehicle (100), which may include persistent data like trip odometers, user preferences, vehicle settings, and diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs), as well as for storing temporary data, such as cached information for navigation maps or real-time sensor readings awaiting processing by the computing unit (104a).
[00032]	In an exemplary embodiment, the memory module (104b) may comprise a combination of both a permanent storage module and a temporary storage module to optimize performance and data integrity. The permanent storage module may be implemented as an embedded multimedia card (eMMC), providing a non-volatile, high-density storage solution for the operating system, application software, and critical vehicle data that must be retained when the system is powered down. The temporary storage module may be implemented as Low-Power Double Data Rate (LPDDR) Synchronous Dynamic Random-Access Memory (SDRAM). The synergistic use of eMMC for persistent storage and LPDDR for volatile, high-speed operations provides an efficient memory architecture for the instrument cluster (102).
[00033]	In an embodiment, the first base board (104) further comprises a power management module (104c), which may be configured to regulate, control, and distribute electrical power to all components of the instrument cluster (102). The power management module (104c) may serve as the primary interface to the vehicle's main power supply, such as the battery and alternator. It is designed to handle fluctuations and transients in the vehicle's electrical system, ensuring a stable and clean power supply to sensitive electronic components like the computing unit (104a) and the memory module (104b).
[00034]	The power management module (104c) may incorporate a Power Management Integrated Circuit (PMIC) and associated circuitry, such as buck-boost converters and Low-Dropout (LDO) regulators, to generate multiple, precise voltage rails required by the microprocessor, microcontroller, memory, and display backlighting. A crucial function of this module (104c) is power sequencing, where it controls the precise order and timing in which different components are powered on and off. This prevents inrush currents and ensures a stable system boot-up and shutdown sequence, which is vital for system integrity.
[00035]	In an embodiment, the power management module (104c) may function to manage the instrument cluster's power consumption and operational state in direct correspondence with the vehicle's status. When the vehicle (100) is in an OFF state, the module (104c) initiates a low-power "sleep" or "dormant" mode, where it ceases to power non-essential components like the main display and microprocessor, while providing minimal standby current only to the core logic of the microcontroller unit (MCU). This allows the instrument cluster (102) to monitor for wake-up signals (e.g., a key fob press or door opening) while ensuring negligible battery drain. Upon detecting an Ignition (IGN) signal, the power management module (104c) may execute a controlled power-up sequence, activating multiple voltage rails in a specific order to safely energize the computing unit (104a), the memory module (104b), and the display unit (110), bringing the instrument cluster (102) to a fully operational state. Additionally, during the Crank phase, when the engine starter causes a significant drop in the vehicle's battery voltage, the power management module (104c) may actively regulate and stabilize the power supply. The power management module (104c) ensures the computing unit (104a) receives a constant, uninterrupted voltage, thereby preventing the instrument cluster (102) from resetting, flickering, or malfunctioning during this electrically volatile event and ensuring its stability and reliability at the moment of engine start.
[00036]	 In an embodiment the power management module (104c) may monitor the vehicle's state via dedicated input lines and communicates with the computing unit (104a) to transition the instrument cluster (102) into low-power sleep or standby modes when the vehicle is off, thereby minimizing current drawn from the battery. This module (104c) is also integral to the functional safety of the instrument cluster (102), often including features like over-voltage protection, under-voltage protection, and thermal protection to safeguard the instrument cluster (102) and ensure its reliable operation under all vehicle conditions.
[00037]	In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the instrument cluster (102) comprises a second base board (106) electrically connected to the first base board (104). The second base board (106) is configured to accommodate a communication module (106a). The second base board (106) is further configured to accommodate a photosensitive module (106b). In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the second base board (106) is physically separated from the first base board (104). In an aspect of the present subject matter, the communication module (106a) may be configured to establish wireless connectivity with at least other vehicular components or auxiliary components. In an embodiment of the present subject matter, the communication module (106a) comprises at least one of a Wi-fi module, a Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) module, a BT module, a GSM module, and a LTE module. The communication module (106a) connects with other vehicular components establishes an intra-vehicle wireless network, reducing the complexity and weight of physical wiring harnesses. For example, the communication module (106a) may be configured to directly receive data from a wireless Tire Pressure Monitoring System (TPMS), displaying real-time tire pressure on the instrument cluster (102). Similarly, it could interface with wireless sensors in smart seats or other intelligent components to configure the vehicle environment based on a recognized driver profile. This connectivity further extends to auxiliary components, such as a technician's diagnostic tablet or detachable entertainment screens, creating a versatile and integrated vehicular ecosystem.
[00038]	In an embodiment, the second base board (106) may function as an connectivity and telematics hub. In an embodiment upon the driver entering the vehicle (100), the Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) transceiver on the communication module (106a) may be configured to detect the driver's authorized smartphone, triggering a secure handshake to unlock the vehicle and load the driver's personalized profile, which includes preferred seating positions and instrument cluster display themes. Once the vehicle (100) is active, the classic Bluetooth (BT) functionality seamlessly pairs with the phone for hands-free calling and audio streaming, with metadata such as song titles and contact names displayed on the instrument cluster. Concurrently, the 4G/LTE modem may be configured to establish a persistent connection to the a cloud services. This communication module (106a) may be configured to retrieve real-time traffic data to be overlaid on the navigation map shown on the cluster display by communication with cloud services. In an embodiment, when the vehicle is parked within range of a trusted network, the Wi-Fi transceiver may perform high-bandwidth tasks, such as downloading an over-the-air (OTA) software update, ensuring the vehicle’s systems are kept current without requiring user intervention or a trip to a service centre.
[00039]	In an embodiment, the photosensitive module (106b) on the second base board (106) may be configured to operate in concert with the communication module (106a). The photosensitive module (106b) may be configured to detect the gradual decrease in ambient light, the ambient light data may be utilized to change from a light mode to night mode and vice versa to reduce eye strain. 
[00040]	In an embodiment, the communication module (106a) may be configured to obtain meteorological data for the vehicle's current location. For example, if the data indicates heavy cloud cover or rain during midday, the processor can override output of the photosensitive module (106b) reading, which might still detect sufficient ambient light, and pre-emptively activate the headlights and adjust the cluster display for the low-visibility conditions, thereby enhancing safety. 
[00041]	In an embodiment, the instrument cluster (102) includes a third base board (108). The third base board (108) is electrically connected to at least one of the first base board (104) and the second base board (106). In an embodiment, the third base board (108) is configured to receive a plurality of indicators (108a), which include the tell-tale drivers ( LED drivers). These drivers are the electronic circuits that control the operation of the standardized visual warning and status lamps, such as the check engine, oil pressure, and turn signal indicators. The third base board (108) may also be configured to accommodate an audio module (108b). The audio module (108b) module may be responsible for generating all system-related audible alerts, including warning chimes and the synchronized clicking of the turn signals. 
[00042]	In an embodiment the instrument cluster (102) may further include a display unit (110). The display unit (110) as described here may function as a visual interface. The display unit (110) may be embodied as a single, panoramic digital surface, or as an assembly of multiple, functionally distinct yet coordinated displays. In an embodiment the display unit (110) may be configured to present a wide range of information, including but not limited to, a digital speedometer, tachometer, navigation maps, infotainment data, and detailed textual or graphical alerts which supplement the tell-tale indicators. To render this information, the display unit (110) may be electrically coupled to the first base board (104). The display unit (110) operates in concert with the aforementioned modules. In an embodiment the display unit (110) brightness may be dynamically controlled based on signals from the photosensitive module (106b) to ensure optimal legibility, and it displays contextual data sourced from the communication module (106a), thereby providing a comprehensive and integrated driver information system.
[00043]	In embodiment of the present subject matter the each of the first base board (104), the second base board (106), and the third base board (108) is  configured with a conductive substrate (112) to electrically connect a plurality of electronic components on respective base board, wherein the plurality of electronic components comprises the at least one computing unit (104a), at least one communication module (106a), the power management module (108a), the memory module, the photosensitive module, etc. Each of these modules may be an integrated circuit or a combination of integrated circuit and antennae or a combination of integrated circuits with individual memory capabilities and wireless capabilities. In an embodiment, each of these modules has wired or wirelessly interfacing with other modules. In an embodiment, the base boards may be a printed circuit board (PCB), flexible printed circuits, rigid-flex PCBs, ceramic substrates, printed electronics, bread boards, etc. In another embodiment, the PCB may be a single sided PCB with provisions to mount the electrical and electronic components on one side, a double sided PCB with conductive substrate on both sides, a multi-layer PCB for complex routing, a flexible PCB, a rigid PCB, Aluminum backed PCB and high frequency PCB.
[00044]	Each of the base board has provisions to receive the modules on them. The provisions may be the vias in the base board, ground and power planes definition on the base board, clearance between conductive substrate/ traces, thermal management provisions, testing and repair provisions, etc. Based on the variant of the vehicle or variant of the instrument cluster that needs to be provided on the vehicle, the number of base boards may vary and the number of modules mounted on the base boards may vary.
[00045]	 Furthermore, each of the first base board (104), the second base board (106), the third base board (108) and the plurality of electronic components being automotive grade compliant. The first base board (104), the second base board (106), and the third base board (108) being electrically and communicatively connected with each other using a plurality of connectors.  
[00046]	In an embodiment of the present invention, the third base board (108) is configured as a dedicated driver alert centre, consolidating the instrument cluster's primary visual and audible feedback systems. It is specifically designed to accommodate a plurality of indicators (108a), which comprise the electronic tell-tale driver circuits. In an embodiment the third base board (108) may be responsible for controlling the illumination of the vehicle's standardized warning and status lamps, such as the turn signals, high-beam indicator, check engine light, and seatbelt reminder. By isolating the telltale indicators and audio module, which manage the higher currents required for the indicator lamps, this board effectively contains potential electrical noise away from the main processing unit. Furthermore, the audio module (108b) may be configured to generate non-infotainment audible alerts, including the synchronized clicking of the turn signals and various warning chimes. 
[00047]	In accordance with the present subject matter, Figure 2 illustrates an alternative embodiment of the instrument cluster (102) wherein the modular configuration is realized on an integrated single base board (201). This embodiment demonstrates that the functional segregation of modules is maintained, irrespective of whether they are implemented on physically separate boards or as distinct, logically separated regions on a unified substrate. The modularity is achieved by the strategic placement and interconnection of the plurality of electronic components on the base board, which are electrically connected to one another through the underlying conductive substrate (112). 
[00048]	The integrated single base board (201), the plurality of electronic components are arranged in functionally distinct zones. At least one computing unit (104a), may be co-located with at least one dedicated memory module (104b) in a high-speed digital processing zone, forming the computational core of the instrument cluster. In a separate region, at least one communication module (106a) is situated, managing all wireless connectivity. The base board may also accommodate at least one power management module (108a), which consolidates the power conversion circuitry responsible for taking the vehicle's supply and generating the stable voltages needed by all other components. This power management module (104c) may be placed in a region optimized for thermal dissipation. Furthermore, at least one photosensitive module (106b) is positioned to accurately detect ambient light for controlling display brightness. All these modules are electrically and communicatively connected to the computing unit (104a) via the traces within the conductive substrate (112).
[00049]	The conductive substrate (112) of the single integrated base board is a complex, multi-layered printed circuit board that provides both the mechanical foundation and electrical interconnection for the plurality of electrical components. While internal connections between modules are handled by the substrate's traces, the instrument cluster still relies on a plurality of connectors for external interfacing. These connectors facilitate the electrical and communicative coupling of the integrated base board to other essential parts of the system, such as the main display unit (110), the vehicle's primary wiring harness, any speakers for an audio module, and any physical gauges or indicators that are part of the final assembly. 
[00050]	Figure 3 illustrates a method (300) for the dynamic configuration of an interface on the display unit (110). This method (300) allows the visual interface to automatically adapt based on the presence or absence of specific hardware modules or base boards. The process commences at step 302 upon the initiation of the vehicle's power-on sequence. At step 304, the control unit, which in an exemplary embodiment may be the computing unit (104a), performs a hardware enumeration and checking sequence. This detection is achieved by polling for responses from connected modules over an internal communication bus or by sensing the state of dedicated presence-detect pins on the physical connectors that link the base boards. The computing unit (104a) compiles a real-time inventory of all detected electronic components, such as the communication module (106a) or a dedicated audio module. At step 306, the computing unit (104a) compares this newly generated inventory against a hardware configuration list stored in non-volatile memory from its previous operational cycle. If a discrepancy is found, such as the identification of a new, previously absent electronic component, the process advances. Upon detecting a new component, the computing unit (104a) loads the corresponding software drivers and simultaneously triggers a predefined UI modification routine. This routine sends signals to the display unit (110) to alter the graphical user interface by activating, deactivating, or modifying display elements at step 308. This ensures the interface always accurately reflects the current hardware capabilities of the instrument cluster, providing an intuitive and uncluttered experience for the user. The process then concludes at step 310, with the instrument cluster operating with its newly configured interface.
[00051]	To further illustrate the aforementioned method (300), consider a detailed exemplary embodiment. A user may purchase a vehicle with a base-model instrument cluster, which includes the first base board (104) with the computing unit (104a) but lacks the second base board (106). In this initial state, the interface on the display unit (110) is streamlined, showing only core driving information and lacking options for external connectivity or automatic brightness control. At a later time, the user may opt for a "Connectivity and Comfort" upgrade, which involves an installation of the second base board (106), containing both the communication module (106a) and the photosensitive module (106b), into a pre-existing expansion slot. The next time the user starts the vehicle (step 302), the computing unit (104a) executes its checking process (step 304) and detects the presence of the new hardware on the second base board (106). Recognizing the new components (step 306), the computing unit (104a) automatically reconfigures the user interface. Consequently, the display unit (110) is dynamically updated to include a cellular signal strength indicator and a Bluetooth icon in its status bar. A previously hidden "Connectivity" menu now appears, allowing the user to pair a smartphone. Simultaneously, upon detecting the photosensitive module (106b), the system activates an "Auto Brightness" toggle within the display settings menu, enabling the display's luminance to adjust automatically. This example demonstrates how the modular configuration allows for post-sale hardware upgrades to seamlessly unlock new software features and UI elements, providing significant value and future-proofing the vehicle's instrumentation without requiring replacement of the entire cluster.
[00052]	Figure 4 exemplarily illustrates an interface configuration in accordance with the present subject matter. In accordance with an embodiment of the present subject matter, Figure 4 exemplarily illustrates a specific interface configuration of the display unit (110), corresponding to an instrument cluster (102) populated with at least the first base board (104) and the second base board (106). The interface is logically partitioned to present distinct categories of information. A primary area of the display is dedicated to rendering core vehicle parameters, which are processed by the computing unit (104a) on the first base board (104). This includes a graphical representation of the prime mover's revolutions per minute (RPM), a prominent digital or analog-style speedometer indicating vehicle speed, and other essential data such as fuel level and engine temperature may also be provided. 
[00053]	In an embodiment, upon detection of the second base board (106), the interface dynamically populates a secondary area with information sourced directly from the communication module (106a). This section may include a status bar or dedicated widgets displaying connectivity details, such as icons indicative of Bluetooth availability and cellular network signal strength. Upon establishing a connection with a peripheral device, this area can be further configured to display information associated with that device, such as a connected smartphone's battery status or the title of a streaming media track. Furthermore, this communication-centric area is configured to display navigation details, such as turn-by-turn directions and distance to the next maneuver, which are generated using GPS data acquired by the communication module (106a), thereby presenting the driver with a seamlessly integrated display of both core vehicle data and advanced connectivity-enabled features.
[00054]	Figure 5 exemplarily illustrates an interface configuration in accordance with the present subject matter. Figure 5 illustrates an adaptive interface configuration that demonstrates the instrument cluster's response to the absence of a specific electronic component. This embodiment represents a scenario where the instrument cluster (102), which may be designed to potentially include a full suite of components such as the computing unit (104a), communication module (106a), power management module (108a), memory module (104b), and photosensitive module (106b), is configured without the photosensitive module (106b). During the vehicle's start-up sequence, the computing unit (104a) performs a hardware checking process and, upon failing to detect a response from the photosensitive module, flags it as absent. Consequently, the system's firmware automatically disables all dependent functionalities to prevent errors and provide a coherent user experience. Specifically, the software algorithms responsible for automatically adjusting the brightness of the display unit (110) and other backlights based on ambient light are deactivated. Similarly, any feature that automatically switches the interface theme, such as from a bright "day mode" to a "dark mode" upon nightfall, is also disabled. To reflect this change in hardware capability, the graphical user interface is reconfigured accordingly. For instance, within the display settings menu, an option for "Automatic Brightness" is hidden or replaced with a purely manual brightness control, such as a slider, empowering the user to set a static preference. This degradation of features and the corresponding adaptation of the interface ensure that the user is presented with a clear and functional system that accurately reflects the hardware present.
[00055]	Figure 6 exemplarily illustrates an interface configuration in accordance with the present subject matter. The depicted figure 6 illustrates the interface of the display unit (110) when all the plurality of electronic components associated with the corresponding dash boards as described in the present subject matter are present. The display unit (110) may be logically segmented, with each segment's content and functionality directly corresponding to one of the underlying base boards. A portion of the interface is dedicated to core vehicle functions driven by the first base board (104), displaying dynamically rendered graphics for the vehicle's speed and the engine's RPM. A second segment, which may include a persistent status bar or a dedicated quadrant, is populated with data sourced from the second base board (106). The second segment area displays connectivity details like Bluetooth status and cellular network strength, as well as turn-by-turn navigation information provided by the communication module (106a). Further, a third segment, may be configured to display status indicators and tell-tales—such as turn signals, gear selection, or alerts for over-speeding—which are controlled by the driver circuits residing on the third base board (108).
[00056]	In an embodiment, the plurality of electronic components may work in tandem to create intelligent, context-aware features. Consider an example, as evening approaches, the photosensitive module (106b) on the second board detects diminishing ambient light. Simultaneously, the communication module (106a) on the same board acquires precise time-of-day and location data via GPS and may pull local weather data (e.g., "heavy cloud cover") from one or more servers. The computing unit (104a) on the first board fuses this data; it doesn't rely solely on the light sensor. If it detects low light, confirms that the time corresponds to sunset, and sees no adverse weather report, it can command the vehicle to activate its headlights while simultaneously instructing the display unit (110) to smoothly transition from its bright "day mode" to a dark, glare-reducing "night mode." This prevents the system from incorrectly reacting to transient changes in light, like driving under a short bridge, creating a truly intelligent and comfortable driver experience reflected directly in the interface.
[00057]	To further elaborate, additional embodiments may incorporate other electronic components to enhance functionality. In an embodiment, the instrument cluster may be enhanced with a forward-facing camera module that is electrically connected to the first base board (104). The display unit (110) is configured to show a live video feed from this camera. The computing unit (104a) processes this video feed and, using precise navigation data supplied by the communication module (106a) on the second board, renders graphical overlays onto the live video. For example, it may be configured to draw arrows directly onto the road in the video feed to indicate an upcoming turn or highlight the correct lane the driver should be in. This feature may provide an intuitive navigation experience by seamlessly blending real-world views with digital directions.
[00058]	A common daily scenario may be provided to improve the understanding of the present subject matter. A driver is streaming a podcast from their smartphone via Bluetooth. The communication module (106a) on the second board manages the wireless audio stream, while the computing unit (104a) on the first board processes the associated metadata (podcast title, artwork) to show it on the display unit (110). When a navigation instruction is imminent, the computing unit (104a) gently fades down the podcast volume by commanding the audio module (108b) on the third board, plays the voice prompt for the turn, and then seamlessly fades the podcast volume back up. 
[00059]	Figure 7 exemplarily illustrates an interface configuration in accordance with the present subject matter. In accordance with the present subject matter, Figure 7 exemplarily illustrates an advanced interface configuration on the display unit (110) that provides the user with detailed, real-time power diagnostics for the instrument cluster's various electronic components. In this embodiment, a smart power management module (104c), which may be a sophisticated Power Management IC (PMIC) with integrated telemetry capabilities, is included on the first base board (104). This module is configured to monitor the voltage and current consumption of each power rail it supplies and communicates this data to the computing unit (104a). In an embodiment the computing unit (104a) then processes this information and renders it on a dedicated "Vehicle Diagnostics & power" screen on the display unit (110). This interface presents a logical list of key hardware modules and their operational states, displaying for each its status (e.g., ACTIVE, STANDBY), its supply voltage, and its real-time current draw. For example, the display could show distinct power metrics for the Computing Unit, an ADAS Module, a 5G Comms module, and the Tell-Tale Drivers. This feature provides diagnostic information for service technicians to identify faulty components and offers transparency to the end-user, particularly in an electric vehicle context where managing the power consumption of various subsystems is critical for maximizing range.
[00060]	The present invention solves the technical problem of high cost and inflexibility associated with traditional, instrument cluster designs. In a conventional approach, all electronic components are integrated onto a single, large printed circuit board (PCB). This creates a rigid architecture were offering different feature sets for various vehicle models—such as a base model versus a premium one—requires a completely separate and expensive redesign of the entire board. This lack of scalability makes it inefficient to produce customized variations or to upgrade to new technologies in the future without a complete and costly overhaul.
[00061]	To overcome these limitations, the present subject matter provides a segmented and modular configuration for the instrument cluster. The cluster's complex electronics are strategically separated into distinct functional blocks, which are typically housed on different, interconnected base boards. For example, a first base board may be dedicated to the core computing unit, while a second base board contains optional, feature-specific components like the communication module. A third base board can then consolidate standard systems like the tell-tale indicator drivers and the audio module. This architecture allows a vehicle manufacturer to easily scale the cluster's capabilities by simply including or omitting certain boards. A base model vehicle might ship with only the core and alert boards, while a premium model would include all three, providing advanced connectivity.
[00062]	This modular design introduces a cost-effective scalability, as manufacturers can serve a full range of vehicle models using a smaller inventory of common, reusable boards, thus reducing design costs and time-to-market. Critically, the computing unit is intelligent and adaptive; upon start-up, the main computing unit automatically detects which boards and components are physically present and configures the user interface on the display unit accordingly. If the communication board is absent, all related menus and icons are automatically hidden from the user, preventing confusion and ensuring a clean interface. This "plug-and-play" capability also enhances future-proofing and serviceability, as upgrading to new technology or repairing a faulty function only requires swapping a single, smaller module rather than the entire instrument cluster assembly.
[00063]	In light of the above-mentioned advantages and the technical advancements provided by the disclosed method and system, the claimed steps as discussed above are not routine, conventional, or well understood in the art, as the claimed steps enable the following solutions to the existing problems in conventional technologies. Further, the claimed steps clearly bring an improvement in the functioning of the configuration itself as the claimed steps provide a technical solution to a technical problem.

[00066]	While various aspects and embodiments have been disclosed herein, other aspects and embodiments will be apparent to those skilled in the art. The various aspects and embodiments disclosed herein are for purposes of illustration and are not intended to be limiting, with the true scope and spirit being indicated by the following claims.
[00067]	While the present disclosure has been described with reference to certain embodiments, it will be understood by those skilled in the art that various changes may be made, and equivalents may be substituted without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. title: A Federated Deep Learning Framework with Adaptive Global Threshold Optimization for Distributed Denial-Of-Service Detection in IoT Edge Networks
abstract: The present invention relates to a federated intrusion detection system for Internet of Things networks. The system comprises a plurality of edge devices, local preprocessing modules, local neural network training modules, a federated aggregation module, a threshold optimization module, and a detection module. Each edge device performs preprocessing of locally collected network traffic data, including normalization and class imbalance reduction, followed by local model training using a focal loss function. Model parameters are transmitted to a central server, where a global model is generated using federated averaging without transferring raw data. Validation predictions from the edge devices are utilized by the threshold optimization module to determine an optimized global decision threshold shared across participating devices. The optimized threshold improves detection consistency among heterogeneous devices, reduces false negatives, enhances resilience to class imbalance, and improves intrusion detection performance while preserving the privacy of locally collected network traffic data.
specification:
Field of the Invention
The present invention relates to a federated intrusion detection system for Internet of Things (IoT) networks that enhances intrusion detection performance of privacy-preserving intrusion detection for distributed IoT environments. 
Background
The present invention relates to the field of cybersecurity, particularly a system for detecting Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks in Internet of Things (IoT) edge networks using a Federated Deep Learning approach. IoT networks are vulnerable to DDoS attacks because of their large scale, diverse devices, and limited resources. Current centralized detection methods are unsuitable because they require the collection of raw and sensitive data at a main server, leading to privacy concerns and communication overhead. Traditional Federated Learning (FL)-based DDoS detectors resolve this issue; however, they have a drawback of using a constant decision threshold (0.5) among all clients, which lowers the performance when data distributions differ among devices. Prior approaches for this had several limitations that the present model overcomes:
(i)	Centralized Systems: Kolias et al. (2017) presented datasets (Bot-IoT and N-BaIoT) for anomaly detection but relied on centralized Machine Learning (ML) methods. These methods lack privacy protection and have a high computational load, which is unsuitable for modern IoT networks.
(ii)	Fixed Threshold FL: Nguyen et al. (2021) proposed Federated Learning model for intrusion detection. However, they did not use any optimization for the dynamic thresholds. This caused a mediocre performance among clients with uneven data distributions, resulting in either high False Positive Rates (FPR) or low Recall.
(iii)	Uniformity Assumptions: Aloqaily et al. (2022) researched FL for IoT security but made simple assumptions, such as a constant attack probability for every device, thus not considering the sensitivity and variability caused by the decision threshold parameter.
Further, it also discloses Federated Deep Learning model built for Detection of Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks in IoT networks, improved by an adaptive global optimization function for decision thresholds. Current federated learning frameworks usually use a fixed 0.5 probability threshold for categorization, whereas this patent presents an adaptive global threshold calculated at the central server using the combined validation outcomes from edge devices. The model improves the balance between precision and recall, decreases the number of false positives, and improves resilience in diverse IoT environments. The model was trained and tested on the N-BaIoT dataset, which showed an improvement in detection reliability and F1-score consistency without increasing the computational load on the edge devices. This model obtained the best global threshold on the benchmark parameters when compared to its current stste of art. 
Summary
The present invention provides a federated intrusion detection system for Internet of Things (IoT) networks that enhances intrusion detection performance while preserving data privacy. The system comprises a plurality of edge devices, a local preprocessing module, a local training module, a communication module, a federated aggregation module, a threshold optimization module, and a detection module. Each edge device collects network traffic data and performs local preprocessing including handling missing values, feature normalization, class imbalance reduction using Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), and partitioning of data into training and testing datasets. A local neural network model is trained at each edge device using a focal loss function to improve learning from imbalanced data. Model parameters and validation predictions are transmitted to a central server, while raw network traffic data remains at the respective edge devices. The central server aggregates the received model parameters using a Federated Averaging (FedAvg) process to generate a global intrusion detection model. The threshold optimization module determines an optimized global decision threshold based on validation predictions received from participating edge devices and distributes the optimized threshold across the network. The invention improves intrusion detection accuracy, enhances F1-score consistency among heterogeneous devices, reduces false negatives, increases resilience to skewed data distributions, and provides privacy-preserving intrusion detection for distributed IoT environments.

METHODOLOGY ADOPTED and RESULTS OBTAINED
The model works using a multistage pipeline built to improve intrusion detection under federated environment constraints.
1.	Data Collection and Preprocessing
Each IoT device collects raw network measurements (e.g., the N-BaIoT dataset). Local prepro-cessing includes:
•	Handling missing values.
•	Feature scaling using StandardScaler.
•	Class imbalance at the edge device is reduced using SMOTE. This preserves the feature space topology while improving the minority class density.
•	Splitting the data for local training and testing(80/20).
This ensures that each client provides a normalized and balanced dataset for federated learning, even in heterogeneous device environments.
2.	Local Model Training
Each edge device trains a lightweight neural model using Focal Loss, which handles class imbal-ance by reducing the weight of simpler samples.
3.	Federated Aggregation (FedAvg)
Edge devices only send model weights, not raw data. The central server performs traditional Federated Averaging. This creates a unified global model while ensuring data privacy.
4.	Global Threshold Optimization
After FedAvg, the proposed model introduces a centralized mechanism for tuning probabilistic decision thresholds. Each edge device sends validation predictions (instead of data) to the central server.
5.	Final Evaluation
The final global model was evaluated using the following:
•	Accuracy
•	Precision
•	Recall
•	F1-score
•	ROC curves
Results Obtained:
The model used the N-BaIoT dataset, which has nine heterogeneous IoT devices. The following results demonstrate the performance benefits of the proposed model.
1.	Best Global Threshold
τ∗ = 0.15
At this threshold, the global performance was as follows:
Metric	Value
•	Accuracy	0.9238
•	Precision	0.9265

•	F1-Score	0.9601
These values prove the effectiveness of global threshold tuning on an imbalanced IoT attack dataset.
2.	Improved F1-score Consistency Across Devices
The adaptive global threshold reduces inter-device variance by synchronizing all clients to a shared optimized decision boundary, improving the F1-score among clients compared with fixed-threshold FL models.
3.	False Positive Reduction
Lower thresholds (τ = 0.15) decreases false negatives without increasing false positives. This is important for real-time IoT security, as unnecessary alerts reduce system reliability.
4.	Reliance to Skewed Data
Devices with a high class imbalance (e.g., device 2 with a poor ROC) showed an improvement with the adaptive global threshold, proving the resilience of the system in heterogeneous systems.
5.	Performance Gain Over Classical FL
Compared with fixed-threshold FL systems, this model achieves the following:
3%–7% improvement in global F1-score
Higher recall without precision loss
More stable cross-client ROC/AUC patterns
