[0041] The Intelligent Recommendation Engine (109) receives the CA-OHS, RUL, 20 PCI, sensor confidence information, oil type, food category, frying temperature, frying duration, frying-cycle history, replenishment history, historical degradation behaviour, and user-defined safety preferences. Based on these parameters, the recommendation engine generates context-aware and personalized recommendations. Such recommendations may include continued use of the oil, use for selected food categories, reduction of frying 25 temperature, reduction of frying duration, replenishment with fresh oil, blending according to predefined criteria, replacement after a specified number of frying cycles, immediate replacement, sensor recalibration, preventive maintenance, or generation of health and safety alerts. The recommendations may be prioritized according to the PCI so that decisions generated under high-confidence conditions are distinguished from decisions 30 generated under lower-confidence conditions.
[0042] The User Interface Module (110) provides visualization of the monitoring and prediction results. The interface may comprise an LCD display, OLED display,
14
touchscreen, mobile application, web dashboard, desktop software, cloud monitoring portal, industrial Human Machine Interface, or smart kitchen display panel. The interface may display real-time sensor readings, current oil condition, CA-OHS, RUL, remaining frying cycles, remaining cooking hours, PCI, degradation trends, historical degradation graphs, sensor confidence levels, personalized recommendations, warning notifications, 5 and maintenance reminders. Audible alarms, visual indicators, push notifications, e-mail notifications, SMS alerts, or equivalent notification mechanisms may be provided when abnormal degradation or low prediction confidence is detected.
[0043] The Historical Database (111) stores operational and predictive information generated during system operation. The stored information may include raw and 10 normalized sensor measurements, sensor confidence values, adaptive weighting coefficients, CA-OHS history, RUL predictions, PCI history, degradation profiles, frying temperatures, frying duration, replenishment events, food categories, cooking frequency, recommendation history, alert history, and Artificial Intelligence prediction outputs. The database may be implemented using local flash memory, embedded memory, SD-card 15 storage, SQL or NoSQL databases, cloud storage, distributed storage, or equivalent storage technologies. The stored information enables long-term degradation analysis, adaptive model retraining, confidence-estimation improvement, report generation, predictive analytics, performance evaluation, maintenance scheduling, and system optimization.
[0044] The Adaptive Self-Learning Module (112) establishes a closed-loop 20 learning mechanism for continuously improving system performance. Newly acquired sensor measurements are compared with previously generated degradation predictions, and a prediction error is calculated. The prediction error is utilized to update sensor confidence scores and corresponding adaptive weighting coefficients. The updated information is supplied to the ACMSFE and the Artificial Intelligence prediction model, which may 25 subsequently be retrained using accumulated historical operational data. The updated model is validated and deployed for subsequent predictions. This process is repeated during later cooking operations so that the system continuously adapts to changing sensor behaviour, oil degradation characteristics, environmental conditions, and operational patterns without requiring continuous manual adjustment of sensor weights. 30
[0045] The communication module provides communication between the embedded system, external devices, cloud platforms, and centralized monitoring systems. Communication may be implemented through Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, ZigBee, Ethernet, LoRa,
15
cellular communication, or equivalent wired or wireless protocols. The communication module enables transmission of processed sensor information, CA-OHS, RUL, PCI, alerts, recommendations, historical information, and system-status information to a mobile application, cloud server, supervisory system, or centralized monitoring platform. In a multi-kitchen deployment, information from multiple cooking stations may therefore be 5 collected for centralized supervision, reporting, trend analysis, and predictive management.
[0046] The power supply unit supplies electrical power to the sensing elements, embedded controller, communication module, display, storage components, and associated electronic circuitry. The power source may comprise mains electricity, rechargeable batteries, external DC supplies, solar-assisted power, or equivalent power sources. The 10 electronic and sensing components may be housed within a protective enclosure formed from heat-resistant, oil-resistant, moisture-resistant, and food-safe material. The enclosure protects the system against oil splashes, dust, humidity, and elevated-temperature kitchen environments while maintaining suitable access for sensing and monitoring operations.
[0047] In operation, the system first initializes the embedded controller, sensing 15 elements, memory, communication interfaces, and user-defined cooking parameters. The selected cooking oil type, food category, frying conditions, and operational preferences are loaded into the system. The sensors then continuously acquire temperature, colour, viscosity, dielectric, and usage-related information. The embedded processing unit synchronizes and pre-processes the acquired measurements, after which the ACMSFE 20 evaluates the confidence of each measurement and dynamically assigns confidence-based weights. The weighted measurements are fused into a unified feature representation and supplied to the Artificial Intelligence Prediction Engine. The prediction engine determines the present degradation state and future degradation trend, while the CA-OHS module generates an overall oil-health score, the RUL engine determines remaining useful life, and 25 the PCI module determines prediction reliability. The recommendation engine subsequently generates an appropriate operational recommendation, which is displayed locally or remotely and stored in the historical database.
[0048] The adaptive learning process subsequently compares predicted degradation with actual subsequently acquired measurements. Prediction error information is used to 30 update the confidence associated with the individual sensors, recalculate adaptive weighting coefficients, and refine the Artificial Intelligence prediction model. The updated model and confidence parameters are then deployed for subsequent monitoring cycles.
16
[0049] Consequently, the system forms a continuous feedback loop in which sensing, confidence evaluation, fusion, prediction, decision-making, feedback, and learning are repeatedly performed during cooking-oil operation. The resulting architecture enables predictive and confidence-aware management of cooking oil rather than solely reactive replacement based on static thresholds. The integrated architecture therefore provides 5 continuous oil-quality assessment, adaptive sensor reliability management, degradation prediction, RUL estimation, prediction-confidence evaluation, personalized decision support, historical learning, and remote monitoring within a single intelligent system.

title: INTEGRATED PROCESSING-IN-MEMORY SYSTEM FOR GRAPH EXECUTION AND VECTOR SIMILARITY SEARCH
abstract: The present invention discloses an integrated processing-in-memory (PIM) system for unified graph execution and high-dimensional vector similarity search. The system comprises a non-volatile resistive random-access memory (ReRAM) crossbar array configured to store graph and vector data and perform mixed-signal vector-matrix multiplication within the memory array. A hardware controller comprises a dynamic graph execution unit and a high-dimensional vector search engine for performing graph traversal and vector similarity computations. An on-chip spiking neural network (SNN) accelerator having spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) circuitry monitors memory access characteristics and controls dynamic data remapping within the ReRAM array. A database software interface compiles graph and vector queries into hardware instructions for direct execution by the PIM architecture, thereby reducing off-chip data movement and enabling coordinated graph and vector processing.
specification:
The present invention relates to an integrated hardware-software Processing-in-Memory (PIM) system for unified execution of graph traversal and high-dimensional vector similarity search. The system integrates a non-volatile resistive random-access memory (ReRAM) crossbar array with mixed-signal computation circuitry, a dynamic graph execution unit, a high-dimensional vector search engine, an on-chip Spiking Neural Network (SNN) accelerator having Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) circuitry, and a hardware-software co-designed database interface. The integrated architecture performs graph and vector computations substantially within the memory subsystem, thereby reducing movement of graph and vector data between an external processor and memory. 
In an embodiment, the system comprises a host interface, a database query compilation engine, an on-chip hardware controller, a plurality of ReRAM compute tiles, a dynamic graph execution unit, a vector similarity search engine, an SNN-based runtime reconfiguration engine, peripheral sensing and conversion circuitry, and an on-chip interconnect. The hardware controller coordinates execution of graph operations, vector computations, memory access operations and runtime reconfiguration operations.
The plurality of ReRAM compute tiles comprises non-volatile ReRAM cells arranged in crossbar structures having wordlines and bitlines. The ReRAM array stores data associated with graph structures and high-dimensional vector embeddings. In an embodiment, adjacency information and edge weights are represented as binary or quantized matrices within respective ReRAM tiles, while node attributes and dense vector embeddings are stored in associated memory regions. 
The physical conductance states of the ReRAM cells represent computational values used during in-memory processing. Accordingly, graph information and vector information remain mapped within the memory array while corresponding computational operations are performed by circuitry coupled to the array.
In an embodiment, each ReRAM memory cell comprises a one-transistor-one-resistor (1T1R) structure comprising an access transistor and a resistive switching element. The resistive switching element is configured to retain a conductance state representing stored information after removal of operating power. The ReRAM cells are arranged along intersecting wordlines and bitlines to form a crossbar array. 
For analog computation, an input vector is supplied to selected wordlines in the form of voltage signals. Each ReRAM cell produces a current corresponding to the applied voltage and its programmed conductance. The currents generated by multiple cells are accumulated along respective bitlines. The accumulation therefore represents a vector-matrix multiplication operation performed directly within the memory array according to the electrical characteristics of the crossbar. 
In an embodiment, differential memory-cell pairs are used to represent positive and negative components of a computational weight. A first conductance represents a positive component and a second conductance represents a negative component, with the difference between the conductances representing the corresponding signed computational value. 
The crossbar is coupled to peripheral circuitry configured to sense and compensate for electrical variations occurring during analog computation. The peripheral circuitry comprises array-edge voltage sensing and closed-loop transconductance calibration circuitry. The hardware controller determines spatial voltage variations associated with wordline and bitline resistance and adjusts the corresponding wordline driving signals to compensate for the detected voltage variation. 
The accumulated bitline current is supplied to a signal conversion path comprising a transimpedance amplifier and an analog-to-digital converter. In an embodiment, a time-interleaved Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC digitizes the converted signal. The conversion path provides different precision modes for approximate graph-vector filtering and higher-precision vector similarity computation. 
The system comprises a dynamic graph execution unit configured to execute graph traversal operations using graph information stored in the ReRAM array. The graph execution unit operates on adjacency information, edge weights and node information mapped to the ReRAM tiles. 
In an embodiment, the dynamic graph execution unit comprises a hardware hash engine configured to translate a graph node identifier into a corresponding physical memory address. The physical memory address identifies a location within the ReRAM architecture for accessing graph information associated with the node. The address mapping enables the hardware controller to directly access the corresponding graph information without requiring the complete graph structure to be transferred to an external processor. 
The dynamic graph execution unit further comprises frontier vector registers configured to maintain active node sets during graph traversal. The frontier information is supplied to wordline drivers of the ReRAM array so that adjacency information corresponding to multiple active nodes is processed in parallel. The architecture thereby supports hardware execution of graph operations including Breadth-First Search (BFS) and PageRank. 
A vector bit-wise intersection engine is further provided for performing logical operations on graph-related bit vectors. In an embodiment, the engine performs AND, OR and XOR operations on bitline outputs for determining relationships between graph node sets, including common neighboring nodes. 
The system further comprises a high-dimensional vector search engine configured to compare a query vector with vector embeddings stored in the ReRAM array. The vector search engine is coupled to the mixed-signal computation circuitry and performs vector similarity calculations directly using the conductance states representing the stored vector embeddings. The disclosed vector search engine supports inner-product, Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity operations. 
For inner-product computation, elements of a query vector are converted into corresponding electrical input signals and applied to the crossbar wordlines. The resulting bitline current represents an accumulated product between the query-vector values and the stored vector values. Multiple stored vectors can thereby be evaluated in parallel across respective portions of the crossbar. 
For Euclidean-distance computation, the vector search engine uses the relationship between the squared magnitudes of the query vector and a stored vector and the inner product between the vectors. The query-vector magnitude is determined by an input controller, while corresponding stored-vector magnitudes are maintained in the memory array. The crossbar performs the inner-product operation and an analog computation circuit combines the resulting value with the stored magnitude values to generate an analog representation of the Euclidean distance before digitization. 
For cosine-similarity computation, the crossbar generates an inner-product value between the query vector and each stored vector. The resulting value is supplied to an analog normalization circuit together with a stored vector magnitude to generate a normalized similarity value. The resulting similarity values are supplied to a hardware ranking circuit for identification of vectors having corresponding similarity values. 
The graph execution unit and the vector search engine are configured to operate on graph and vector information mapped within the same ReRAM-based memory architecture. In an embodiment, graph information is represented using a Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format, while dense vector embeddings are maintained in associated memory regions. 
The architecture further supports graph-vector index structures including Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) structures. Upper graph layers are processed by the dynamic graph execution unit, while vector evaluations at a lower search layer are performed by the mixed-signal vector search engine. The graph traversal and vector similarity operations are consequently executed using coordinated processing paths within the memory-centric architecture. 
The system comprises an on-chip SNN accelerator configured to monitor operating conditions of the ReRAM crossbar and control runtime memory reconfiguration. The SNN accelerator is integrated within the hardware controller and operates as a closed-loop control subsystem associated with the physical memory array. 
In an embodiment, the SNN accelerator comprises Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons and STDP learning circuitry. The input neurons receive signals corresponding to physical operating conditions of the ReRAM array. Such conditions include local temperature, memory access frequency, read latency and error occurrence. The monitored parameters are converted into input signals that influence the membrane potentials of the LIF neurons. 
When the membrane potential of an LIF neuron reaches a threshold, the neuron generates a spike. The temporal relationship between pre-synaptic and post-synaptic spikes is processed by the STDP circuitry to update corresponding synaptic weights. The updated SNN state represents a runtime condition of one or more ReRAM regions. 
The output of the SNN is supplied to the hardware controller. When the SNN identifies an operating condition corresponding to a reconfiguration requirement, the controller initiates a background data migration operation. Data associated with a selected ReRAM tile is transferred to another memory tile through an on-chip interconnect. A pointer redirection table is updated to associate the logical data location with the new physical location. The original tile is subsequently subjected to recalibration and reprogramming operations. 
The SNN-based reconfiguration therefore establishes a closed-loop relationship between physical operating conditions of the ReRAM array and logical data mapping. The physical memory state is monitored during execution, and the resulting SNN decision is used to dynamically modify the physical placement of data without requiring the host processor to perform the corresponding memory-management operation. 
The system further comprises a database software interface configured to translate high-level graph and vector queries into hardware-executable instructions. The database interface receives a declarative query and generates a corresponding sequence of micro-instructions according to the PIM-ISA. The micro-instructions are transmitted to an on-chip hardware instruction scheduler and executed by the respective processing units. 
In an embodiment, the PIM-ISA comprises instructions for loading a query vector, initiating inner-product computation, initiating Euclidean-distance computation, executing a graph traversal step and obtaining the state of the SNN-based reconfiguration engine. The instructions are decoded by the on-chip controller and routed to the corresponding hardware units. 
The software layer further manages physical organization of graph and vector information according to a ReRAM-compatible storage format. Graph information is mapped into CSR-based structures and vector embeddings are mapped into corresponding dense-vector regions. Dynamic indexing is maintained by the software and hardware components in accordance with changes in physical memory mapping generated by the runtime reconfiguration engine. 
During operation, a graph-vector query is received by the database interface. The query compiler analyzes the graph traversal requirement and vector similarity requirement and generates a corresponding PIM-ISA instruction sequence. The instruction sequence is provided to the on-chip hardware controller for execution. 
The hardware controller decodes the instruction sequence and determines the physical ReRAM locations corresponding to graph nodes, adjacency information and vector embeddings. The hardware hash engine performs graph-node address mapping and the graph execution unit establishes the active traversal frontier. 
For vector evaluation, the query vector is supplied to the wordline drivers as electrical input signals. The ReRAM crossbar performs parallel VMM operations through cell-level conductance modulation and bitline current accumulation. The resulting analog signals are converted into digital values by the ADC circuitry for subsequent ranking, filtering or query-result generation. 
During execution, the SNN accelerator continuously monitors selected physical operating parameters of the ReRAM array. The SNN processes the monitored parameters through its LIF and STDP circuitry and generates control outputs corresponding to detected memory conditions. Where reconfiguration is triggered, the hardware controller dynamically remaps the affected data between physical ReRAM locations and updates the corresponding address mapping while maintaining the logical data association. 
Thus, the system provides a closed-loop hardware-software architecture in which data storage, analog computation, graph traversal, vector similarity evaluation and physical memory management are coordinated within a common ReRAM-based processing environment. The combination of the mixed-signal ReRAM compute array, unified graph-vector execution engine, SNN-based runtime reconfiguration and PIM-ISA query interface enables graph-vector queries to be processed with reduced dependence on off-chip data movement. 
In an embodiment, the ReRAM array is implemented using a plurality of crossbar tiles interconnected through an on-chip network. Different tiles store different portions of graph adjacency information, node attributes and vector embeddings.
In an embodiment, the vector search engine operates using selectable inner-product, Euclidean-distance or cosine-similarity computation according to the query instruction received through the PIM-ISA.
In an embodiment, the graph execution unit performs BFS, PageRank or set-intersection operations using frontier registers, address-mapping circuitry and bit-vector processing.
In an embodiment, the SNN accelerator uses physical monitoring signals associated with temperature, access activity, read latency and error occurrence to generate runtime reconfiguration decisions.
In an embodiment, the database interface generates hardware instruction sequences corresponding to hybrid graph-vector queries and directly communicates the instruction sequences to the on-chip execution scheduler. ,

title: METHOD FOR DETECTING AN OCCUPANCY STATE WITH A VIRTUAL ANTENNA
abstract:
The invention relates to a method for detecting an occupancy state (B) of seat (201, 202) in a vehicle (200), a computer program, a computer-readable data carrier, a control unit (ECU), and a vehicle (200).
Fig. 1
specification:
Description

The invention relates to a method for detecting an occupancy state of at least one seat in a vehicle, a computer program product, a computer-readable data carrier, a control unit, and a vehicle.

Vehicles are known to have sensors, for example, UWB devices, LIDAR, cameras, and/or ultrasonic sensors, in order to detect static objects (and/or moving objects). It may be provided that a UWB device (e.g., a UWB anchor) is set up for detecting and/or authenticating a vehicle access and/or a driving license, for example, by detecting and/or recognizing and/or localizing a person in the vicinity of the vehicle (and/or an ID transmitter). In this context, a UWB device can receive and/or provide a plurality of channel impulse responses. Depending on this, the distance to objects (such as an ID transmitter for the vehicle) can be determined, for example. It is also known to provide seat occupancy detection (SOD) for at least one seat in the interior of the vehicle, for example, for the driver's seat. In known solutions, capacitive or pressure-sensitive seat mats can be integrated in one/each seat. These sense deformation, and a weight and, if applicable, also a profile of the weight distribution on the seat can be determined therefrom.

The prior art has disadvantages in this regard. For example, capacitive or pressure-sensitive seat mats can be cost-intensive, since in addition to the seat mat, they also need to be integrated into the seat and the associated wiring in/on the seat and in the vehicle. In addition, evaluation electronics are required. This can lead to costs, increased complexity, increased assembly effort, reduced robustness, increased maintenance effort, and/or additional weight. Another disadvantage is that the existing technology cannot distinguish between objects and living persons/humans. Finally, it is not possible to make a robust distinction between adults and children, who are located on the seat.

It is therefore an object of the present invention to at least partially overcome at least one of the disadvantages described above. In particular, it is an object of the invention to enable detection of an occupancy state that optimizes costs, weight, assembly, complexity, accuracy, robustness (of the detection), speed, and/or maintenance effort.

The above object is achieved by a method having the features of the independent method claim, a computer program product having the features of the independent patent claim relating to a computer program product, a computer-readable data carrier having the features of the independent patent claim relating to a computer-readable data carrier, a control unit having the features of the independent patent claim relating to a control unit, and a vehicle having the features of the independent vehicle claim.

Further features and details of the invention are apparent from the respective dependent claims, the description, and the drawings. In this context, features and details described in connection with the method according to the invention naturally also apply in connection with the computer program product according to the invention and/or in connection with the computer-readable data carrier according to the invention and/or in connection with the control unit according to the invention and/or in connection with the vehicle according to the invention and vice versa, such that with respect to the disclosure of the individual aspects of the invention, mutual reference is always made or can be made. In particular, advantages described in the context of the first, second, third, fourth, and/or fifth aspect also apply to the first, second, third, fourth, and/or fifth aspect, respectively.

According to a first aspect, the present invention relates to a method for detecting an occupancy state of at least one seat, in particular a first seat and/or a second seat in a vehicle, the vehicle having:
-	a first antenna, which is set up for transmitting and receiving UWB waves and is arranged in the interior of the vehicle, wherein in particular the first antenna is arranged above the first seat, the second seat, and/or the at least one seat, for example, in a headliner of the vehicle, and
-	a second antenna, which is set up to transmit and receive UWB waves and is arranged in the interior of the vehicle, wherein the first antenna is spaced apart from the second antenna, in particular along a transverse direction, wherein in particular the second antenna is arranged above the first seat, the second seat, and/or the at least one seat, for example, in the headliner of the vehicle,
the method comprising:
-	transmitting by the first antenna the first UWB waves, the reflections of which are received by the first antenna in order to provide a first plurality of channel impulse responses,
-	transmitting by the second antenna the second UWB waves, the reflections of which are received by the second antenna in order to provide a fourth plurality of channel impulse responses,
-	providing
•	a second plurality of channel impulse responses as a function of reflections of the first UWB waves received by the second antenna, and/or
•	a third plurality of channel impulse responses as a function of reflections of the second UWB waves received by the first antenna,
-	calculating by the control unit an occupancy state, which is specific to the at least one seat, as a function of the first plurality of channel impulse responses, the fourth plurality of channel impulse responses, and
•	the third plurality of channel impulse responses, and/or
•	the second plurality of channel impulse responses, and
-	operating the vehicle by the control unit as a function of the occupancy state.

The method according to the first aspect may be computer-implemented and/or performed repeatedly and/or continuously. Preferably, the method can be carried out during, before, and/or (preferably) while operating or using a vehicle and/or a control unit. Operating may in this case be (manual) driving, autonomous driving, and/or (at least partially) automated driving. Alternatively or additionally, the method may be carried out at (regular) intervals (e.g., as a function of speed and/or as a function of a time of use, for example, within a time interval after unlocking the doors of the vehicle). In this context, the control unit can (at least partially) implement the method, for example, by performing the (above-mentioned) steps (in combination) and/or by activating corresponding components (e.g., a UWB device). The method can be used to detect the occupancy state of at least one seat.

Within the scope of the invention, a vehicle may comprise a motor vehicle and/or a commercial truck. A vehicle may be set up for operating, in particular for autonomous and/or (at least partially) automated driving.

The vehicle may, in this case, have a first antenna and a second antenna. The first and/or second antenna can be set up to transmit and/or receive UWB waves. The first and/or second antenna can be combined and/or arranged in a (common) UWB device (UWB, Ultra-Wide-Band), in particular a UWB anchor. The first and/or second antenna can be connected to each other, for example, via a transmit/receive switch (of the UWB device). For example, the first antenna, the second antenna, and/or the UWB device may perform transmitting of first and/or second UWB waves into the vehicle interior of the vehicle, for example, by being arranged (pointing downward) in the roof and/or headliner of the vehicle, preferably above a first and/or second seat or a bench seat (with at least two seats). For example, a vehicle may have at least one UWB device for the front, rear, and/or each row of seats. The first antenna, second antenna, and/or UWB device can (additionally) be set up for another function, for example, a keyless entry system or the like. For example, the UWB device or the first and/or second antenna can be set up for detecting and/or authenticating a vehicle access and/or a driving license, for example, by detecting and/or recognizing and/or localizing a person (and/or an ID transmitter) in front of the UWB device. This means that existing UWB devices or an existing (already installed) first and/or second antenna may also be used. Accordingly, the function or the method may also be retrofitted.

The control unit may be integrated into the UWB device. Alternatively or additionally, a (central and/or separate) control unit may be comprised by the vehicle. The control unit may be connected to the first antenna, the second antenna, a transmit/receive switch, and/or the UWB device for data communication, for example, via a respective data connection.

Detecting an occupancy state of at least one seat, in particular a first seat and/or a second seat, may in this case in particular comprise detecting a first target, in particular on a first seat (e.g., a seat on the right relative to the direction of travel or along the transverse direction), and/or detecting a second target, in particular on a second seat (e.g., a seat on the left relative to the direction of travel or along the transverse direction). The first target may in this case comprise a first object, in particular an (immovable) first object or a first person (in particular an adult or a child). Detection of a (first) animal would also be conceivable. The second target may in this case comprise a second object, in particular an (immovable) second object or a second person (in particular an adult or a child). Detection of a (second) animal would also be conceivable. The occupancy state may in this case have a data structure that is in particular specific to the occupancy and/or type of occupancy of the at least one seat, the first seat (by a first target) and/or the second seat (by a second target), in particular, for example, via a respective occupancy value (0 or 1) or in each case "occupied yes" or "occupied no". Additionally or alternatively, the occupancy state may be specific to a type of the object, in particular whether the first and/or second target is (likely to be) a (first and/or second) object or a (first and/or second) person, and in particular whether it is (likely to be) an adult or a child (or possibly an animal).

Within the scope of the invention, a right-handed coordinate system may be provided (in particular for illustration). In this context, a direction of travel (of the vehicle) may be configured, for example, as a direction of movement and/or an x-direction and/or pointing forward. In this context, a transverse direction and/or y-direction may be configured perpendicular to the direction of travel and/or (in the direction of travel) from right to left (or vice versa). In this context, a vertical direction and/or z-direction may be configured from bottom to top (or vice versa) and/or perpendicular to the direction of travel and/or perpendicular to the transverse direction.

Here, the first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses may be (directly) calculated and/or provided by a/the UWB device, and subsequently transmitted to the control unit. Alternatively or additionally, the control unit may calculate these, e.g., based on the raw data (transmitted and/or received).

The first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses may in this case be provided by the first and/or second antenna. Alternatively or additionally, other antennas may also be used. It is therefore conceivable that a third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and/or eighth antenna (et cetera) may also be used in an antenna array. Accordingly, the first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses may be provided by transmitting with one of the antennas and receiving with the same antenna and/or at least one other antenna (and subsequent further processing, see above). In this context, virtual (receiving) antennas may also be provided in each case. The angular separation capability may be further improved by using multiple (virtual and/or physical) antennas. The principle may (already) be illustrated using a first and a second antenna, which is why the method with a first and second antenna is described here in particular. Nevertheless, it is conceivable to apply the method to further antennas and/or an arbitrary number of antennas (in an antenna array).

In particular, it may be provided that the (different) channel impulse responses (e.g., in the form of a 1D vector with amplitudes) are received for the (first, second, third, and/or fourth) plurality of channel impulse responses at different (successive) points in time and/or each have different amplitude values, which are in particular specific to successive distance values (e.g., specific to certain distances in front of/below the first and/or second antenna or UWB device). Accordingly, the first and/or second UWB waves may be at least partially reflected by an object or a first and/or second target and subsequently received (by the first and/or second antenna). By means of an (auto) correlation between the transmitted (first and/or second UWB waves) and (first reflected and then) received (first and/or second) UWB waves (received signal), a (respective) channel impulse response (e.g., in the form of a 1D vector with amplitudes) may be provided, in particular by the UWB device. The channel impulse response(s) may be transmitted to the control unit, for example, via a (wired or wireless) data connection. Accordingly, the control unit may receive the channel impulse responses and/or a plurality of channel impulse responses (for example, by lining up the channel impulse responses into a 2D matrix, which in particular sorts the channel impulse responses in time). Alternatively or additionally, the UWB device may also provide (and subsequently transmit to the control unit) the (first, second, third, and/or fourth) plurality of channel impulse responses. In this context, a (first, second, third, and/or fourth) plurality of channel impulse responses may (in each case) have at least 10, at least 50, at least 100, at least 500, or at least 1000, for example 10000 channel impulse responses, which are preferably (all) determined one after the other in time, in particular at different successive points in time. In this context, one (each) channel impulse response may have successive distance values or CIR taps (e.g., 300), each of which comprises a (corresponding) amplitude. In this context, the amplitude may be specific to (all) signals (e.g., of different objects, such as the first and/or second target), which are detected or were detected for a particular distance value (in particular at a certain distance, preferably [or more precisely] in a certain distance range, e.g. [a bin] of 30 cm). Simplified accordingly, a first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses may be understood as a 2D matrix, wherein the channel impulse responses are arranged in the rows and/or along the x-coordinates, and wherein successive measurement time points are arranged along the columns and/or along the y-coordinates.

The (first) transmitting by the first antenna of the first UWB waves, reflections of which are received by the first antenna (to obtain a first received signal) to provide a first plurality of channel impulse responses, may be performed in a (so-called) radar mode, in particular not in sensing mode and/or for time-of-flight (ToF) measurement, in particular because (unlike, e.g., ID transmitters) the objects or a first and/or second target do not "send back" but merely reflect the UWB waves. The radar mode in a UWB device may be characterized by the capability to capture precise and detailed information about the vehicle interior, in particular by emitting UWB signals and analyzing the reflected signals. This enables the precise determination of distances, movements, and positions of objects. The radar mode may offer the advantage of high precision in detecting and localizing, even in complex environments or with moving objects. In addition, the radar mode may be considered robust against environmental influences, such as light conditions and/or acoustic disturbances. For example (with reference to the above), a first plurality of channel impulse responses (or the corresponding individual channel impulse responses) may be provided by (auto)correlating between the first UWB waves and their reflections (such as at the first and/or second target). For example, the received signal received by the first antenna or the channel impulse response (when reflected at a first target) may have a (relative) phase of 〖2Φ〗_d (see explanations below), wherein in particular d may represent the distance between the first antenna and the (first) target and Φ_d the corresponding phase (when transmitting and receiving). Accordingly, the first antenna may (thereby) be operated in a transmit/receive mode (both transmitting and [subsequently or in parallel] receiving). Accordingly, it may be provided that the first plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses) have a phase of 〖2Φ〗_d.

The (second) transmitting by the second antenna of second UWB waves, reflections of which are received by the second antenna (to obtain a fourth received signal) in order to provide a fourth plurality of channel impulse responses, may be performed in a (so-called) radar mode. For example (with reference to the above), a fourth plurality of channel impulse responses (or the corresponding individual channel impulse responses) may be provided by (auto)correlation between the second transmitted) UWB waves and their reflection (such as at the first and/or second target). For example, the received signal received by the second antenna or the channel impulse response (when reflected at a first target) may have a (relative) phase of 〖2Φ〗_d+ 〖2Φ〗_x, wherein d may represent the distance between the first antenna and the (first) target and Φ_d may represent the phase difference present twice (due to transmitting and receiving), caused by the additional distance x (covered by the UWB waves) between the second antenna and the first target (relative or compared to the distance between the first antenna and the first target in this example). This means that the second antenna may be operated in a transmit/receive mode (both transmitting and receiving [subsequently or in parallel]). Accordingly, it may be provided that the fourth plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses) have a phase of 〖2Φ〗_d+ 〖2Φ〗_x.

Providing a second plurality of channel impulse responses as a function of reflections of the first UWB waves that are received by the second antenna may accordingly be specific to the first UWB waves reflected at the first (and/or second) target. To return to the above example, the second plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses) may therefore (due to reception by the second antenna while transmitting with the first antenna) have a phase of 〖2Φ〗_d+ Φ_x, in particular since the (first) UWB waves have to cover the additional distance x, which results in particular from the distance (e.g., a=λ/2) between the first and second antennas.

Providing a third plurality of channel impulse responses as a function of reflections of the second UWB waves received by the first antenna, may accordingly be specific to second UWB waves reflected at the first (and/or second) target. To return to the above example, the third plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses) may therefore (due to reception by the first antenna while transmitting with the second antenna) have a phase of (also) 〖2Φ〗_d+ Φ_x, in particular since the (second) UWB waves have to cover the additional distance x, which results in particular from the distance (e.g., a=λ/2) between the first and second antennas. Accordingly, the second and third plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses and/or phases) may each be configured to be reciprocal and/or interchangeable. This may advantageously be used to use only the second or third plurality of channel impulse responses (within the scope of the method). In particular, this can reduce the total time required for transmitting and receiving. As a result, accuracy can be increased.

By using the first and fourth plurality of channel impulse responses in conjunction with the second or third plurality of channel impulse responses, a (third) virtual (receiving) antenna may therefore be provided, which in particular (virtually) extends the antenna array formed by the first and second antennas by a further third antenna (at a distance a). Furthermore, it may be provided that the UWB device has additional (real and/or physical) antennas. Thus, the UWB device may have a first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and/or eighth antenna (et cetera), which in particular together form an antenna array. Preferably, the antennas may be spaced apart from each other (at a distance of half a wavelength, see below), in particular along the transverse direction. In this respect, the embodiments of the first and/or second antenna may apply analogously to other antennas. In other words, a larger aperture may thereby be provided. Advantageously, this may enable improved separation between objects, in particular between a first target (such as on the first seat) and a second target (on the second seat). This means that with two (real or physical) antennas (namely, the first and second antennas), it is still possible to resolve two objects (the first and second target). In particular, this may apply approximately, especially if the distance to the objects d is (significantly) greater than the distance a between the first and second antenna, e.g., the following applies:
d≫a
The principle described above can also be extended to other antennas, such as a third, fourth, and/or fifth (and so on) antenna. Accordingly, a first, second, and third antenna may also be used, for example, to improve the separation of three targets (e.g. neighboring targets in a row of seats).

The first and second UWB waves may have the same wavelength. It may also be provided that these differ.

Preferably, at least the first and the second plurality of channel impulse responses are different. Particularly preferably, the first, second, and third (or fourth) plurality of channel impulse responses are different.

Calculating an occupancy state may comprise detecting by the first detection algorithm, detecting by the second detection algorithm, and/or determining an occupancy state (quasi-merging the detection results).

The calculating, in particular a detecting (by the first and/or second detection algorithm), may detect a first and/or second target, preferably on the at least one seat, the first seat and/or second seat. In this context, preferably a first target (or lack thereof) may be determined on a first seat and/or a second target (or lack thereof) on a second seat. In the simplest case, this may be done by comparing with reference data and/or replacement data, which are specific to an unoccupied first and/or second seat. In other words, an occupancy state may have a negative first and/or second target value and/or occupancy may be excluded if the first, second, third and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses are not different from a corresponding plurality of channel impulse responses measured while the first and/or second seat was unoccupied. This makes it easy to determine whether (at all) a first and/or second target is located on the first and/or second seat.

The operating may be specific and/or used for a plurality of different vehicle functions (see also below).

Within the scope of the invention, it may be advantageous that transmitting with the first antenna and transmitting with the second antenna are carried out alternately, in particular at (directly) successive time intervals.

In other words, the first and the second antenna may transmit alternately. It may be provided that the first and/or second antenna performs receiving in parallel with transmitting (by the first and/or second antenna) (or that receiving is performed with this antenna).

The determining by the control unit of an occupancy state of at least one seat of the vehicle, a first seat and/or a second seat, wherein the occupancy state is specific to the first target and preferably to the second target, wherein the determining of the occupancy state is performed as a function of the first target detection and the second target detection, may thus have a merging and/or combining the first target detection and the second target detection. In this context, the results may be validated by comparison and/or plausibility checking and/or may be made more robust. This may be particularly advantageous when the first and the second detection algorithms are configured to be at least partially complementary and/or have different strengths (e.g., good detection of movement vs. high robustness even in the absence of movement).

Within the scope of the invention, it can be advantageous that the first detection algorithm and the second detection algorithm differ, wherein in particular
-	the first detection algorithm is optimized for detecting moving targets, and/or
-	the second detection algorithm is optimized for detecting static targets.

The robustness and/or accuracy can thus be increased by using the first and the second detection algorithms. If, for example, only the first detection algorithm were used, a first and/or second target could (potentially) generate no amplitude maximum in some or all of the first amplitude-angle profiles, for example, due to a lack of movement. Accordingly, it would (incorrectly) be assumed that there is either no first and/or no second target, or at least no person or animal is positioned on the first or second seat (but rather an object). In other words, false detections could occur (e.g., false negatives). By optimizing the second detection algorithm for detecting static targets, the robustness of detecting (at least temporarily) static first and/or second targets may advantageously be optimized. This can increase the overall robustness.

The adaptive beamforming algorithm, in particular the Minimum-Variance Distortionless Response Algorithm (MVDR), may in this case be optimized for movement and/or moving first and/or second targets. This algorithm (see above) may be less optimal for static targets. However, this may be compensated for by using a second detection algorithm. The adaptive beamforming algorithm, in particular the minimum-variance distortionless response algorithm (MVDR), may be provided with the first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses as input and/or can be implemented in the control unit. The adaptive beamforming algorithm, in particular Minimum-Variance Distortionless Response Algorithm (MVDR), may provide the first plurality of amplitude-angle profiles as output. The Minimum-Variance Distortionless Response algorithm may advantageously maintain the gain in the direction of arrival of a desired signal and attenuate interference from other directions. This may provide particularly precise detection, especially angular resolution, for the first and/or second target. This may be particularly advantageous when detecting living beings (people and/or animals) (due to their movement).

It may be provided within the scope of the invention that the first detection algorithm is set up to provide a first plurality of (1D) amplitude-angle profiles and/or that the second detection algorithm is set up to provide a second plurality of (1D) amplitude-angle profiles.

The first plurality of amplitude-angle profiles may result (as output) from the first detection algorithm. The second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles may result (as output) from the second detection algorithm. In this context, the first and/or second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles may each have 1D vectors. In this context, the first and/or second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles may each have a number of amplitude-angle profiles that are in particular (successively) specific to different (concrete) distance values or distance ranges. For example, it may be provided that the first and/or second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles each has 10 (different) amplitude-angle profiles, wherein these are specific to (successive and/or discrete) distance values or distance ranges, e.g.:
-	a first distance value of 10 cm or a distance range from 0 to 10 cm,
-	a first distance value of 20 cm or a distance range from 10 to 20 cm,
-	a first distance value of 30 cm or a distance range from 20 to 30 cm,
-	a first distance value of 40 cm or a distance range from 30 to 40 cm,
-	a first distance value of 50 cm or a distance range from 40 to 50 cm,
-	a first distance value of 60 cm or a distance range from 50 to 60 cm,
-	a first distance value of 70 cm or a distance range from 60 to 70 cm,
-	a first distance value of 80 cm or a distance range from 70 to 80 cm,
-	a first distance value of 90 cm or a distance range from 80 to 90 cm, and/or
-	a first distance value of 100 cm or a distance range from 90 to 100 cm,
wherein in particular the (radial) distance or a distance range starting from the first and/or second antenna and/or the UWB device may be assumed. For example, the first and/or second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles and/or each first and/or second amplitude-angle profile may represent and/or have an angle range, e.g., from between -90° and -90°. In this context, a separation may be provided in the middle of the range. In other words, it may be provided that a first target angle range, e.g., between 90° and 0°, is provided, which is in particular specific to the first seat and/or an (expected) first target. For example, 0° may represent the center of the seat bench and/or a position between the first and second seat (e.g., when the first and/or second antenna is positioned in the center and/or in the headliner of the vehicle). Similarly, a second target angle range, e.g., between 0° and +90°, is provided, which is in particular specific to the second seat and/or an (expected) second target. It may be provided that positive angles correspond to the first and/or right seat. It may be provided that negative angles correspond to the second and/or left seat. Naturally, this may also be defined the other way round. A separation range between the sides may also be provided, such that, for example, a first target angle range of between -80° and -20° and a second target angle range of between +20° and -80° are provided. It may also be provided that the angular ranges of the first and second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles overlap only partially and/or are (partially) different. It may be provided that (additional) normalization (e.g., of the amplitudes) and/or interpolation (e.g., between adjacent angular values) is carried out to achieve comparability.

It is furthermore conceivable that the second detection algorithm, in particular during calculating and/or detecting by the second detection algorithm, has an angular Fourier transformation, in particular an angle FFT, from which in particular the second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles results (as output), wherein in particular calculating a first Fourier transformation is performed, preferably with respect to a time axis, along which successive channel impulse responses are arranged one after the other (wherein the result can correspond to a "range-velocity" representation), followed by a second Fourier transformation, preferably with respect to a direction corresponding to a juxtaposition of the different antennas and/or a plurality of channel impulse responses, in order to obtain the plurality of amplitude-angle profiles (in particular a corresponding plurality of amplitude-angle profiles for each [real and physical] antenna).

The angular Fourier transformation, in particular angle FFT, may be calculated as a function of the first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses, in particular the respective channel impulse responses and/or the respective phases. These can be used as input. This may advantageously provide high efficiency (computationally efficient, which enables real-time application), and/or improved or additional angular information or angular resolution (with a sufficient number of antennas, even with two real antennas and one virtual antenna, a fine and/or additional angular resolution may be achieved). The number of amplitude values for each amplitude-angle profile of the second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles may, in this case, correspond to the number of (real and/or virtual) antennas. Accordingly, the (angular) resolution and/or angular separation capability may be improved with an increasing number of antennas. However, two real and/or one virtual antenna may already be sufficient to provide the second plurality of amplitude-angle profiles.

It is also conceivable, in particular as an alternative to the angle FFT, that the second detection algorithm (essentially as a conventional beamformer) is designed such that antenna weights (weights w) are determined by it. In this context, the antenna weights may be selected such that the resulting strongest beam of the beam pattern points into a predefined angle zone (e.g., left (driver side) (-60..-30°) or right (30..60°) (passenger side)) and it is thus checked for the respective angle zone as to whether sufficiently strong reflections are coming from this respective direction. In other words, the antenna weights may be selected in order to obtain a comparatively high (reflection) intensity from the direction of the first and/or second seat when these are occupied. For this purpose, at each measurement time t, the complex signal presents at antennas 1..n (in-phase component I and quadrature-phase component Q) a_i (i=1..n_ant) may be multiplied by the associated complex (the magnitude manipulates the signal amplitude and the angle the phase position) antenna weight w_i (i=1..n_ant) and summed over the number of antennas. This result sum may substantially have the effect of the incoming reflections from this angular zone.

Additional information may also be included, for example, the width of the amplitude maximum (e.g., FWHM for a Gaussian fit), the prominence and/or the area enclosed by the maximum. The use of this information can further increase robustness. For example, this information may be used as part of thresholding methods and/or used for improved (more robust) detection using machine learning (e.g., with respect to their significance).

Description

The invention relates to a method for detecting an occupancy state of at least one seat in a vehicle, a computer program product, a computer-readable data carrier, a control unit, and a vehicle.

Vehicles are known to have sensors, for example, UWB devices, LIDAR, cameras, and/or ultrasonic sensors, in order to detect static objects (and/or moving objects). It may be provided that a UWB device (e.g., a UWB anchor) is set up for detecting and/or authenticating a vehicle access and/or a driving license, for example, by detecting and/or recognizing and/or localizing a person in the vicinity of the vehicle (and/or an ID transmitter). In this context, a UWB device can receive and/or provide a plurality of channel impulse responses. Depending on this, the distance to objects (such as an ID transmitter for the vehicle) can be determined, for example. It is also known to provide seat occupancy detection (SOD) for at least one seat in the interior of the vehicle, for example, for the driver's seat. In known solutions, capacitive or pressure-sensitive seat mats can be integrated in one/each seat. These sense deformation, and a weight and, if applicable, also a profile of the weight distribution on the seat can be determined therefrom.

The prior art has disadvantages in this regard. For example, capacitive or pressure-sensitive seat mats can be cost-intensive, since in addition to the seat mat, they also need to be integrated into the seat and the associated wiring in/on the seat and in the vehicle. In addition, evaluation electronics are required. This can lead to costs, increased complexity, increased assembly effort, reduced robustness, increased maintenance effort, and/or additional weight. Another disadvantage is that the existing technology cannot distinguish between objects and living persons/humans. Finally, it is not possible to make a robust distinction between adults and children, who are located on the seat.

It is therefore an object of the present invention to at least partially overcome at least one of the disadvantages described above. In particular, it is an object of the invention to enable detection of an occupancy state that optimizes costs, weight, assembly, complexity, accuracy, robustness (of the detection), speed, and/or maintenance effort.

The above object is achieved by a method having the features of the independent method claim, a computer program product having the features of the independent patent claim relating to a computer program product, a computer-readable data carrier having the features of the independent patent claim relating to a computer-readable data carrier, a control unit having the features of the independent patent claim relating to a control unit, and a vehicle having the features of the independent vehicle claim.

-	a second antenna, which is set up to transmit and receive UWB waves and is arranged in the interior of the vehicle, wherein the first antenna is spaced apart from the second antenna, in particular along a transverse direction, wherein in particular the second antenna is arranged above the first seat, the second seat, and/or the at least one seat, for example, in the headliner of the vehicle,

For example, the first antenna, the second antenna, and/or the UWB device may perform transmitting of first and/or second UWB waves into the vehicle interior of the vehicle, for example, by being arranged (pointing downward) in the roof and/or headliner of the vehicle, preferably above a first and/or second seat or a bench seat (with at least two seats). For example, a vehicle may have at least one UWB device for the front, rear, and/or each row of seats. The first antenna, second antenna, and/or UWB device can (additionally) be set up for another function, for example, a keyless entry system or the like. For example, the UWB device or the first and/or second antenna can be set up for detecting and/or authenticating a vehicle access and/or a driving license, for example, by detecting and/or recognizing and/or localizing a person (and/or an ID transmitter) in front of the UWB device. This means that existing UWB devices or an existing (already installed) first and/or second antenna may also be used. Accordingly, the function or the method may also be retrofitted.

The control unit may be integrated into the UWB device. Alternatively or additionally, a (central and/or separate) control unit may be comprised by the vehicle. The control unit may be connected to the first antenna, the second antenna, a transmit/receive switch, and/or the UWB device for data communication, for example, via a respective data connection.

Detecting an occupancy state of at least one seat, in particular a first seat and/or a second seat, may in this case in particular comprise detecting a first target, in particular on a first seat (e.g., a seat on the right relative to the direction of travel or along the transverse direction), and/or detecting a second target, in particular on a second seat (e.g., a seat on the left relative to the direction of travel or along the transverse direction). The first target may in this case comprise a first object, in particular an (immovable) first object or a first person (in particular an adult or a child). Detection of a (first) animal would also be conceivable. The second target may in this case comprise a second object, in particular an (immovable) second object or a second person (in particular an adult or a child). Detection of a (second) animal would also be conceivable. The occupancy state may in this case have a data structure that is in particular specific to the occupancy and/or type of occupancy of the at least one seat, the first seat (by a first target) and/or the second seat (by a second target), in particular, for example, via a respective occupancy value (0 or 1) or in each case "occupied yes" or "occupied no". Additionally or alternatively, the occupancy state may be specific to a type of the object, in particular whether the first and/or second target is (likely to be) a (first and/or second) object or a (first and/or second) person, and in particular whether it is (likely to be) an adult or a child (or possibly an animal).

Here, the first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses may be (directly) calculated and/or provided by a/the UWB device, and subsequently transmitted to the control unit. The first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses may in this case be provided by the first and/or second antenna. Alternatively or additionally, other antennas may also be used. It is therefore conceivable that a third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and/or eighth antenna (et cetera) may also be used in an antenna array. Accordingly, the first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses may be provided by transmitting with one of the antennas and receiving with the same antenna and/or at least one other antenna (and subsequent further processing, see above). In this context, virtual (receiving) antennas may also be provided in each case. The angular separation capability may be further improved by using multiple (virtual and/or physical) antennas. The principle may (already) be illustrated using a first and a second antenna, which is why the method with a first and second antenna is described here in particular. Nevertheless, it is conceivable to apply the method to further antennas and/or an arbitrary number of antennas (in an antenna array).

In particular, it may be provided that the (different) channel impulse responses (e.g., in the form of a 1D vector with amplitudes) are received for the (first, second, third, and/or fourth) plurality of channel impulse responses at different (successive) points in time and/or each have different amplitude values, which are in particular specific to successive distance values (e.g., specific to certain distances in front of/below the first and/or second antenna or UWB device). Accordingly, the first and/or second UWB waves may be at least partially reflected by an object or a first and/or second target and subsequently received (by the first and/or second antenna). By means of an (auto) correlation between the transmitted (first and/or second UWB waves) and (first reflected and then) received (first and/or second) UWB waves (received signal), a (respective) channel impulse response (e.g., in the form of a 1D vector with amplitudes) may be provided, in particular by the UWB device. The channel impulse response(s) may be transmitted to the control unit, for example, via a (wired or wireless) data connection. Accordingly, the control unit may receive the channel impulse responses and/or a plurality of channel impulse responses (for example, by lining up the channel impulse responses into a 2D matrix, which in particular sorts the channel impulse responses in time). Alternatively or additionally, the UWB device may also provide (and subsequently transmit to the control unit) the (first, second, third, and/or fourth) plurality of channel impulse responses. In this context, a (first, second, third, and/or fourth) plurality of channel impulse responses may (in each case) have at least 10, at least 50, at least 100, at least 500, or at least 1000, for example 10000 channel impulse responses, which are preferably (all) determined one after the other in time, in particular at different successive points in time. In this context, one (each) channel impulse response may have successive distance values or CIR taps (e.g., 300), each of which comprises a (corresponding) amplitude. In this context, the amplitude may be specific to (all) signals (e.g., of different objects, such as the first and/or second target), which are detected or were detected for a particular distance value (in particular at a certain distance, preferably [or more precisely] in a certain distance range, e.g. [a bin] of 30 cm). Simplified accordingly, a first, second, third, and/or fourth plurality of channel impulse responses may be understood as a 2D matrix, wherein the channel impulse responses are arranged in the rows and/or along the x-coordinates, and wherein successive measurement time points are arranged along the columns and/or along the y-coordinates.

The (first) transmitting by the first antenna of the first UWB waves, reflections of which are received by the first antenna (to obtain a first received signal) to provide a first plurality of channel impulse responses, may be performed in a (so-called) radar mode, in particular not in sensing mode and/or for time-of-flight (ToF) measurement, in particular because (unlike, e.g., ID transmitters) the objects or a first and/or second target do not "send back" but merely reflect the UWB waves. The radar mode in a UWB device may be characterized by the capability to capture precise and detailed information about the vehicle interior, in particular by emitting UWB signals and analyzing the reflected signals. This enables the precise determination of distances, movements, and positions of objects. The radar mode may offer the advantage of high precision in detecting and localizing, even in complex environments or with moving objects. In addition, the radar mode may be considered robust against environmental influences, such as light conditions and/or acoustic disturbances. For example (with reference to the above), a first plurality of channel impulse responses (or the corresponding individual channel impulse responses) may be provided by (auto)correlating between the first UWB waves and their reflections (such as at the first and/or second target). For example, the received signal received by the first antenna or the channel impulse response (when reflected at a first target) may have a (relative) phase of 〖2Φ〗_d (see explanations below), wherein in particular d may represent the distance between the first antenna and the (first) target and Φ_d the corresponding phase (when transmitting and receiving). Accordingly, the first antenna may (thereby) be operated in a transmit/receive mode (both transmitting and [subsequently or in parallel] receiving). Accordingly, it may be provided that the first plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses) have a phase of 〖2Φ〗_d.

The (second) transmitting by the second antenna of second UWB waves, reflections of which are received by the second antenna (to obtain a fourth received signal) in order to provide a fourth plurality of channel impulse responses, may be performed in a (so-called) radar mode. For example (with reference to the above), a fourth plurality of channel impulse responses (or the corresponding individual channel impulse responses) may be provided by (auto)correlation between the second transmitted) UWB waves and their reflection (such as at the first and/or second target). For example, the received signal received by the second antenna or the channel impulse response (when reflected at a first target) may have a (relative) phase of 〖2Φ〗_d+ 〖2Φ〗_x, wherein d may represent the distance between the first antenna and the (first) target and Φ_d may represent the phase difference present twice (due to transmitting and receiving), caused by the additional distance x (covered by the UWB waves) between the second antenna and the first target (relative or compared to the distance between the first antenna and the first target in this example). This means that the second antenna may be operated in a transmit/receive mode (both transmitting and receiving [subsequently or in parallel]). Accordingly, it may be provided that the fourth plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses) have a phase of 〖2Φ〗_d+ 〖2Φ〗_x.

Providing a second plurality of channel impulse responses as a function of reflections of the first UWB waves that are received by the second antenna may accordingly be specific to the first UWB waves reflected at the first (and/or second) target. To return to the above example, the second plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses) may therefore (due to reception by the second antenna while transmitting with the first antenna) have a phase of 〖2Φ〗_d+ Φ_x, in particular since the (first) UWB waves have to cover the additional distance x, which results in particular from the distance (e.g., a=λ/2) between the first and second antennas.

Providing a third plurality of channel impulse responses as a function of reflections of the second UWB waves received by the first antenna, may accordingly be specific to second UWB waves reflected at the first (and/or second) target. To return to the above example, the third plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses) may therefore (due to reception by the first antenna while transmitting with the second antenna) have a phase of (also) 〖2Φ〗_d+ Φ_x, in particular since the (second) UWB waves have to cover the additional distance x, which results in particular from the distance (e.g., a=λ/2) between the first and second antennas. Accordingly, the second and third plurality of channel impulse responses (or their channel impulse responses and/or phases) may each be configured to be reciprocal and/or interchangeable. This may advantageously be used to use only the second or third plurality of channel impulse responses (within the scope of the method). In particular, this can reduce the total time required for transmitting and receiving. As a result, accuracy can be increased.

By using the first and fourth plurality of channel impulse responses in conjunction with the second or third plurality of channel impulse responses, a (third) virtual (receiving) antenna may therefore be provided, which in particular (virtually) extends the antenna array formed by the first and second antennas by a further third antenna (at a distance a). Furthermore, it may be provided that the UWB device has additional (real and/or physical) antennas. Thus, the UWB device may have a first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and/or eighth antenna (et cetera), which in particular together form an antenna array. Preferably, the antennas may be spaced apart from each other (at a distance of half a wavelength, see below), in particular along the transverse direction. In this respect, the embodiments of the first and/or second antenna may apply analogously to other antennas. In other words, a larger aperture may thereby be provided. Advantageously, this may enable improved separation between objects, in particular between a first target (such as on the first seat) and a second target (on the second seat). This means that with two (real or physical) antennas (namely, the first and second antennas), it is still possible to resolve two objects (the first and second target). In particular, this may apply approximately, especially if the distance to the objects d is (significantly) greater than the distance a between the first and second antenna, e.g., the following applies:
d≫a
The principle described above can also be extended to other antennas, such as a third, fourth, and/or fifth (and so on) antenna. Accordingly, a first, second, and third antenna may also be used, for example, to improve the separation of three targets (e.g. neighboring targets in a row of seats).

Within the scope of the invention, it can be advantageous that the first detection algorithm and the second detection algorithm differ, wherein in particular
-	the first detection algorithm is optimized for detecting moving targets, and/or
-	the second detection algorithm is optimized for detecting static targets.

The robustness and/or accuracy can thus be increased by using the first and the second detection algorithms. If, for example, only the first detection algorithm were used, a first and/or second target could (potentially) generate no amplitude maximum in some or all of the first amplitude-angle profiles, for example, due to a lack of movement. Accordingly, it would (incorrectly) be assumed that there is either no first and/or no second target, or at least no person or animal is positioned on the first or second seat (but rather an object). In other words, false detections could occur (e.g., false negatives). By optimizing the second detection algorithm for detecting static targets, the robustness of detecting (at least temporarily) static first and/or second targets may advantageously be optimized. This can increase the overall robustness.

This may be particularly advantageous when detecting living beings (people and/or animals) (due to their movement).
