PREAMBLE TO THE DESCRIPTION:
The following specification particularly describes the invention and the
40 manner in which it is to be performed:
2
[1] The invention relates to a switching device for high-voltage direct electric
current. Such devices are designed for implementation in networks or
HVDC network units in case of electrical malfunction generating a fault
current through at least one electrical conductor of the network.
5 [2] HVDC networks are particularly considered as a solution for the
interconnection of heterogeneous or asynchronous power generation sites.
HVDC networks are particularly considered for the transmission and
distribution of power from offshore wind farms rather than alternative
current technologies, thanks to lower line loss and no effect of parasitic
10 capacitances of the network on long distances. Such networks typically
have nominal service voltage levels higher than 75 kV, in particular ca.
100 kV or more.
[3] In the present text, it is considered as a direct high-voltage device either a
“high-voltage A” device, wherein the nominal service direct voltage is
15 more than 1500 V but not more than 75 000 V, or a “high-voltage B”
device, wherein the nominal service direct voltage is more than 75 000 V.
Thus, the direct high-voltage domain includes the “high-voltage A”
domain and the “high-voltage B” domain.
[4] Power breaks in such networks are a crucial security issue that directly
20 determines the feasibility and the development of such networks.
[5] Nowadays, the evolution of these networks tends toward interconnecting
infrastructures to get meshed networks, i.e. networks featuring a plurality
of possible pathways between two given locations in the network.
[6] In an electric circuit, there is generally at least one power source and at
25 least one power consumer, which can comprise any device or set of
devices or any network including such devices that consume electrical
energy to turn it into another kind of energy. In an electric circuit, there is
generally at least one electric switching device that makes it possible to
3
disrupt the flow of electrical current through the circuit, generally between
the power source and the power consumer, or between the power source
and the ground.
[7] Various types of switching devices are known that are designed to be
5 introduced in a conductor of an electric circuit. For example, circuit
breakers are known that are mechanical switching devices and that are
designed and scaled to allow, in particular, an opening under load or a
default mode of the electrical circuit, in which they are positioned.
Furthermore, switching devices are known with simpler designs, such as
10 circuit breakers, which are generally not designed to break circuits under
load, but rather to provide, in a circuit where the flow of the current is
already interrupted by another switch device, an electric isolation with a
preset high level between an upstream part of a conductor of the circuit,
for example connected to the power source, and a downstream part of this
15 conductor of the circuit.
[8] In a main switch device of mechanical type, the power break results only
from the opening of a mechanical switch item. Such a mechanical switch
item comprises two contact conductive parts that are in mechanical and
electrical contact when the switch is closed and mechanically separate
20 when the switch is open.
[9] In the presence of a direct high current and/or voltage, the mechanical
separation can result in the establishment of an electric arc between the
two conductive parts because of the high energy levels in the network that
the device protects. As long as the electric arc remains through the
25 mechanical separation, the mechanical switch device does not complete
the power break, since some current keeps on flowing through the device
with the arc. The power break, in terms of effective interruption of the
flow of electric current, is sometimes particularly difficult in the context of
4
direct high-voltage current, these conditions having the tendency to
maintain the electric arc.
[10] It is more complex to break direct high-voltage currents than
alternative high-voltage currents. Indeed, during the break of an
5 alternative high-voltage current, it is taken advantage of a zero crossing of
the current to get the electric break, which is not possible with a direct
high-voltage current.
[11] Hybrid circuit breakers have been developed to break direct current.
Thus, hybrid circuit breakers use a main branch with the direct current
10 through it in normal mode, and a parallel branch of electronic power
components. The main branch usually comprises a vacuum tube switch
mounted in series with a switch help module. In case of malfunction, the
opening of the vacuum tube initiates an arc voltage. The switch help
module by impedance increase makes it possible to increase the
15 impedance in the main branch to compel the current through the parallel
branch. Then, the electronic power components of the parallel branch
open to disrupt the flow of the current.
[12] A drawback of the switch help module by impedance increase is that it
is connected in series on the main branch. Thus, it induces losses by Joule
20 heating in normal mode and requires cooling.
[13] In order to limit this loss, the document EP3072143 discloses to
connect a reverse current injection module as a switch help module. A
transformer is then used to inject a reverse current into the main branch
when switching.
25 [14] The FR2103336 patent discloses a reverse current injection module
relying on the discharge of a capacitor.
5
[15] The purpose of the invention is to solve one or several of these
drawbacks. Thus, the invention relates to a switching device for direct
high-voltage electric current, as described in the appended claim 1.
[16] The invention also relates to the variants of the dependent claims. A
5 person skilled in the art shall understand that each characteristic of the
dependent claims and of the description can be independently combined to
the characteristics of claim 1 without constituting an intermediate
generalization however.
[17] Other characteristics and advantages of the invention will clearly
10 appear thanks to the following description produced as a guide and nonlimitative with a reference to the appended schematic pictures, where:
[18] [Fig. 1] is a schematic view of an embodiment of a switching device for
direct high-voltage electric current of the invention;
[19] [Fig. 2] is a schematic view of a first example of switch module for a
15 switching device;
[20] [Fig. 3] is a schematic view of a switch module of a first type for a
second example of switch module;
[21] [Fig. 4] is a schematic view of another embodiment of a switching
device of the invention;
20 [22] [Fig. 5] shows a variant of a switch module in association with a surge
suppressor;
[23] [Fig. 6] shows another variant of a switch module in association with a
surge suppressor;
[24] [Fig. 7] shows yet another variant of a switch module in association
25 with a surge suppressor;
6
[25] [Fig. 8] shows another variant of a switch module in association with a
surge suppressor;
[26] [Fig. 9] shows another variant of a switch module in association with a
surge suppressor.
5 [27] In an electric network, the transmission of power between two given
locations is made by a power transmission line that generally comprises a
plurality of conductors, each corresponding to a terminal of the power
transmission line. Thus, in a HVDC network, the transmission of power
between two given locations in the network is made by a power
10 transmission line that generally comprises two terminals. So, in this case,
the power transmission line comprises two conductors with different
polarities with, under load, for example, a conductor with a positive
potential and a conductor with a negative or neutral potential.
[28] Still in the same unit of the HVDC network, the power transmission
15 between two given locations of the network can also be made by a power
transmission line with three terminals, comprising three conductors with,
under load, a conductor with a positive potential, a conductor with a
negative potential and a conductor with a neutral potential. In some cases,
the transmission of power between two given locations of the network can
20 be made by a power transmission line with only one terminal, with a
conductor at the same potential as the line and with an earth return.
[29] [Fig. 1 shows a first embodiment of the switching device 10 to break a
high-voltage DC current through a conductor 11. For example, the
conductor 11 can belong to a power transmission line in a HVDC network
25 unit under a nominal service direct voltage of more than 1500 V, possibly
more than 75 000 V (75 kV). Thus, the switching device 10 is located in
the conductor 11 between a primary location 12 of the switching device 10
and a secondary location 14 of the switching device 10. The primary
7
location 12 and the secondary location 14 can be respectively connection
terminals of the device 10. Thus, the switching device 10 divides the
conductor 11 in two sections, a first section 111 that is connected to the
primary location 12 and a second section 112 that is connected to the
5 secondary location 14.
[30] Thus, the switching device 10 comprises a main circuit 16 between the
primary location 12 of the switching device 10 and the secondary location
14 of the switching device 10. In a conductive configuration of the
switching device 10, a working electric current flows with a nominal
10 service direct high voltage of the switching device 10. It is the working
current that flows through the conductor 11, whose intensity is not more
than the nominal intensity of the device. Indeed, in case of electrical
malfunction, the intensity of current through the switching device may
briefly exceed this nominal intensity.
15 [31] The switching device 10 is configured to act as a circuit breaker, i.e. it
breaks a current with an intensity less than its breaking capacity, so either
in load at nominal or partial intensity, or in case of default current.
[32] The switching device 10 comprises at least one switch module 18 in the
main circuit 16 between a first location 20 and a second location 22. In the
20 example of Fig. 1 (that comprises only one switch module 18), the first
location 20 and a second location 22 of the main circuit 16 are locations
on the main circuit 16 at respectively the same electrical potential as the
primary location 12 and the secondary location 14 of the switching device
10 that delineate the main circuit 16 of the switching device 10.
25 [33] The switching device can comprise a plurality of switch modules that
can be mounted in series in the main circuit 16 between the primary
location 12 and the secondary location 14 of the switching device 10.
8
[34] A switch module 18 comprises three branches that are mounted in
parallel to each other between the first location 20 and the second location
22.
[35] The switch module 18 comprises a main branch 24 between the first
5 location 20 and the second location 22, with at least one main switching
unit 26 in the main branch 24 between the first location 20 and the second
location 22, which is of mechanical type to get an electrical break in the
main branch 24. The main switching unit 26 can switch between a closed
state, where it allows the flow of the current through the main branch 24,
10 and an open state, where it breaks the current through the main branch 24
by disrupting the flow of current at the zero crossing of the intensity in the
main branch 24. The main branch 24 of the module 18 is the one through
which the working current flows in normal condition of the network,
when the switching device 10 is in conductive configuration. Thus, in
15 normal condition of the network, when the switching device 10 is in
conductive configuration, the working current in the conductor 11 flows
through the main switching unit 26 in a steady or nearly steady state.
[36] For example, the main switching unit 26 can be a circuit breaker, a
load switch or a disconnector.
20 [37] In the main switching unit 26 of mechanical type, the electric break is
obtained by moving, in particular by moving aside, at least one pair of
electrical contacts. The spreading of the electrical contacts is generally
made by mechanic, pneumatic, hydraulic or electric adjusting mechanisms
or actuators. This movement can be electronically monitored, for example
25 by an electronic control unit 100. In the presence of a high current and/or
voltage, the mechanical separation of the electric contacts can result in the
establishment of an electric arc between the two electric contacts of the
device. As long as the electric arc remains through the mechanical
separation, the mechanical switching unit 26 does not complete the power
9
break, since some current keeps on flowing through the device with the
arc.
[38] As seen below, the invention includes means to provide the power
break, in terms of effective interruption of the flow of electric current. The
5 main switching unit 26 can be made of only one main switching device or
can be made of a plurality of main switching devices mounted in series
and/or in parallel. The main switching unit 26 can be a “gas insulated
substation”, where the electric contacts are enclosed in a watertight
housing filled with an isolating fluid or, more preferably, a unit under
10 vacuum (sometimes called “vacuum tube switch”), where the electric
contacts are enclosed in a watertight housing with a pressure less than the
ambient, in particular less than 100 millibar, notably less than 10
microbar. The main switching unit 26 will be advantageously able to break
the electric arc of a current with a high speed of intensity variation (di/dt)
15 at the moment of a zero crossing of the intensity, typically with a speed of
variation of at least 100 A per microsecond.
[39] A switch module 18 also comprises an absorption branch 28,
electrically mounted parallel to the main branch 24 between the first
location 20 and the second location 22 of the considered switch module
20 18, with at least one general surge suppressor 30 between the absorption
branch 28 between the first location 20 and the second location 22 of the
considered switch module.
[40] Such a general surge suppressor 30 makes it possible to restrict the
amplitude of the voltage difference at the terminals of any component or
25 set of components it is mounted parallel to. Thus, a surge suppressor is a
device that restricts the voltage peaks at its terminals. A surge suppressor
generally comprises an electric component with a resistance that varies
with the electric voltage at its terminals. The surge suppressor acts by
limiting the voltage at its terminals on the current interval, for which it
10
was selected. It puts up a protective voltage when submitted to the highest
current, for which the surge suppressor was sized. At less than the
transition voltage, it tends to prevent the flow of the current. At more than
the transition voltage, it lets the current flow through the surge suppressor
5 for a small increase of the voltage at its terminals. It is known that the
transition voltage is generally not an accurate value, but rather
corresponds to a transition voltage range. However, in the present text, it
shall be considered as a definition that the transition voltage of a surge
suppressor is the voltage value, at which the surge suppressor allows a 1-
10 Ampere (A) current. The protective voltage is the voltage at the terminals
of the surge suppressor when submitted to the biggest intensity it was sized
for. Among surge suppressors are known lightning conductors, which can
notably include varistors and “TVS” diodes (Transient Voltage
Suppressor), such as “Transil™” diodes. In particular, in the context of the
15 invention, a surge suppressor, notably the general surge suppressor 30, can
comprise a metal oxide varistor (MOV).
[41] In the example as pictured in figure 1, the absorption branch 28 does
not comprise a switch. Because of this, it is necessary to select the general
surge suppressor 30 so that its protective voltage is higher than the possible
20 voltage at the terminals of the switch module 18 when the switching

30 is selected, so that its protective voltage is between 1.2 and 2 times, for
example 1.6 times the nominal service voltage of the module 18, which is
25 the voltage where the switch module 18 is working when the switching
device 10 is working under the nominal service voltage of the network.
[42] Because of the presence of the general surge suppressor 30 in the
absorption branch 28, and because of the selection of its transition voltage
value, it can be considered that in normal mode of the network, when the
11
switching device 10 is in conductive configuration, there is no current
through the absorption branch 28.
[43] A switch module 18 of the invention also comprises a switch branch
32, electrically mounted parallel to the main branch 24 and of the
5 absorption branch 28 between the first location 20 and the second location
22 of the considered switch module 18.
[44] There are several switch modules 34 mounted in series in the switch
branch 32 between the first location 20 and the second location 22. The
switch modules 34 are controlled by the electronic control unit 100.
10 [45] Enough switch modules 34 are connected in series to break high
currents (for example more than 500 A, for example ca. 10000 A) under a
direct voltage of at least 50 kV in the branch 32. The number of switch
modules 34 connected in series can also be adapted so that this current
break is possible event if the monitoring or the function of one of the
15 modules 34 failed.
[46] To control the switch modules 34, the electronic control unit 100
makes it possible to switch them either to their open state or to their closed
state.
[47] As detailed below, the switch modules 34 are designed to be switched
20 to closed state only during switching stages of the main switching unit 26,
in particular during switching stages of the main switching unit 26 from
closed to open state. When not in these switching stages (in particular
during nominal conduction stages, when the main switching unit 26 is
maintained in closed state or in isolation stage, where the main switching
25 unit 26 is maintained in open state), the switch modules 34 are designed to
be maintained in open state, so that no current flows through the switch
branch 32.
12
[48] For each switch module 34, a switch capacitor 38 is connected in series
with at least one semiconductor switch.
[49] Figure 2 shows an embodiment of the switch module 34. A switch
capacitor 38 is connected in series between one-way semiconductor
5 switches 41 and 42. The switch capacitor 38 acts as a generator for an
oscillating current in the switch branch 32 to inject a counter-current into
the main branch 24, in order to promote the extinction of the electric arc
that may happen between the electrodes of the main switching device 26
when opening. The device 1 of the invention makes it possible to
10 implement the opening functions of the switch 26 with switch capacitors
38 that have a voltage withstand far less than the nominal service voltage
of the switch module 18, hence far less than the nominal service voltage of
the network, in which the conductor 11 is inserted.
[50] A plurality of one-way switches 41 and 42 can be connected in parallel
15 to increase the capacity of the system.
[51] The switch 38 also acts as a power supply for a control system 561.
Because of the use of a plurality of modules 34 in series, the voltage at the
terminals of the various capacitors 38 can be lowered enough for getting
close to the power supply voltage of the control systems 561.
20 Alternatively, the control system 561 advantageously comprises a preload
circuit for the switch capacitor 38. This preload circuit makes it possible to
apply a preset voltage between the two plates of the switch capacitor 38
before any switching of the main switching device 26. In the example, the
preload circuit comprises a DC power source 501 that selectively applies a
25 voltage to the terminals of the switch capacitor 38. Here, this voltage is
applied through a resistor 531 and through another resistor 551. The
resistors 531, 551 of the preload circuit can have the same or different
resistance values. Practically, only one of the two resistors may be enough.
The at least one resistor 531, 551 are designed to restrict the
13
load/discharge current to provide by the DC power source 501. In order to
secure the power supply of the control system 561 by its capacitor 38, a
DC-to-DC converter can be located between the control system 561 and
this capacitor 38 or can be located inside the control system 561.
5 [52] The module 34 comprises, electrically in parallel to the switch
capacitor 38, a switch surge suppressor 801. This switch surge suppressor
801 is connected by its two terminals respectively to two locations in the
first part of the switch branch 32 on both sides of the switch capacitor 38.
The switch surge suppressor 801 makes it possible to restrict the voltage at
10 the terminals of the switch capacitor 38, hence to use capacitors for lower
voltage. For example, such a surge suppressor 801 is of ZnO type.
Typically, in a switching device 1 designed for a very-high-voltage
network, the voltage at the terminals of the switch capacitor 38 can then
be restricted by the first switch surge suppressor 801 to a level that depends
15 on the number of modules 34 in series. For example, it can be planned to
connect at least 8 modules 34 in series.
[53] Here, the switches 41 and 42 are of IGBT type (Insulated Gate Bipolar
Transistor). The IGBTs 41 and 42 are here in opposite directions. The
IGBTs 41 and 42 constitute a two-way switch capable to selectively
20 conduct or block the current in both directions. Using two IGBTs 41 and
42 makes a two-way current and voltage switch possible.
[54] Each IGBT 41, 42 comprises a free-wheeling diode mounted
antiparallel to the IGBT. When working, the two IGBTs 41 and 42 are
normally open. The IGBTs 41, 42 are commanded to their closed state to
25 initiate the discharge of the capacitor 38.
[55] The IGBTs 41 and 42 are monitored by the control system 561. The
control system 561 is dedicated to the module 34 and is powered by the
capacitor 38. Such a configuration makes it possible to prevent issues with
14
a common power supply of the control systems 561 with a corresponding
galvanic isolation. The control systems 561 are controlled by the electronic
control unit 100.
[56] As detailed below, the generation of a switching current oscillation in
5 the switch branch 32, when the modules 34 are in closed state, results from
a modulation of the current in the loop made of the main branch 24 and
the switch branch 32 of the switch module 18. This loop, which notably
comprises the switch capacitors 38, necessarily and naturally, as any loop,
has some inductance, such that the loop constitutes a LC circuit that
10 generates a current ripple in the transitory stages. This current ripple is
used to disrupt a potential electrical arc in the main switching device 26 in
its open state.
[57] The switching inductance can result from the proper inductance of the
components of the loop, in particular from the proper inductance of the
15 main branch 24 and/or from the proper inductance of the switch branch
32. However, if the proper inductance of the components is not enough,
the loop formed by the main branch 24 and the switch branch 32 can
comprise a coil 82. This coil is preferably located in the switch branch 32.
The switching inductance will be so sized that it restricts the speed of the
20 current variation through the main switching device 26, the variation
happening when the switch branch 32 closes. The speed of current
variation in the loop made of the switch branch 32 and the main branch 24
must be restricted by the components in the switch branch 32 to a value
corresponding to the ability by the main switching device 26 to disrupt the
25 electric arc. Thus, the device is sized, so that it secures the disruption of
the arc in the main switching device 26 when the current through this
main switching device 26 crosses a zero value.
[58] The device 1 can comprise or be associated with at least one electronic
control unit 100 to monitor/control the modules 34. An electronic control
15
unit 100 typically comprises at least one processor and at least one
electronic memory, and can comprise or be linked to at least one
communication electronic circuits, for example for communication with at
least one computer network, and/or at least one interface electronic
5 circuit, and/or at least one input/output electronic circuit. An electronic
control unit 100 can comprise or be associated with at least one display.
An electronic control unit can comprise or be associated with at least one
sensor, for example at least one intensity sensor and/or at least one
voltage sensor, configured to measure a value for a physical parameter in
10 the switching device 1 or in the electric set-up, to which the device 1 is
meant to be integrated. The at least one electronic control unit is
programmed to implement all or a part of a process to open a device such
as described above. Advantageously, the at least one electronic control
unit 100 may communicate their commands/control instructions, in
15 particular to the control units 561, by signals with galvanic isolation
against high voltage. These signals can be optical signals transported by
optical fibers. They can be electrical signals isolated by transformers.
These signals can be electromagnetic signals transported by wireless
communication links.
20 [59] Thus, the switching device 1 as described above constitutes a circuit
breaker particularly suitable for high-voltage DC currents, in particular
under high-voltage DC of more than 75 kV. This device 1 makes it
possible to get sufficient circuit break performances with components that,
globally, mean reduced volume and cost, with minimum energy loss in
25 normal work condition.
[60] In case of malfunction, the working sequence of the device 1 is
following. In service, the switches of the modules 34 are open and the
switch 26 is closed. When detecting a fault (for example by information or
detection at the electronic control unit 100), a command to open the
30 switch 26 is sent by the electronic control unit 100. Because of an arc at
16
the opening of the switch 26, the break of the current through this switch
26 is not effective yet. A command to generate a switching is sent to the
modules 34 in a synchronic way. The duration of the switching of the
current through the main branch 24 toward the switch branch 32 is
5 maximum equal to three quarters of the oscillation period in the loop
made of the main branch 24 and the switch branch 32, considering that
this oscillation can be equated with the discharge of the capacitors into a
LC or RLC circuit. After a delay or after checking that the circuit break is
effective through the switch 26, the switches of the modules 34 are opened
10 again. Then, the surge suppressor 30 reduces the default current and takes
up the residual energy from the network.
[61] The invention advantageously makes it possible to reduce the loss by
Joule heating in the main branch 24 while reducing the risks of
malfunction in the switch branch 32. Indeed, because of the presence of a
15 plurality of modules 34 connected in series, the switching can be obtained
anyway, even if the command of one of the modules 34 were faulty.
Furthermore, such a device 1 makes it possible to maintain an effective
speed of circuit break in the main branch 24, which reduces the erosion of
the electrodes of the switch 26.

BACKGROUND
Systemic sclerosis (SSc) (also known as systemic scleroderma) is a devastating
autoimmune disease characterized by excessive production and accumulation of extracellular
matrix leading to fibrosis of skin and other internal organs. Systemic sclerosis is associated
20 with mortality rates that in its most severe form are comparable to metastatic cancers (1,2).
The etiology of SSc remains poorly understood but involves genetic predisposition (3),
female sex (4), and environmental exposures (5,6), resulting in autoimmunity, fibrosis in the
skin and internal organs, along with prominent microvasculopathy (7).
Skin thickening in SSc is due to increased deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM)
25 components, most prominently type I collagen (9,10). With disease progression, there is
increasing dermal fibrosis and loss of adnexa (11). The increased skin tightness correlates
with accumulation of myofibroblasts in the skin (12,13). Myofibroblasts are mesenchymal
cells of fibroblast lineage that are transiently activated during normal wound healing (14). In
contrast to fibroblasts, myofibroblasts express the contractile protein alpha smooth muscle
30 actin, and form characteristic stress fibers (15). Myofibroblasts are commonly first detected
in the deep dermis (16), and their persistence in SSc (17,18) is thought to be responsible for
3
the exaggerated and uncontrolled ECM production (15,18). The factors driving differentiation
and accumulation of myofibroblasts in SSc have been extensively investigated. It is currently
thought that TGF-β and mechanical forces are key factors in myofibroblast development
(14,19). Notably, mechanical stiffness itself activated latent TGF-β (20-23), setting up a self5 sustaining amplification circuit for tissue fibrosis in SSc skin (10).
Vascular dysfunction and structural abnormalities, particularly involving the
arterioles, are among the earliest manifestations of SSc and precede development of fibrosis
(24). This vascular dysfunction results in altered capillary architecture with reduced vessel
density, a hallmark of SSc, causing decreased capillary blood flow and tissue hypoxia (25).
10 Clinically, these microvascular changes underlie painful digital ulcerations, pulmonary
arterial hypertension, gastric vascular ectasia, mucocutaneous telangiectasia and scleroderma
renal crisis (26-28). Larger vessels, including arterioles in the lung and the kidney, may show
intimal proliferation (onion skinning) and adventitial fibrosis, accompanied by loss of
pericytes. Apoptosis of endothelial cells in SSc was first noted over 25 years ago (29), and
15 there is accumulating evidence that this endothelial damage may be immune-mediated (30).
Immune mechanisms underlying the endothelial damage in SSc include cytotoxic T cells (8)
and anti-endothelial autoantibodies (31). Upon microvascular injury, endothelial cells can
acquire a mesenchymal phenotype through a process termed endothelial-to-mesenchymal
transition (EndoMT) (32). EndoMT is characterized by the loss of cell-cell junctions and
20 endothelial markers, such as von Willebrand factor, CD31, and VE-cadherin, coupled with
the acquisition of invasive properties and gain of mesenchymal markers such as alpha SMA
and collagens (33). EndoMT has been implicated in driving the pathogenesis of fibrosis in
multiple fibrotic conditions, including SSc (34).
The mechanisms and the main cellular participants in SSc skin fibrosis remain
25 incompletely understood. Current treatment paradigms can slow, but not halt or reverse,
fibrosis (8). There are no treatments that can cure or stop the fibrosis associated with SSc.
Antifibrotic agents (D-penicillamine, interferon alfa and interferon gamma, and
immunomodulatory agents (photopheresis, corticosteroids, methotrexate, chlorambucil,
mycophenolate mofetil cyclosporine, FK506, thalidomide, cyclophosphamide, and statins))
30 have been investigated, although results have varied and none is clearly shown to be of
consistent benefit. Treatments are primarily limited to attempts to help control symptoms and
prevent complications.
4
SUMMARY
Experiments conducted during the development of embodiments of the present
technology demonstrated a dual source of extracellular matrix deposition in SSc skin from
both myofibroblasts and endothelial to mesenchymal transitioning cells (EndoMTs),
5 characterized their differentiation trajectories at a single cell level, and defined a central role
of Hippo pathway effectors in promoting and maintaining myofibroblast differentiation and
EndoMT. Further, ligand-receptor analysis revealed that myofibroblasts and EndoMTs act as
central communication hubs that drive key pro-fibrotic signaling pathways in SSc. Together,
these discoveries provide comprehensive and detailed characterization of myofibroblast
10 differentiation and EndoMT in SSc skin and demonstrate that modulation of the Hippo
pathway can reverse the pro-fibrotic phenotypes in myofibroblasts and EndoMTs. As such,
Hippo pathway modulators find use in the treatment and/or prevention SSc.
The Hippo pathway is a highly conserved signaling pathway that regulates cell
proliferation, apoptosis, and stemness in response to a wide range of extracellular and
15 intracellular signals. Downstream effects of Hippo pathway signaling are mediated by the
YAP and TAZ transcription co-activators through binding with members of the TEAD family
of transcription factors (35). When the Hippo pathway is inactive, YAP/TAZ enters the
nucleus, competes with VGLL family of transcription co-factors for binding to TEADs, and
recruits other factors to induce gene transcription (35,36). When Hippo pathway is active,
20 YAP/TAZ is phosphorylated by LATS1/2 on multiple sites and is retained in the cytoplasm
due to interaction with 14-3-3 proteins and eventually removed through poly-ubiquitination
and degradation (35). Hippo signaling has been shown to regulate the expression of ligands
for WNT, TGF-β, JAK-STAT, EGFR, and Notch pathways (37), placing this pathway at the
nexus of multiple biological processes, many of which have been implicated in SSc
25 pathogenesis (38-42).

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
25 Fibroblast-myofibroblast transition and vascular dysfunction have long been
recognized as key pathologic features in SSc (17,18,24). Vascular abnormalities involving the
arterioles are among the earliest manifestations occurring in almost every SSc patient (25).
This vascular dysfunction precedes development of fibrosis and manifests clinically as
Raynaud’s phenomenon, digital ulcerations, and increased prominence of nailfold capillary
30 loops (24,25). The subsequent fibrosis is thought to result from exaggerated and uncontrolled
production of ECM components mainly by myofibroblasts in SSc skin (15,18). However, the
relationship between the vascular dysfunction and triggering of fibrosis has remained unclear.
15
Experiments conducted during the development of embodiments of the present
invention demonstrated that, in the SSc environment, the SFRP2+ FB progressively acquires
qualities of myofibroblasts as it transitions into fully developed myofibroblasts defined by
ACTA2 and COL8A1 expression. The SFRP2+ FB and myofibroblasts are the major source
5 of COL1A1 expression by fibroblastic lineage cells in SSc skin. Strikingly, with spatial-seq
and scRNA-seq integration, we observe prominent compartmentalization of the fibrotic
process in SSc skin, with increased COL1A1 expression and ECM activity occurring in
localized areas both superficially and deep in the dermis. Those areas correspond to the
SFRP2+ FB and myofibroblast signatures, with the SFRP2+ FB being most prominent in the
10 superficial dermis whereas myofibroblasts predominate in the deeper layers of the dermis.
The experiments further demonstrate that EndoMT represents another source of ECM in SSc
skin, which provides novel insight into the molecular mechanisms driving EndoMT at single
cell resolution.
Notably, most of the cellular interactions activated in SSc skin involved only two
15 major cell types, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts. Of those, the most pronounced cell-cell
interactions were seen between the EndoMTs (EC2) and myofibroblasts (COL8A1+ FB).
These interactions involve different chemokines (CCL2, CCL8, CCL11, CXCL1), cytokines
(IL6, IL11, TGFB1, TFGB3, TNFSF4, TNFSF9, TNFSF12), growth factors (FGF2, FGF7,
FGF18, VEGFA, VEGFB), and WNT ligands (WNT2, WNT4). Many of these mediators
20 have been implicated in SSc pathogenesis including CCL2 and CCL8 in promoting dendritic
cell differentiation (66), IL6 and IL11 in promoting fibrosis (39,59,67), TNFSF4 as genetic
predisposition in SSc (68), FGF7 in fibroblast activation (69), VEGF in vascular dysfunction
(70), and WNT2 in dermal fibrillin deposition (40).
The data presented here also implicate non-stromal cell populations in SSc
25 pathogenesis, particularly immune cells including B cells and T cells. B cells were highly
enriched in SSc skin and may provide a link between pathological processes in the skin and
development of autoantibodies, found in most patients with SSc (88). CD8 T cells have been
postulated to serve as key drivers in the prominent endothelial dysfunction in SSc (8), with
some of the earliest features SSc being perivascular edema along with perivascular
30 mononuclear infiltrate particularly in the upper and mid-dermis (11). These early changes
coincide with the same dermal locations where EndoMTs, characterized by SMA+CD31+,
are prominent. Besides immune cells, other stromal cells, such as the smooth muscle cells,
which were primarily derived from the SSc biopsies, may also play a role in pathogenesis.
16
It is demonstrated herein that the profibrotic phenotypes of myofibroblasts and
EndoMTs in SSc are reversed by inhibiting TEAD transcriptional activity.
Thus, in some embodiments, provided herein are compositions and methods for the
treatment of SSc and related and other fibrotic diseases and conditions (e.g., diseases and
5 conditions showing a similar profibrotic phenotype of myofibroblasts and EndoMTs), as well
as inflammatory diseases and conditions (e.g., inflammatory diseases and conditions that
include scarring, such as cutaneous lupus), by the administration of a Hippo pathway effector
(e.g., TEAD inhibitor) to a subject having, or suspected of having, the disease or condition.
In some embodiments, the related and/or other fibrotic diseases and conditions are idiopathic
10 pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), cardiac fibrosis, kidney fibrosis, and liver fibrosis. In some
embodiments, the related and/or other fibrotic and/or inflammatory disease and condition is
Hidradenitis Suppurativa. Systemic sclerosis is classified into two subsets based on the
extent of skin involvement – limited systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) and diffuse systemic sclerosis
(dsSSc). Patients with fibrosis of the skin affecting acral parts of the body – face and limbs
15 (distal to the knees and elbows) – are classified as having lcSSc, whereas those with fibrosis
of the trunk and proximal parts of the limbs are classified as having dsSSc. Although lcSSc
has slow progression of skin fibrosis and Raynaud’s phenomenon starts long before the skin
symptoms, it is not limited to skin involvement and is also associated with the involvement of
the esophagus and lungs. However, late and slow organ involvement in lcSSc is associated
20 with relatively good prognosis with 10-year survival over 90%. Patients with dsSSc have
poorer prognosis because of fast progression of skin and organ involvement including
cardiovascular system, lungs, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract and even central and peripheral
nervous system. In dsSSc there is typically a shorter time period between the onset of
Raynaud’s phenomenon and skin symptoms. The overall 10-year survival rate in dsSSc
25 ranges from 65 to 82%, which is a result of the wide range of systemic complications. The
most life-threatening of them affect the heart, lungs and kidneys.
Gastrointestinal tract (GIT) involvement is common (90%) in patients with SSc,
affecting all parts of the GIT. Within the oral cavity the most frequent complications of SSc
are microstomia and xerostomia. The latter can be an effect of a concomitant Sjögren’s
30 syndrome. The esophagus is the most frequently involved organ of GIT in SSc – almost 67%
of patients complaint of one or more symptoms: dysphagia, odynophagia, regurgitation,
pyrosis, chronic cough or hoarseness. They are a result of structural and functional
alterations of the esophagus, such as amyotonia contributing to dilation of the lumen,
17
dysfunction of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and hiatal hernia – which lead to the
increased incidence of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in SSc. Additionally, reduced
LES pressure may lead to chronic reflux changes such as strictures and Barrett’s esophagus.
The predominant alteration of the stomach in SSc is gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE).

EXAMPLES
5 Methods
Human sample acquisition
22 systemic sclerosis patients and 18 healthy donors were recruited for single cell
RNA sequencing, and additional 4 systemic sclerosis patients were recruited for spatial
sequencing. Skin biopsies were taken from the affected forearm of patients. The study was
10 approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board (IRB), and all patients
gave written consent. The study was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki
Principles.
Single-cell RNA-seq library preparation, sequencing, and alignment
Generation of single-cell suspensions for scRNA-seq was performed as follows: Skin
15 biopsies were incubated overnight in 0.4% dispase (Life Technologies) in Hank’s Balanced
Saline Solution (Gibco) at 4°C. Epidermis and dermis were separated. Epidermis was
digested in 0.25% Trypsin-EDTA (Gibco) with 10U/mL DNase I (Thermo Scientific) for 1
hour at 37°C, quenched with FBS (Atlanta Biologicals), and strained through a 70μM mesh.
Dermis was minced, digested in 0.2% Collagenase II (Life Technologies) and 0.2%
20 Collagenase V (Sigma) in plain medium for 1.5 hours at 37°C and strained through a 70μM
mesh. For the samples collected from the University of Pittsburgh, epidermal and dermal
cells were combined in 1:1 ratio. For three of the samples collected from the University of
Michigan, the epidermal and dermal cells were prepared in different libraries that were
constructed by the University of Michigan Advanced Genomics Core on the 10X Chromium
25 system with chemistry v3. For the remaining samples the epidermis and dermis were
combined in 1:1 ratio. Libraries were then sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000
sequencer to generate 150 bp paired-end reads. Data processing including quality control,
read alignment (hg38), and gene quantification was conducted using the 10X Cell Ranger
software. The samples were then merged into a single expression matrix using the cellranger
30 aggr pipeline.
23
Cell clustering and cell type annotation
The R package Seurat (v3.1.2) was used to cluster the cells in the merged matrix.
Cells with less than 500 transcripts or 100 genes or more than 1e5 transcripts or 15% of
mitochondrial expression were first filtered out as low-quality cells. The NormalizeData
5 function was used to normalize the expression level for each cell with default parameters.
The FindVariableFeatures function was used to select variable genes with default parameters.
The ScaleData function was used to scale and center the counts in the dataset. Principal
component analysis (PCA) was performed on the variable genes. The RunHarmony function
from the Harmony package was applied to remove potential batch effect among samples
10 processed in different batches. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)
dimensional reduction was performed using the RunUMAP function. The clusters were
obtained using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions with the resolution set to 0.6.
The cluster marker genes were found using the FindAllMarkers function. The cell types were
annotated by overlapping the cluster markers with the canonical cell type signature genes. To
15 calculate the disease composition based on cell type, the number of cells for each cell type
from each disease condition were counted. The counts were then divided by the total number
of cells for each disease condition and scaled to 100 percent for each cell type. Differential
expression analysis between any two groups of cells were carried out using the FindMarkers
function.
20 Cell type sub-clustering
Sub-clustering was performed on the abundant cell types. The same functions
described above were used to obtain the sub-clusters. Sub-clusters that were defined
exclusively by mitochondrial gene expression, indicating low quality, were removed from
further analysis. The subtypes were annotated by overlapping the marker genes for the sub25 clusters with the canonical subtype signature genes. The module scores were calculated using
the AddModuleScore function on the intended gene lists. The ECM score was calculated on
the genes from the extracellular matrix pathway from the Gene Ontology database. The TGFβ and IL-4 score for fibroblast subtypes were calculated on induced genes in fibroblasts after
stimulation with TGF-β or IL-4 (89). The module scores for the upstream regulators were
30 calculated on the target gene lists from the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software.
Ligand receptor interaction analysis
24
CellphoneDB (v2.0.0) was applied for ligand-receptor analysis. Each subtype was
separated by their disease classifications (SSc or NS), and a separate run was performed for
each disease classification. If a subtype contains fewer than 10 cells for a disease
classification, it was not considered in the ligand-receptor analysis for this disease
5 classification. Pairs with p value > 0.05 were filtered out from further analysis. To compare
between the two disease conditions, each pair was assigned to the condition in which it
showed the higher interaction score. The number of interactions between each subtype pair
was then calculated. The connectome web was plotted using the R package igraph.
Pseudotime trajectory construction
10 Pseudotime trajectories for the fibroblast and endothelial transitions were constructed
using the R package Monocle (v2.22.0). The raw counts for cells were extracted from the
Seurat analysis and normalized by the estimateSizeFactors and estimateDispersions functions
with the default parameters. Genes detected in >10 cells were retained for further analysis.
Variable genes were determined by the differentialGeneTest function with a model against
15 the group identities for the fibroblast transition and the Seurat sub-cluster identities for the
endothelial transition. The orders of the cells were determined by the orderCells function, and
the trajectory was constructed by the reduceDimension function with default parameters.
Differential expression analysis was carried out using the differentialGeneTest function with
a model against the pseudotime, and genes with an adjusted p value smaller than 0.05 were
20 clustered into five patterns and plotted in the heatmap. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis was used
to determine the upstream regulators for the genes in each expression pattern. A module score
was calculated for each upstream regulator on the target genes from all five patterns. The
module scores were calculated using the Seurat function AddModuleScore with default
parameters. Pearson correlation was then performed between the upstream regulator module
25 scores and the pseudotime.
Spatial sequencing library preparation
Skin samples were frozen in OCT medium and stored at -80°C until sectioning.
Optimization of tissue permeabilization was performed on 20 μm sections using Visium
Spatial Tissue Optimization Reagents Kit (10X Genomics, Pleasanton, CA, USA), which
30 established an optimal permeabilization time to be 9 minutes. Samples were mounted onto a
Gene Expression slide (10X Genomics), fixed in ice-cold methanol, stained with hematoxylin
and eosin, and scanned under a microscope (Keyence, Itasca, IL, USA). Tissue
25
permeabilization was performed to release the poly-A mRNA for capture by the poly(dT)
primers that are precoated on the slide and include an Illumina TruSeq Read, spatial barcode,
and unique molecular identifier (UMI). Visium Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kit (10X
Genomics) was used for reverse transcription to produce spatially barcoded full-length cDNA
5 and for second strand synthesis followed by denaturation to allow a transfer of the cDNA
from the slide into a tube for amplification and library construction. Visium Spatial Single
Cell 3ʹ Gene Expression libraries consisting of Illumina paired-end sequences flanked with
P5/P7 were constructed after enzymatic fragmentation, size selection, end repair, A-tailing,
adaptor ligation, and PCR. Dual Index Kit TT Set A (10X Genomics) was used to add unique
10 i7 and i5 sample indexes and generate TruSeq Read 1 for sequencing the spatial barcode and
UMI and TruSeq Read 2 for sequencing the cDNA insert, respectively. Libraries were then
sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 sequencer to generate 150 bp paired end reads.
Spatial sequencing data analysis
After sequencing, the reads were aligned to the human genome (hg38), and the
15 expression matrix was extracted using the spaceranger pipeline. Seurat was then used to
analyze the expression matrix. Specifically, the SCTransform function was used to scale the
data and find variable genes with default parameters. PCA and UMAP were applied for
dimensional reduction. The FindTransferAnchors function was used to find a set of anchors
between the spatial-seq data and scRNA-seq data, which were then transferred from the
20 scRNA-seq to the spatial-seq data using the TransferData function. These two functions
construct a weight matrix that defines the association between each query cell and each
anchor. These weights sum to 1 for each spot and were used as the percentage of the cell type
in the spot.
Immunofluorescence and Immunohistochemistry staining
25 Formalin-fixed embedded human tissues were sectioned and heated at 65 ºC for 30
minutes, deparaffinized, and rehydrated. Slides were placed in pH 6 or pH 9 antigen retrieval
buffer according to manufacture structure and heated at 125 ºC for 30 seconds in a pressure
cooker water bath. After cooling, slides were blocked and incubated with primary rabbit and

Statistical analysis for in vitro experiments
For the in vitro experiments, normality test was first conducted to determine whether
the data is normally distributed or skewed. To determine the differences between groups,
unpaired t test, Mann–Whitney U test, one-way ANOVA with Sidak test, Kruskal–Wallis test

Results
10 scRNA-seq and spatial-seq reveal diverse cell types and their spatial locations in
SSc skin
To understand the unbiased cellular composition and cell states of healthy normal skin
(NS) and systemic sclerosis (SSc) skin, we generated single cell suspensions of skin biopsies
from 18 NS donors and 22 SSc patients and performed scRNA-seq. The resulting quality15 controlled SSc plus NS single cell atlas contained a total of 96,174 cells, with an average of
2,258 genes and 9,263 transcripts detected per cell. The cells were clustered based on
differential expression of marker genes and visualized on a uniform manifold approximation
and projection (UMAP) plot. Cluster annotation was corroborated by overlapping the cluster
markers with the canonical lineage-specific genes reported in previous skin disease scRNA20 seq studies (10,30,43-45). We recovered 12 major cell types across all the samples (FIG. 1ad), including keratinocytes, melanocytes, eccrine gland cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts,
pericytes, smooth muscle cells, nerve cells, T cells, myeloid cells, mast cells, and B cells.
Most of these cell types contained cells from both NS and SSc samples (FIG. 1b, c). Notably,
two small populations, smooth muscle cells, and B cells, were primarily derived from the SSc
25 samples (FIG. 1c). Interestingly, clear separations were observed in keratinocytes, fibroblasts,
pericytes, and endothelial cells between the NS and SSc cells, suggesting fundamental
transcriptional differences between them (FIG. 1b). By contrast, the other cell types displayed
overlapping patterns for the NS and SSc cells.
To localize the major cell types detected by scRNA-seq in SSc skin, we performed
30 spatial sequencing (spatial-seq) on four independent SSc skin samples using the 10X Visium
platform. After the quality control steps, we detected 951 spatially defined spots with an
29
average of 805 genes and 1,647 transcripts per spot (FIG. 7a). We deconvoluted the spatial
spots by the major cell types detected in scRNA-seq using the Seurat anchor-based label
transfer method (Methods). The deconvolution scores for each cell type were displayed on
the tissue (FIG. 1e) and combined into a scatter-pie plot representing the relative cell type
5 composition for each spot (FIG. 7a). As expected, keratinocytes localized to the epidermis
and the hair follicle. Melanocytes were enriched along the basal epidermis. Myeloid cells and
T cells were primarily located in the superficial dermis in proximity to the epidermis and the
hair follicle. B cells were aggregated adjacent to the hair follicle. Strikingly, fibroblasts,
pericytes, and endothelial cells were distributed throughout a large proportion of the spots in
10 the dermis, covering the regions of fibrosis. The other cell types represent small populations
and were lowly detected in the spatial-seq sample. Spatial-seq of three additional SSc skin
biopsy specimens analyzed in parallel revealed similar results (FIG. 7b-d).
Hippo pathway effectors promote and maintain myofibroblast differentiation in
SSc skin
15 Due to their capacity to produce large amounts of pro-fibrotic extracellular matrix
(ECM) components, myofibroblasts have long been regarded as central to the fibrotic
response in SSc. A recent scRNA-seq study proposed SFRP2hi fibroblasts as the potential
progenitors of myofibroblasts in SSc skin (10). To understand the heterogeneity of the
fibroblasts and the myofibroblast differentiation process in SSc skin, we selected all the
20 fibroblasts from our scRNA-seq dataset and performed sub-clustering (FIG. 8a). Based on
previously published marker genes (10,47-49), we annotated the fibroblast sub-clusters into
seven subtypes including SFRP2+ fibroblasts (FB), COL8A1+ FB, CCL19+ FB, FMO1+ FB,
FMO2+ FB, TNN+ FB, and CLDN1+ FB (FIG. 2a, e). The COL8A1+ FB expressed high
levels of ACTA2, SFRP4, POSTN, and PRSS23, representing myofibroblasts in our dataset
25 (10). Strikingly, the COL8A1+ FBs, which were derived exclusively from the SSc samples,
were contiguous with the SFRP2+ FB on the UMAP (FIG. 2b, c). Notably, the NS and SSc
SFRP2+ FB were largely distinct on the UMAP, suggesting fundamental transcriptional
differences between these two cell populations. Furthermore, only the SSc SFRP2+ FB, not
the NS ones, connected to the COL8A1+ FB (FIG. 2a, b), suggesting that only in SSc did
30 SFRP2+ FB have the potential of directly differentiate into myofibroblasts. To illustrate the
capacity for ECM production by the different fibroblast subtypes, we calculated an ECM
module score using the gene list from the extracellular matrix pathway from Gene Ontology
(FIG. 2d) and plotted all the collagen genes across the subtypes (FIG. 8b). The COL8A1+ FB
30
had the highest ECM score and highest expression pattern of the collagen genes, including
COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL5A1, COL5A2, COL6A3, COL8A1, COL8A2,
COL10A1, and COL12A1. The SFRP2+ FB ranked the second highest for the ECM score
and collagen gene expression. To corroborate the spatial locations of the fibroblasts, we next
5 plotted the expression of COL1A1 and the ECM score across the four spatial-seq samples and
found them highly correlated with the fibroblast deconvolution scores (FIG. 1e, 2f, 7a-d). We
then deconvoluted the fibroblast-rich spots (with fibroblast deconvolution score > 0.25) using
the fibroblast subtypes (FIG. 2f, 8c). The SFRP2+ FB were primarily located in the
superficial dermis, while the COL8A1+ FB were localized to the deeper dermis. We did not
10 detect COL8A1+ FB in the third and fourth spatial-seq samples, likely due to sample
heterogeneity and that we did not cut deep enough in these two tissue sections.
Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence of SMA (encoded by ACTA2) validated the
location of myofibroblasts in the deeper dermis of SSc skin (FIG. 2g, h), overlapping with
areas of intense fibrosis. Interestingly, SMA from the upper dermis of the SSc skin tissue was
15 observed mainly in and around the blood vessels (FIG. 2g, h), suggesting endothelial to
mesenchymal transition (EndoMT) in SSc skin.
To better characterize the differentiation process from SFRP2+ FB to COL8A1+ FB,
we focused on these two subtypes and split them into three groups based on the fibroblast
sub-clusters (FIG. 3a, 8a). Group 1 and 2 were mainly composed of NS SFRP2+ FB and SSc
20 SFRP2+ FB, respectively, and group 3 was composed of COL8A1+ FB (FIG. 3b). The
expression of myofibroblast marker genes ACTA2, TAGLN, and COL8A1 and the ECM
score increased from group 1 to 2 to 3 (FIG. 3c, e). We calculated module scores using genes
induced in cultured fibroblasts stimulated by two pro-fibrotic cytokines, TGF-β or IL-4, and
found that these two module scores escalated from group 1 to 2 to 3 (FIG. 3e, Methods).
25 Interestingly, the expression of two Hippo pathway target genes, CTGF and CYR61,
displayed increasing trends from group 1 to 2 to 3 (FIG. 3f), suggesting involvement of the
Hippo pathway in myofibroblast differentiation in SSc skin. Furthermore, CytoTRACE
analysis (50) suggested that group 1 represented less differentiated cells and group 3
represented the most differentiated cells (FIG. 3d). Based on these observations, we
30 performed pseudotime analysis on the three groups using Monocle and arranged the cells into
a linear trajectory from group 1 to 2 to 3 (FIG. 3g, h). To identify the potential cytokines and
transcription factors that drive the myofibroblast differentiation, we split the variable genes
along the pseudotime into five expression patterns (FIG. 9a). We then inferred the upstream
31
regulators for genes in each pattern using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. For each upstream
regulator, we calculated a module score using all target genes gathered from the five
expression patterns (Methods). Consistent with the cytokine stimulation experiment, both
TGF-β1 and IL-4 target scores were highly correlated with the pseudotime (FIG. 3i).
5 Previously reported transcription factors, STAT1, IRF7, RUNX1 and SMAD3, that promote
the differentiation from SFRP2hi fibroblast to myofibroblasts (10), displayed a module score
positively correlated with the pseudotime (FIG. 3i). The module scores for WWTR1 (TAZ)
and TEAD1 were also highly correlated with the pseudotime, suggesting a contribution of the
Hippo pathway in the differentiation from the SFRP2+ FB to the COL8A1+ FB. Indeed,
10 multiple key molecules involved in Hippo pathway, including WWTR1, CTGF, CYR61,
TEAD1, TEAD2, TEAD3, TEAD4, and VGLL3, were highly expressed in group 3 compared
to groups 1 and 2 (FIG. 9b).
To determine the functional relevance of the Hippo pathway in SSc fibroblasts, we
used primary dermal fibroblasts isolated from patients with early diffuse cutaneous (dc)SSc.
15 Two inhibitors relevant to the Hippo pathway were used; TRULI, a LATS1/2 (large tumor
suppressor kinase 1 and 2) inhibitor that decreases phosphorylation of YAP to promote its
entry into the nucleus (51), and verteporfin, an inhibitor of YAP-TEAD interaction (52). In
all assays, the two inhibitors showed opposite effects. TRULI treatment led to a significant
increase in pro-fibrotic markers in dcSSc fibroblasts including ACTA2 and COL1A1 (FIG.
20 3j), and we validated this for SMA with western blotting, but the increase in COL1A1 did not
reach significance (FIG. 3k). Further, these findings were validated by immunofluorescent
staining with increased expression of SMA but only slight to moderate increase in COL1A1
expression (FIG. 3l). Specifically for verteporfin, we found that its treatment in dcSSc
fibroblasts downregulated both SMA and COL1 to levels comparable to what was observed
25 in healthy fibroblasts at baseline (FIG. 9c, d). Since myofibroblasts exhibit higher
contractility, increased proliferation, and migration capacities, we also measured these as
functional endpoints. We found that TRULI enhanced gel contraction, proliferation, and
migration in dcSSc fibroblasts (FIG. 3m-o), suggesting that TRULI promotes a pro-fibrotic
phenotype in these cells. In contrast, verteporfin downregulated SMA and COL1 in dcSSc
30 fibroblasts at both mRNA levels and protein levels (FIG. 3j-l). Verteporfin also inhibited gel
contraction, proliferation, and migration in a dose-dependent manner (FIG. 3m-o). We also
determined the impact of these inhibitors in healthy dermal fibroblasts. Verteporfin did not
appear to have any effect on fibrotic gene expressions, proliferation, and migration in healthy
32
fibroblasts, while TRULI upregulated SMA, though to a lesser extent compared to dcSSc
fibroblasts, it did not affect proliferation or migration in healthy fibroblasts (FIG. 9e, f). To
further delineate the roles of key mediators in the Hippo pathway in SSc fibroblasts, we
knocked down YAP1, TEAD1, TEAD3, VGLL3, or TEAD1/TEAD3 simultaneously in these
5 cells (FIG. 3p) and measured ACTA2 and COL1A1 levels. Similar to what was observed
with verteporfin treatment, knockdown of these key mediators resulted in downregulation of
ACTA2 and COL1A1 (FIG. 3q). Altogether, these results point to a role for Hippo pathway
effectors in promoting and maintaining the pro-fibrotic signal in dcSSc fibroblasts.
Hippo pathway effectors promote and maintain endothelial to mesenchymal
10 transition in SSc skin
To characterize the heterogeneity of endothelial cells, we sub-clustered all the
endothelial cells from the scRNA-seq dataset and obtained seven sub-clusters (FIG. 4a-c).
Sub-cluster 6 represented the lymphatic endothelial cells with high expression of LYVE1 and
MMRN1 (FIG. 4c). Sub-clusters 3, 4, and 5 represented the activated endothelial cells with
15 high expression of SELP and SELE (FIG. 10a). Interestingly, sub-clusters 0, 1, and 2,
expressed GJA4, a marker of arteriolar endothelial cells 53, and were aligned contiguously on
the UMAP, suggesting a potential transition among these sub-clusters. Close examination of
lineage marker genes in the three sub-clusters reinforced this transition hypothesis:
expression of endothelial cell markers PECAM1 and CDH5, as well as Notch signaling genes
20 NOTCH1, JAG2, and DLL4, decreased, while mesenchymal cell markers COL1A1, ACTA2,
and TAGLN increased from sub-cluster 0 to 1 to 2 (FIG. 4d). Immunofluorescence confirmed
co-expression of SMA and CD31 (encoded by PECAM1) in SSc but not NS skin (FIG. 4g).
Sub-cluster 2 also had the highest ECM score (FIG. 4e) and expressed the highest level of
collagen genes among all the endothelial sub-clusters (FIG. 10b). The disease composition
25 revealed increasing proportions of SSc endothelial cells from sub-cluster 0 to 1 to 2 (FIG.
10c). Furthermore, the CytoTRACE score indicated that the cells in sub-cluster 2 were more
differentiated compared to the cells in subcluster 0 and 1 (FIG. 4f). Taken together, the above
evidence suggests EndoMT occurs during progression from sub-cluster 0 to 1 to 2.
To better characterize the EndoMT progression at the single cell level, we performed
30 pseudotime analysis on these three sub-clusters using Monocle and aligned them into a linear
trajectory (FIG. 4h). The pseudotime was assigned from early to late from sub-cluster 0 to 1
to 2. In parallel to the fibroblast trajectory analysis, we calculated the correlation coefficient
33
between the target score for different upstream regulators and the pseudotime in the
endothelial trajectory analysis (FIG. 10d). We focused on the key upstream regulators that
promote the SFRP2+ FB to the COL8A1+ FB transition and plotted the correlation
coefficients in both fibroblast and endothelial trajectory analyses (FIG. 4i). TGF-β
5 transcription factors displayed positive correlation in both the fibroblast and the endothelial
transitions. Intriguingly, TEAD transcription factors were also highly correlated with both
transitions, suggesting that Hippo pathway effectors promote both myofibroblast transition
and EndoMT. Accordingly, key molecules involved in Hippo pathway, including YAP1,
WWTR1, CTGF, CYR61, TEAD1, TEAD2, TEAD3, TEAD4, and VGLL3, were all
10 expressed in higher percentage of cells in sub-cluster 2 compared to sub-clusters 0 and 1
(FIG. 4k). By contrast, the target scores of HIF1A, STAT1, IRF7, and RUNX1 were only
positively correlated with the fibroblast pseudotime but not the endothelial pseudotime (FIG.
4i). We validated the expression of TEAD1 and TEAD3 by immunofluorescence and
demonstrated their colocalization with CD31 in SSc but not NS samples (FIG. 4j). Given the
15 similarity between fibroblast transition and endothelial transition, we sought to determine the
common programs that were upregulated in both processes. To do so, we overlapped the upregulated genes in group 3 compared to group 1 and 2 in the fibroblast transition and those in
sub-cluster 2 compared to sub-cluster 0 and 1 in the endothelial transition. Enrichment
analysis on the 240 common up-regulated genes implicated the extracellular matrix
20 organization as the most prominent program commonly induced in both transitions (FIG. 4l).
We next determined whether the Hippo pathway is functionally involved in EndoMT
in endothelial cells isolated from dcSSc skin. TRULI increased ACTA2 and COL1A1
expression in dcSSc endothelial cells while verteporfin downregulated these genes (FIG. 5a).
Interestingly, TRULI had inconsistent effects on endothelial markers PECAM1 and CDH5,
25 while verteporfin blocked the expression of both at the mRNA levels. The effect of these
inhibitors on dcSSc endothelial cells were further validated using Western blotting (FIG. 5b).
The expression levels in SSc ECs treated with verteporfin appeared to be comparable to the
expression levels in ECs isolated from healthy controls. Of note, we were unable to detect
COL1 expression in healthy ECs. By immunofluorescent staining we showed that TRULI
30 enhanced EndoMT as shown by cell morphology and loss of endothelial marker VWF. In
contrast, verteporfin reversed EndoMT by downregulating SMA expression in dcSSc
endothelial cells (FIG. 5c). We also determined the effects of these inhibitors on ECs isolated
from healthy subjects. It appears that TRULI induced EndoMT by downregulating VWF,
34
upregulating SMA, and also induced morphological changes, while verteporfin appeared to
increase VWF (FIG. 5c). The discrepancy of the effect of the inhibitors on EC markers in
FIG. 5a-c could be due to posttranscriptional or translational modifications, or differences in
protein and RNA degradation rates. To further dissect the roles of YAP1, TEAD3, or VGLL3
5 in mediating EndoMT in dcSSc endothelial cells, we knocked these genes down individually
(FIG. 5d) and measured EndoMT markers. Knockdown of YAP1, TEAD3, or VGLL3,
resulted in lower ACTA2 and COL1A1 levels, similar to what was observed with verteporfin
treatment (FIG. 5e). TEAD3 and VGLL3 knock-down appeared to promote endothelial
markers PECAM1 and CDH5, while YAP1 knock-down had minimal effect.
10 Myofibroblasts and EndoMTs act as central hubs in cell-cell communications
To comprehensively study the cell type composition and cell-cell communications in
SSc skin, we sub-clustered the other cell types in the scRNA-seq dataset. We identified four
subtypes of keratinocytes: basal, spinous, supraspinous, and inflammatory keratinocyte (FIG.
11a). The T cells were sub-clustered and annotated into five subtypes: CD4 T cell (CD4T),
15 regulatory T cell (Treg), CD8 T cell (CD8T), nature killer cell (NK cell), and innate
lymphoid cell (ILC) (FIG. 11b). For myeloid cells, we annotated six subtypes, including
Langerhans cell (LC), conventional type 1 DC-like cell (cDC1), conventional type 2A DClike cell (cDC2A), conventional type 2B DC-like cell (cDC2B), monocyte (Mono), and
macrophage (Mac) (FIG. 11c). We sub-clustered the pericytes and smooth muscle cells
20 together due to their transcriptional similarities. We obtained four pericyte sub-clusters and
two smooth muscle cell sub-clusters (FIG. 11d). For the other cell types, we obtained five
eccrine gland cell sub-clusters, six melanocyte sub-clusters, four nerve cell sub-clusters, five
mast cell sub-clusters, and three B cell sub-clusters (FIG. 12a-e).
We then performed separate ligand-receptor analyses on the SSc and NS cellular
25 subtypes using CellPhoneDB (Methods). To assess the changes that occur in SSc, we
analyzed ligand-receptor pairs from the subtypes that had higher interaction scores in SSc
compared to NS. By aggregating the total number of interactions for each cell type, we
observed the largest ligand-receptor pair number changes in endothelial cells and fibroblasts
(FIG. 6a). Connectome web analysis revealed endothelial sub-cluster 2 (EC2, EndoMTs) and
30 the COL8A1+ FB (myofibroblasts) as the central communication hubs. Of note, EC2 and
COL8A1+ FBs had the greatest number of self-interactions (FIG. 13a), many of which
overlapped between EC2 and COL8A1+ FB cells as these two subtypes share fibrotic
35
features. Thus, these overlapping self-interactions account for some of the interactions
highlighted between the two groups. Taken together, these data suggest dynamic interaction
between these two key subtypes and other skin cell subtypes during the EndoMT and
fibroblast to myofibroblast transition (FIG. 6c). Of note, several other endothelial and
5 fibroblast subtypes were also relatively more active, including EC0, EC1, EC3, EC4,
SFRP2+ FB, FMO1+ FB, and CCL19+ FB, which mainly interacted with the two hubs. By
contrast, fewer ligand-receptor interactions were higher in NS compared to SSc, with the
majority of these representing keratinocyte-keratinocyte crosstalk (FIG. 13b, c). To this end,
we focused on the interactions within the SSc endothelial cells and fibroblasts. To emphasize
10 the roles of the two hubs, we selected the pairs from which the ligands were subtype-specific
marker genes for either EC2 or COL8A1+ FB, which uncovered various validated and
uncharacterized signaling pathways implicated in fibrosis (FIG. 6c). Fibroblast growth factors
(FGF2, FGF7, and FGF18) (54), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGFA and PDGFC)
(55,56), transforming growth factor beta (TGFB1 and TGFB3), and vascular endothelial
15 growth factor (VEGFA and VEGFB) (57) were known to be involved in fibrosis. WNT2 and
WNT4 were specifically expressed by the COL8A1+ FB and have been reported to promote
cardiac fibrosis by activating NF-κB signaling 58. IL6 and IL11 served as pro-fibrotic
cytokines; both have been reported to be elevated in SSc and proposed as therapeutic targets
for SSc (59,60). Notably, our analysis revealed several other pro-inflammatory mediators,
20 including CCL2, CCL8, CCL11, TNFSF4, TNFSF9, and TNFSF12, that were highly
expressed by EC2 or the COL8A1+ FB. Together, these data illustrate pro-fibrotic shifts
within the interactome in SSc and reinforce the essential roles of EC2 and the COL8A1+ FB
in SSc skin fibrosis.
Ex Vivo Testing
25 Ex vivo testing was conducted with results shown in FIG. 15. Distinct steps of the
Hippo pathway were tested using Verteporfin that was applied to SSc skin biopsies ex vivo
(n=3 patients per treatment group). TRULI and MGH-CP1 were also tested. Biopsies from
the same patients were treated in parallel with DMSO to be used as a patient-specific vehicle
control. Molecular changes in affected cell populations were assessed by extensive scRNA30 Seq analyses.
It was found that Verteporfin selectively depleted myofibroblasts and endothelialmesenchymal transition cells (EndoMTs) – the stromal cells pathologically activated in SSc.
36
It also reduced expression of inflammatory, pro-fibrotic, and endothelial activation markers.
Moreover, cell-cell interactions that sustain disease signaling were markedly hindered by
Verteporfin. There was a striking overlap between the genes downregulated by Verteporfin
and those upregulated in SSc versus healthy patients across cell populations. Thus, targeting
5 Hippo pathway by Verteporfin effectively reversed molecular hallmarks of SSc. The data
further demonstrate the utility of this approach for modeling drug targeting ex vivo.
FIG. 15A shows the processing steps. Cells were obtained from a scleroderma skin
sample and placed in suspension ex vivo. Cells were treated with Verteporfin or a control
(DMSO). Cells were captured and barcoded and a sequencing library was prepared and
10 sequenced. FIG. 15B shows identified cell populations in both vehicle and treatment
samples. FIG. 15C and D shows shifts in cell populations, including disappearance of
myofibroblasts with verteporfin treatment (C and D). FIG. 15E shows collapse in pathogenic
cell-cell interactions in scleroderma with verteporfin treatment. FIG. 15F shows that
Verteporfin selectively targeted myofibroblast differentiation with no effect on cell death.

CLAIMS
We claim:
1. A method comprising: treating a subject having systemic sclerosis (SSc) or a
fibrotic disease or condition with a Hippo pathway effector under conditions that reduce or
prevent fibrosis.
2. The method of claim 1, wherein the Hippo pathway effector is a TEAD
inhibitor.
3. The method of claim 2, wherein the TEAD inhibitor is a protein-protein
interaction disruptor of TEAD/YAP.
4. The method of claim 2, wherein the TEAD inhibitor prevents YAP
translocation to the nucleus to activate TEAD.
5. The method of claim 2, wherein the TEAD inhibitor is Verteporfin.
6. The method of claim 1, wherein Hippo pathway effector regulates an
association between VGLL3 and TEAD.
7. The method of claim 1, further comprising the step of assessing efficacy of the
Hippo pathway effector in reducing or preventing fibrosis.
8. The method of claim 6, wherein said assessing comprises evaluating a sign or
symptom of SSc.
9. The method of claim 6, wherein said assessing comprises evaluating a cellular
or molecular biomarker.
10. The method of claim 9, wherein said biomarker comprises profibrotic
phenotype or reversal of profibrotic phenotype of myofibroblasts.
11. The method of claim 9, wherein said biomarker comprises profibrotic
phenotype or reversal of profibrotic phenotype of endothelial to mesenchymal transitioning
cells (EndoMTs).
12. The method of claim 1, wherein said treating comprises systemic delivery of
the Hippo pathway effector to the subject.
45
13. The method of claim 12, wherein said systemic delivery comprises injection,
oral, or transdermal delivery.
14. The method of claim 13, wherein said injection comprises intravenous,
subcutaneous, or intraperitoneal administration.
15. The method of claim 1, wherein said treating further comprises coadministering an agent or conducting a procedure that controls symptoms and/or prevents one
or more complications of SSc.
16. The method of claim 15, wherein the symptoms comprise one or more
Raynaud syndrome, polyarthralgia, dysphagia, heartburn, skin swelling, skin tightening, and
contractures of fingers.
17. The method of claim 15, wherein said complications comprise one or more of
interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and scleroderma renal crisis.
18. An ex vivo method of determining effect of a therapeutic agent, comprising:
a) obtaining a tissue sample from a subject, b) contacting said tissue sample with an agent ex
vivo to produce treated cells, c) isolating treating cells to generated isolated cells, d)
preparing a nucleic acid sequencing library from said isolated cells; e) sequencing the
sequencing library to generate sequencing data, and f) analyzing the sequencing data to
determine an effect of said agent on said tissue.
19. The method of claim 18, wherein said analyzing comprises comparing
sequencing data to data obtained from a control sample not contacted with the agent.
20. The method of claim 18, wherein the analyzing comprises determining an
effect of said agent on two or more different cell types found in said tissue sample.
21. The method of claim 18, wherein said analyzing comprises determining cell
differentiation status of one or more cell types found in said tissue sample.
22. The method of claim 19, wherein said analyzing comprises generating a report
that identifies shifts in cell populations between treated cells and control cells.
23. The method of claim 18, wherein said analyzing comprises identifying a
change in pathogenic cell-cell interactions in response to treatment with said agent.
46

COMPOSITIONS AND METHODS FOR THE TREATMENT OF SYSTEMIC
SCLEROSIS AND OTHER FIBROTIC DISEASES AND CONDITIONS
Provided herein are compositions and methods for the treatment of systemic sclerosis
and related diseases and conditions. In particular, provided herein are Hippo pathway
effectors and their uses in the treatment of systemic sclerosis and related and other fibrotic
diseases and conditions.

title: METHOD FOR CONTROLLING A MATERIAL FEED, AND METERING SYSTEM
abstract: The method is suitable for controlling or regulating a material feed for filling a first container with a material from a second container. In the method, a rate of change of a fill level of the first container is determined. If the rate of change is positive, the material feed is reduced and, if the rate of change is negative, the material feed is increased. The rate of change is determined by means of a capacitive sensor.
