[039] The process described herein comprises at least two sets of steps, i.e. a first set comprising
steps a’), b’) and c’) and at least a second set comprising steps a’’), b’’) and c’’). The process described
herein is thus a continuous process meaning that the second set of steps is carried out directly after the
25 first set (in other words, the step a’’) of the second set is carried out subsequently and directly after step
c’) of the first set while the substrate carrying the first coating layer (x20’) is not removed from the printing
machine, i.e. is continuously fed, to carry out the second set of steps. In other words, the multi-sets of
steps process described herein is a continuous process using a single machine, said machine allowing
the application, preferably printing, of coating composition, the exposure of said compositions to
30 magnetic fields and the at least partial curing of said compositions. An example of such a single machine
allowing the multi-sets of steps described herein is disclosed in US 2021/0316545, said machine
comprising in the following order: at least a first printing unit, a first orientation unit, a first curing unit, a
second printing unit to downstream apply compositions, a second orientation unit and a second curing
unit. As mentioned therein, the process described herein allows the preparation of OELs comprising the
35 first motif and the second motif described herein, said OELs exhibiting a continuous effect as observed
by the naked eye at one first viewing angle (as obtained by the use of magnetic fields being symmetric
with respect to a mirror plane which is parallel to the substrate (x10)), and said effect originating from
the first and second magnetic patterns and consisting of a continuous image extending continuously
from the first motif to the second motif, wherein said effect splits upon tilting and recombines to form the
40 same continuous image upon tilting to come back to the first viewing angle; this highly dynamic effect
12
results from the perfect register of not only the applied first and second motifs but also originated from
the first and second magnetic patterns.
[040] The OEL is seen by an observer at a first viewing angle as a continuous image extending
continuously from one motif to the other described herein, wherein said continuous image may or may
5 not be centrally aligned in said OEL, i.e., may or may not be centrally aligned within the combination of
the first and second motifs described herein.
[041] Should the first and/or second motifs described herein independently consist of sub-first-motifs
and sub-second-motifs (as shown for example in Fig. 1), the continuous effect/image results from the
combination of a plurality or of all sub-motifs.
10 [042] Fig. 1 schematically shows the first and second magnetic pattern of an OEL produced by the
process described herein, wherein said OEL exhibits a single bar at one first viewing angle and two bars
moving in opposite direction when the OEL is tilted; wherein said effect is based on pigment particles
orientations independently imitating a curved surface across the coating layers. The OEL exhibiting two
bars moving in opposite directions upon tilting comprises the first and second motifs described herein
15 (in the form of the first cured coating layer 120’ and the cured second coating layer 120’’ on the substrate
110). Thanks to the symmetry of the first and second magnetic patterns with respect to a mirror plane
which is parallel to the substrate (110), an observer sees at viewing angles being different from the one
at which both bars appear as a single bar one as a bright bar moving in one direction upon tilting and
the other as a bright bar moving in the opposite direction upon tilting. In other words, the observer sees
20 one bright bar moving away from said observer upon tilting of the OEL and another one bright bar
moving towards said observer upon tilting of the OEL. The observation of a bar which moves away or
towards the observer upon tilting of the OEL originates from the specific magnetic orientation patterns of
the pigment particles. Two patterns are shown in Fig. 1: a magnetic orientation pattern comprising particles
oriented according to a concave fashion and following a positively curved surface is shown in Fig. 1 for
25 motif 120’ and a magnetic orientation pattern comprising particles oriented according to a convex fashion
and following a negatively curved surface is shown in Fig. 1, motif 120’’. The terms “convex fashion” or
“convex curvature” and the terms “concave fashion” or “concave curvature” refer to the apparent
curvature of the curved surface as seen by an observer (Fig. 1) viewing the OEL from the side of the
substrate (110) carrying the first coating layer (120’) (as shown by the eye in Fig. 1). The curvature of
30 the curved surface follows the magnetic field lines produced by the magnetic field-generating device at
the position where the OEL is produced. A “convex curvature” refers to a negatively curved magnetic
field line (as shown in Fig 1, motif 120’’); a “concave curvature” refers to a positively curved magnetic
field line (as shown in Fig 1, motif 120’). A convex curvature leads to a visual effect characterized by a
downward movement of the bright bar when the OEL is tilted backwards and a concave curvature (positive
35 curve orientation) leads to a visual effect characterized by a upward movement of the bright bar when the
OEL is tilted backwards.
[043] The OEL described herein comprises the first and second motifs (i.e. the first and second cured
coating layers 120’ and 120’’) on opposite sides of the substrate (110), wherein said substrate (110) is
preferably transparent, and wherein said first and second motifs are at least partially adjacent to each
40 other (i.e. the second motif is adjacent to at least a part of the first motif) and in proper register so that
13
an observer sees the OEL as a continuous feature at a first viewing angle in a see-through observation
mode or in a transparency observation mode. By “adjacent”, it means that the first and second motifs
(first coating layer (x20’) and second coating layer (x20’’) have their projections on each side of the
substrate (110) (see dotted line in Fig. 1) being contiguous (i.e. they share at least one region together
5 and have a common border). The projections of first and second motifs on each side of the substrate
(110) are at least partially adjacent (i.e. the second motif is adjacent to at least a part of the first motif)
and in proper register, preferably at least partially juxtaposed and in proper register or at least partially
interlaced and in proper register. The first and second motifs may be continuous or discontinuous.
[044] The process described herein comprises at least two independent steps a’) and a’’) consisting
10 of applying onto the first side of the substrate (x10) the first radiation curable coating composition so as
to form the first coating layer (x20’) (step a’) and consisting of applying onto the second side of the
substrate (x10) (i.e. the side of the substrate(x10) lacking the first coating layer (x20’)) and in register
the second radiation curable coating composition so as to form the second coating layer (x20’’) (step
a’’), wherein said first and second radiation curable coating compositions are in a first physical state
15 which allows their application as layers and which are in a not yet hardened (i.e. wet) state wherein the
platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles can move and rotate within the binder
material. The process described herein comprises at least two independent steps b’) and b’’) consisting
of independently exposing the first and second radiation curable coating compositions of step a’) and
step a’’) to a magnetic field so as to magnetically orient at least a part of the platelet-shaped magnetic
20 or magnetizable pigment particles and forming the first and second coating layers (and forming the first
and second motifs), the so-obtained first and second motifs having specific magnetic orientation patterns
in register, i.e. the process described herein allows to control the position the magnetic assemblies (x30’
and x30’’) during step b’) and step b’’) so that the effect/image of the OELs described herein is observed
at one first viewing angle as an image extending continuously from the first motif to the second motif
25 thus wherein said image splits upon tilting and recombines to form the same effect upon tilting to come
back to the first viewing angle thus allowing an easy authentication due to the continuity of said effect
at one viewing angle resulting from the perfect register of not only the applied first and second motifs
but also the effect originated from the first and second magnetic patterns.
[045] As mentioned therein, the first and second coating layers (x20’ and x20’’) (and the first and
30 second motifs, respectively) are at least partially adjacent to each other (i.e. the second motif is adjacent
to at least a part of the first motif) and in proper register, meaning that not only the radiation curable
coating composition is applied without or with a very limited (smaller than 1 mm, preferably smaller than
0.5 mm, more preferably smaller than or equal to 0.2 mm) misalignment and misplacement between the
second coating layer (x20’’) and the first coating layer (x20’) but also that the provided first magnetic
35 pattern and second magnetic patterns of the obtained OEL appear to the naked eye as a continuous
layer (i.e. no breakup image) at one first viewing angle. Said register is allowed by the claimed
continuous process. According to one embodiment, the first and second coating layers (x20’ and x20’’)
are within a register of ± 1 mm, preferably ± 0.5 mm and more preferably ± 0.2 mm. Said in register is
allowed by the claimed continuous process using a single machine.
40 [046] Preferably, said steps a’) and a’’) are independently carried out by a printing process, preferably
14
independently selected from the group consisting of screen printing, rotogravure printing, flexography
printing and intaglio printing (also referred in the art as engraved copper plate printing and engraved
steel die printing), more preferably selected from the group consisting of screen printing, rotogravure
printing and flexography printing and still more preferably by screen printing.
5 [047] Screen printing (also referred in the art as silkscreen printing) is a stencil process wherein an
ink is transferred to a surface through a stencil supported by a fine fabric mesh of silk, mono- or multifilaments made of synthetic fibers such as for example polyamides or polyesters or metal threads
stretched tightly on a frame made for example of wood or metal (e.g. aluminum or stainless steel).
Alternatively, the screen-printing mesh may be a chemically etched, a laser-etched, or a galvanically
10 formed porous metal foil, e.g. a stainless steel foil. The pores of the mesh are blocked in the non-image
areas and left open in the image area, the image carrier being called the screen. Screen printing might
be of the flat-bed or rotary type. Screen printing is further described for example in The Printing ink
manual, R.H. Leach and R.J. Pierce, Springer Edition, 5th Edition, pages 58-62 and in Printing
Technology, J.M. Adams and P.A. Dolin, Delmar Thomson Learning, 5th Edition, pages 293-328.
15 [048] Rotogravure (also referred in the art as gravure) is a printing process wherein the image
elements are engraved into the surface of a cylinder. The non-image areas are at a constant original
level. Prior to printing, the entire printing plate (non-printing and printing elements) is inked and flooded
with ink. Ink is removed from the non-image by a wiper or a blade before printing, so that ink remains
only in the cells. The image is transferred from the cells to the substrate by a pressure typically in the
20 range of 2 to 4 bars and by the adhesive forces between the substrate and the ink. The term rotogravure
does not encompass intaglio printing processes (also referred in the art as engraved steel die or copper
plate printing processes) which rely for example on a different type of ink. More details are provided in
“Handbook of print media”, Helmut Kipphan, Springer Edition, page 48 and in The Printing ink manual,
R.H. Leach and R.J. Pierce, Springer Edition, 5th Edition, pages 42-51.
25 [049] Flexography preferably uses a unit with a doctor blade, preferably a chambered doctor blade,
an anilox roller and plate cylinder. The anilox roller advantageously has small cells whose volume and/or
density determines the ink application rate. The doctor blade lies against the anilox roller, and scraps
off surplus ink at the same time. The anilox roller transfers the ink to the plate cylinder which finally
transfers the ink to the substrate. Specific design might be achieved using a designed photopolymer
30 plate. Plate cylinders can be made from polymeric or elastomeric materials. Polymers are mainly used
as photopolymer in plates and sometimes as a seamless coating on a sleeve. Photopolymer plates are
made from light-sensitive polymers that are hardened by ultraviolet (UV) light. Photopolymer plates are
cut to the required size and placed in an UV light exposure unit. One side of the plate is completely
exposed to UV light to harden or cure the base of the plate. The plate is then turned over, a negative of
35 the job is mounted over the uncured side and the plate is further exposed to UV light. This hardens the
plate in the image areas. The plate is then processed to remove the unhardened photopolymer from the
nonimage areas, which lowers the plate surface in these nonimage areas. After processing, the plate is
dried and given a post-exposure dose of UV light to cure the whole plate. Preparation of plate cylinders
for flexography is described in Printing Technology, J. M. Adams and P.A. Dolin, Delmar Thomson
15
Learning, 5th Edition, pages 359-360 and in The Printing ink manual, R.H. Leach and R.J. Pierce,
Springer Edition, 5th Edition, pages 33-42.
[050] The first and second radiation curable coating compositions are independently applied during
steps a’) and a’’) thus forming the first coating layer (x20’) and the second coating layer (x20’’),
5 respectively. The first and second radiation curable coating compositions independently comprise a
binder and the platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles described herein. As shown
in Figs 1, 3, 5 and 6, the first radiation curable coating composition is applied during step a’) on the first
side of the substrate (x10) thus forming the first coating layer (x20’) and the second radiation curable
coating composition is applied on the second side of the substrate (i.e. the side of the substrate lacking
10 the first coating layer (x20’) in register during step a’’) thus forming the second coating layer (x20’’).
[051] According to one embodiment, the first radiation curable coating composition exhibits a color
and the second radiation curable coating composition exhibits the same color with the naked eyes.
According to one embodiment, the first and second radiation curable coating compositions have different
binders but comprise the same platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles so that they
15 exhibit the same color with the naked eyes. According to another embodiment, the first and second
radiation curable coating compositions are the same, i.e. they comprise the same binder and comprise
the same platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles.
[052] According to one embodiment, the first radiation curable coating composition exhibits a first
color and the second radiation curable coating composition exhibits a second color, said second color
20 being different color from the first color as observed with the naked eyes. OELs comprising the first and
second motifs of different colors not only exhibit an eye catching effect due to its dynamic effect
(continuous effect observed at one first viewing angle, wherein said effect splits upon tilting and
recombines to form the same effect upon tilting to come back to the first viewing angle) but also combine
a high level of counterfeit resistance due to the sophisticated adjacent motifs of different colors.
25 [053] According to one embodiment, the first and second radiation curable coating compositions
comprise the same platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles but comprise a different
binder, the binder of the first composition comprising a dye and/or a colorant so that the compositions
exhibit a different color with the naked eyes. According to one embodiment, the first and second radiation
curable coating compositions comprise the same platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment
30 particles but comprise a different binder, the binder of the second composition comprising a dye and/or
a colorant so that the compositions exhibit a different color with the naked eyes. According to one
embodiment, the first and second radiation curable coating compositions comprise the same plateletshaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles but comprise a different binder, the binder of the
first composition comprising a dye and/or colorant and the binder of the second composition comprising
35 a dye and/or a colorant having a different color so that the compositions exhibit a different color with the
naked eyes. For optically variable platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles, i.e.
pigments exhibiting a different color upon tilting (i.e. exhibiting a face color and a different angle color),
“different colors” refer to different face colors or different angle colors or different face and angle colors.
According to one embodiment, the first radiation curable coating composition comprises optically
40 variable platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles having a first face color and a first
16
angle color and the second radiation curable coating composition comprises optically variable plateletshaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles having a second face color and a second angle
color, wherein the first face color is different from the second face color and the first angle color is
different from the second angle color. According to one embodiment, the first radiation curable coating
5 composition comprises optically variable platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles
having a first face color and a first angle color and the second radiation curable coating composition
comprises optically variable platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles having a
second face color and a second angle color, wherein the first face color is the same as the second face
color and the first angle color is different from the second angle color. According to one embodiment,
10 the first radiation curable coating composition comprises optically variable platelet-shaped magnetic or
magnetizable pigment particles having a first face color and a first angle color and the second radiation
curable coating composition comprises optically variable platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable
pigment particles having a second face color and a second angle color, wherein the first face color is
different from the second face color and the first angle color is the same as the second angle color.
15 [054] The first and second coating compositions described herein as well as the first coating layer
(x20’) and the second coating layer (x20’’) described herein comprise the platelet-shaped magnetic or
magnetizable pigment particles described herein. In contrast to needle-shaped pigment particles which
can be considered as quasi one-dimensional particles, platelet-shaped pigment particles are quasi twodimensional particles due to the large aspect ratio of their dimensions. As shown in Fig. 2, platelet20 shaped pigment particle can be considered as a two-dimensional structure wherein the dimensions X
and Y are substantially larger than the dimension Z. Platelet-shaped pigment particles are also referred
in the art as oblate particles or flakes. Such pigment particles may be described with a main axis X
corresponding to their longest dimension crossing the pigment particle and a second axis Y
perpendicular to X and corresponding to the second longest dimension crossing the pigment particle. In
25 other words, the XY plane roughly defines the plane formed by the first and second longest dimensions
of the pigment particle, the Z dimension being ignored.
[055] The platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles described herein have, due to
their non-spherical shape, non-isotropic reflectivity with respect to incident electromagnetic radiation for
which the hardened/cured binder material is at least partially transparent. As used herein, the term “non30 isotropic reflectivity” denotes that the proportion of incident radiation from a first angle that is reflected
by a particle into a certain (viewing) direction (a second angle) is a function of the orientation of the
particles, i.e. that a change of the orientation of the particle with respect to the first angle can lead to a
different magnitude of the reflection to the viewing direction.
[056] In the first and second motifs of the OELs described herein, the platelet-shaped magnetic or
35 magnetizable pigment particles described herein are dispersed in the first and second coating layer
(x20’ and x20’’), respectively, said layers comprising a hardened binder material that fixes the orientation
of the platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles. The binder material is at least in its
hardened or solid state (also referred to as second state herein), at least partially transparent to
electromagnetic radiation of a range of wavelengths comprised between 200 nm and 2500 nm, i.e. within
40 the wavelength range which is typically referred to as the “optical spectrum” and which comprises
17
infrared, visible and UV portions of the electromagnetic spectrum. Accordingly, the particles contained
in the binder material in its hardened or solid state and their orientation-dependent reflectivity can be
perceived through the binder material at some wavelengths within this range. Preferably, the hardened
binder material is at least partially transparent to electromagnetic radiation of a range of wavelengths
5 comprised between 200 nm and 800 nm, more preferably comprised between 400 nm and 700 nm.
Herein, the term “transparent” denotes that the transmission of electromagnetic radiation through a layer
of 20 µm of the hardened binder material as present in the OEL (not including the platelet-shaped
magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles, but all other optional components of the OEL in case such
components are present) is at least 50%, more preferably at least 60 %, even more preferably at least
10 70%, at the wavelength(s) concerned. This can be determined for example by measuring the
transmittance of a test piece of the hardened binder material (not including the platelet-shaped magnetic
or magnetizable pigment particles) in accordance with well-established test methods, e.g. DIN 5036-3
(1979-11).
[057] The platelet-shaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles described herein are defined
15 as having, due to their non-spherical shape, non-isotropic reflectivity with respect to an incident
electromagnetic radiation for which the cured binder material is at least partially transparent. As used
herein, the term “non-isotropic reflectivity” denotes that the proportion of incident radiation from a first
angle that is reflected by a particle into a certain (viewing) direction (a second angle) is a function of the
orientation of the particles, i.e. that a change of the orientation of the particle with respect to the first
20 angle can lead to a different magnitude of the reflection to the viewing direction. Preferably, the plateletshaped magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles described herein have a non-isotropic reflectivity
with respect to incident electromagnetic radiation in some parts or in the complete wavelength range of
from about 200 to about 2500 nm, more preferably from about 400 to about 700 nm, such that a change
of the particle’s orientation results in a change of reflection by that particle into a certain direction. As
25 known by the man skilled in the art, the magnetic or magnetizable pigment particles described herein
are different from conventional pigments, in that said conventional pigment particles exhibit the same
color and reflectivity, independent of the particle orientation, whereas the magnetic or magnetizable
pigment particles described herein exhibit either a reflection or a color, or both, that depend on the
particle orientation.

title: COMPUTER-IMPLEMENTED METHOD FOR DECODING A MARKING ENCODING INFORMATION AND COMPUTER-IMPLEMENTED METHOD FOR ENCODING INFORMATION IN A MARKING
abstract: Method for decoding a marking, the marking including a specific layout of symbols encoding information, each symbol including a pair of differential elements having different values, the marking including a first and a second portion each including multiple symbols, the method comprising: scanning the marking using a scanning device to obtain scanned information; using the scanning device, decoding the first portion by applying a first decoding algorithm on the scanned information, the first decoding algorithm being stored on the scanning device and including information to decode only the symbols of the first portion; sending a characterization of the second portion to a remote server; and using the remote server, decoding the second portion by applying a second decoding algorithm on the characterization of the second portion, the second decoding algorithm being stored on the remote server and including information to decode the symbols of the second portion.
specification:
The present invention is directed at a computer-implemented method for decoding a marking
encoding information. The present invention is further directed at a computer-implemented method
for encoding information in a marking.
10 BACKGROUND ART
Currently, articles and security devices can be identified by a mark or a logo inscribed on a package
of the article or on the article itself. These inscriptions are visible and enable the article to be identified
by all users. It is also possible to use other visible identifiers which contain encrypted information so
that the content of the identifier cannot be recognized by all users. There are, for example, one15 dimensional identifiers of the barcode type or two-dimensional identifiers of the data matrix type,
usually printed on a surface, and which are the most widely used.
One type of two-dimensional code used to encode information on articles is described in the patent
application WO 2013/071960 A1. This code is based on differential pairs of symbols of different
20 values and can only be decoded if one knows the pattern according to which the differential pairs are
arranged in the code. If the entire decoding process of such a code is contained in a smartphone
application, for example, by reversing the decoding algorithm, one can know what the decoder
expects to read and create false codes which comply with the secret pattern and/or unallowably
decode the code. An objective of the invention as defined herein is to increase the security of the
25 code and decrease any security breaches incurring through the smartphone decoding.
An objective of the present invention is the provision of a method for encoding and decoding a
marking encoding information, and of a corresponding marking.
30 SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
According to a first aspect, a computer-implemented method for decoding a marking encoding
information is provided, the marking including a specific layout of symbols for encoding the
information, wherein each symbol includes at least one pair of differential elements arranged in a
specific manner, each element being characterized by a parameter, the parameter of a first element
35 of each differential element having a first value and the parameter of a second element of each
differential element having a second value different from the first value, wherein the marking includes
a first portion including multiple symbols and a second portion including multiple symbols, the method
comprising:
scanning the marking using a scanning device to obtain a scanned information;
3
using the scanning device, decoding the first portion of the marking by applying a first
decoding algorithm on the scanned information, the first decoding algorithm being stored on the
scanning device and including information to decode only the symbols of the first portion of the
marking;
5 sending a characterization of the second portion to a remote server; and
using the remote server, decoding the second portion of the marking by applying a second
decoding algorithm on the characterization of the second portion, the second decoding algorithm
being stored on the remote server and including information to decode the symbols of the second
portion of the marking.
10
The described method allows decoding part of the marking using a scanning device and part of the
marking using a remote server. The decoding of the marking hence requires two participants (the
scanning device and the remote server), which are each capable of decoding one part of the marking.
The full marking can only be decoded using both the scanning device and the remote server. As
15 compared to a case where the decoding is fully performed by the scanning device, the described
method allows for a more secure marking, which can be decoded only by acknowledged participants.
Fully decoding and authenticating the code remotely on a secure server (instead of on a smartphone)
would require transmitting a video stream to the secure server, which is unrealistic because it is
20 cumbersome and expensive in terms of data transmission. If compression is applied to the video
stream to allow transmission to the remote server, then the quality of the video will be impacted and
thus decoding can fail. The described method is in particular advantageous in that it does not require
transmitting a cumbersome video to the server.
25 As used herein, the expression “computer-implemented method” indicates that the method is realized
using a computer, a computer network and/or another programmable apparatus, wherein the method
is in particular implemented by executing a computer program on such a computer, computer network
and/or other programmable apparatus.
30 The marking can include a mark, a code or the like in which information is stored. The marking can
be printed on an article or security device, or the marking may be attached to the article or security
device. The article or security device may be included in the group formed by a label, a package, a
cartridge, a container containing foodstuffs, nutraceutical products, pharmaceutical products or
drinks, a bank slip, a credit card, a stamp, a revenue stamp, a tamper indicator, a secure document,
35 a passport, an identity card, a driving license, an access card, a transport ticket, an admission ticket,
a coupon, a printing form, a reflecting film, aluminum foil and a commercial article.
4
The information encoded in the marking can be numerical and/or alpha-numerical information. The
information is in particular encoded such that it cannot easily be read and/or decoded by a human
and rather needs to be decoded by an appropriate decoding algorithm.
5 The marking encodes the information in line with the algorithm presented in the patent application
WO 2013/071960 A1. The information is in particular encoded using a specific layout of symbols,
which can be specific for the article type and/or specific for the article on which the marking is
provided. The specific layout of symbols can be considered as a pattern along which the symbols
are arranged. Each symbol includes at least one pair of differential elements arranged in a specific
10 manner. The differential elements can be designated as “dots” or the like and can correspond to a
smallest unit of information of the marking. In some embodiments, a dot can correspond to a pixel.
Each differential element is characterized by a parameter, which in particular means that each
differential element has a value associated therewith, which encodes the information. The parameter
15 of a first element of each differential element has a first value and the parameter of a second element
of each differential element has a second value different from the first value. In particular, the first
value and the second value of different differential elements are not necessarily identical. Each
symbol can encode one binary number as information, the binary number being obtained based on
a difference between the first value and the second value.
20
The marking includes a first portion including multiple symbols and a second portion including
multiple symbols. The marking can be split into at least two parts, these parts being the first portion
and the second portion. Each portion includes multiple symbols having differential pairs, as described
above. The first and the second portion in particular encode information by following the same
25 differential pair scheme described herein. The difference between the symbols of the first and the
second portion is that they are not decodable by a single algorithm and rather require decoding by
different algorithms (namely, the first decoding algorithm and the second decoding algorithm).
The first portion may comprise a public and/or non-sensitive information, such as a serial number
30 (serialization sequence) of the article comprising the marking, or the like. Consequently, the first
decoding algorithm may be a publicly available and/or non-sensitive algorithm, which is why it may
be stored on the scanning device where it can be subject to reverse-engineering. The second portion
may comprise a private, secret and/or sensitive information, such as an information allowing to
determine the authenticity of the article comprising the marking. Consequently, the second decoding
35 algorithm may be a private, secret and/or sensitive algorithm, which is why it may be stored on the
remote server where it cannot be subject to reverse-engineering because the remote server is not
accessible to a user decoding the marking.
5
The scanning device can be a device used by the person wanting to decode the marking, for example
to verify the authenticity of the article. The scanning device can be a portable device (such as a
smartphone, tablet or laptop), a device dedicated for the tasks described herein, a computer, and/or
a device for verifying the readability of the marking during product manufacture. Scanning the
5 marking implies capturing at least one image of the marking, for example using a camera or a
scanner (said scanner being capable of reading a two-dimensional array) of the scanning device.
The scanned information obtained from the scanning device can be an image or video of the marking
and/or information extracted from the scan, such as the values of the individual differential pairs of
the marking.
10
The first decoding algorithm is in particular only capable of decoding the first portion of the marking.
To this end, the first decoding algorithm is knowledgeable of the specific layout of the symbols of the
first portion, but not of the second portion. In particular, the first decoding algorithm does not know
which differential elements form pairs in the second portion and hence cannot decode the second
15 portion (even when seeing or knowing the values of the differential elements of the second portion).
When decoding the first portion, the first decoding algorithm in particular identifies the location of the
symbols in the first portion (using the specific layout knowledge of the first portion) and determines
the value of each differential pair of the symbols of the first portion. The information comprised in the
first portion and decoded by the first decoding algorithm can be referred to as “first information”. The
20 first decoding algorithm (which can be provided as an app) is stored in the scanning device, meaning
that the scanning device can only decode the first information.
The second decoding algorithm is in particular capable of decoding the second portion of the
marking. To this end, the second decoding algorithm is knowledgeable of the specific layout of the
25 symbols of the second portion, but not necessarily of the first portion. It is in particular not necessarily
expected from the second decoding algorithm to decode the first portion. In some embodiments, the
second decoding algorithm is not capable of decoding the first portion. When decoding the second
portion, the second decoding algorithm in particular identifies the location of the symbols in the
second portion (using the specific layout knowledge of the second portion) and determines the value
30 of each differential pair of the symbols of the second portion. The information comprised in the
second portion and decoded by the second decoding algorithm can be referred to as “second

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
The method for encoding and decoding a marking as well as the marking described herein all rely
20 on the encoding of information through symbols including pairs of differential elements as described
in view of Fig. 1. The concept shown in Fig. 1 is based on the encoding of information in a twodimensional pattern as known from WO 2013/071960 A1. As used herein, a differential element
corresponds to a dot, and a differential pair corresponds to a dot pair.
25 As shown in Fig. 1, each dot pair A - D encodes one bit of information. As defined therein, a twodimensional code is created using dot pairs A - D. Each dot can have to different states E1 and E2
(black and white dots for simplicity), which correspond to a first value and a second value,
respectively. A dot pair A – D can thus have four different states corresponding to all possible ways
of combining the two possible states of the two dots forming the dot pair (namely E1-E2, E2-E1, E1-
30 E1 and E2-E2). Out of these four states, only the states in which the two dots of the dot pair have
opposite states are valid (that is, E1-E2 and E2-E1 are valid, while E1-E1 and E2-E2 are invalid). In
Fig. 1, the dot pair A – D have the following allowable states: A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2, D1 and D2.
The dot pairs A – D are arranged according to a predetermined pattern P1 (specific layout) offering
the possibility of encoding multiple valid two-dimensional codes P1’ and P1’’.
35
Although for simplicity the first and the second value are respectively represented as black and white
dots, it is preferable to instead use various values of grey. For each differential pair A – D, the two
dots have different grey values (corresponding to the first and second values). The binary value of
one differential pair A – D is determined by calculating the difference between the first and the second
15
values. Different differential pairs A – D can have dots having different first and second values
associated thereto, so that the code comprises multiple shades of grey and is difficult to copy and
counterfeit.

16
requires two actors: the smartphone 110 and the remote server 120. The smartphone 110 is a

title: ROAMING PROCEDURE FOR CONTEXT TRANSFER DURING ROAMING IN A MULTI-LINK OPERATION NETWORK
abstract: In one aspect, a method includes initiating a roaming procedure for a Non-Access Point Multi-Link Device (Non-AP MLD) to roam from a current Access Point Multi-Link Device (AP MLD) onto a target AP MLD; determining whether a multi-phased roaming procedure for the Non-AP MLD to roam to the target AP MLD is possible; performing the multi-phased roaming procedure when the multi-phased roaming procedure is possible; and performing a single-phased roaming procedure when the multi-phased roaming procedure is not possible.
specification:
The present technology pertains to wireless communication network, and more
specifically, to signaling procedures for enabling context transfer when a device roams from one
access point to another in a Multi-Link Operation wireless network.
BACKGROUND
[0002] Wi-Fi technology has undergone continuous evolution and innovation since its
inception, resulting in significant advancements with each new generation. Following Wi-Fi 5
(802.11ac) there has been Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax), Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be), and soon there will be Wi-Fi
8 (802.11bn) and Wi-Fi 9, each new Wi-Fi generation brings notable improvements in speed,
capacity, efficiency, and overall performance.
[0003] Wi-Fi 5 introduced substantial upgrades over its predecessor, Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n). It
introduced the use of wider channel bandwidths, multi-user Multiple-Input Multiple-Output
(MIMO), and beamforming technologies. These advancements significantly increased data
transfer rates and improved network capacity, allowing multiple devices to simultaneously
connect and communicate more efficiently. Wi-Fi 6/6E included enhanced orthogonal frequencydivision multiple access (OFDMA) and target wake time (TWT) mechanisms and included
greater frequency and improved overall spectral efficiency and power management and better
performance in crowded areas. Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) delivers speeds of up to 30 Gbps, utilizing
multi-band operation, wider bandwidth, advanced MIMO techniques, and improved modulation
schemes. Wi-Fi 7 also focuses on reducing latency and enhancing security features.
[0004] Wi-Fi 8 (802.11bn) aims to revolutionize wireless connectivity by providing ultra-high
reliability enabling rich experiences for QoS demanding applications such as cloud gaming,
AR/VR, industrial IoT, wireless TSN etc. Wi-Fi 8 is expected to introduce advancements like
seamless roaming, multi-AP coordination for predictable QoS, enhanced power saving and
advanced beamforming techniques paving the way for futuristic applications and seamless
connectivity experiences.
[0005] As Wi-Fi technology continues to evolve, each new Wi-Fi generation brings
improvements that address the growing demands of modern networks, including increased device
density, higher data rates, lower latency, improved reliability and better overall network
3
performance. These advancements play a crucial role in enabling emerging technologies,
supporting the proliferation of smart devices, and transforming the way we connect and
communicate in an increasingly interconnected world.

[0027] IEEE 802.11, commonly referred to as Wi-Fi, has been around for three decades and has
become arguably one of the most popular wireless communication standards, with billions of
devices supporting more than half of the worldwide wireless traffic. The increasing user demands
in terms of throughput, capacity, latency, spectrum, and power efficiency calls for updates or
amendments to the standard to keep up with them. As such, Wi-Fi generally has a new
amendment after every few years with its own characteristic features. In the earlier generations,
the focus was primarily higher data rates, but with ever increasing density of devices, area
efficiency has become a major concern for Wi-Fi networks. Due to this issue, the last (802.11 be
(Wi-Fi 7)) amendments focused more on efficiency though higher data rates were also included.
The next expected update to IEEE 802.11 is coined as Wi-Fi 8. Wi-Fi 8 will attempt to further
enhance throughput and minimize latency to meet the ever-growing demand for the Internet of
Things (IoT), high resolution video streaming, low-latency wireless services, etc.
[0028] Multiple Access Point (AP) coordination and transmission in Wi-Fi refers to the
management of multiple access points in a wireless network to avoid interference and ensure
efficient communication between the STA devices and the network. When multiple access points
are deployed in a network – for instance in buildings and office complexes – they operate on the
same radio frequency, which can cause interference and degrade the network performance. To
mitigate this issue, access points can be configured to coordinate their transmissions and avoid
overlapping channels.
[0029] Wi-Fi 7 introduced the concept of multi-link operation (MLO), which gives the devices
(Access Points (APs) and Stations (STAs)) the capability to operate on multiple links (or even
bands) at the same time. MLO introduces a new paradigm to multi-AP coordination which was
not part of the earlier coordination approaches. MLO is considered in Wi-Fi-7 to improve the
throughput of the network and address the latency issues by allowing devices to use multiple
links.
[0030] A multi-link device (MLD) may have several “affiliated” devices, each affiliated device
having a separate PHY interface, and the MLD having a single link to the Logical Link Control
(LLC) layer. In IEEE 802.11be, a multi-link device (MLD) is defined as: “A device that is a
logical entity and has more than one affiliated station (STA) and has a single medium access
control (MAC) service access point (SAP) to logical link control (LLC), which includes one
MAC data service” (see: LAN/MAN Standards Committee of the IEEE Computer Society,
8
Amendment 8: Enhancements for extremely high throughput (EHT), IEEE P802.11 be™/D0.1 ,
Sep. 2020, section 3.2). Connection(s) with an MLD on the affiliated devices may occur
independently or jointly. A preliminary definition and scope of a multi-link element is described
in section 9.4.2.247b of aforementioned IEEE 802.11 be draft. An idea behind this information
element/container is to provide a way for multi-link devices (MLDs) to share the capabilities of
different links with each other and facilitate the discovery and association processes. However,
this information element may still be changed, or new mechanisms may be introduced to share
the MLO information (e.g., related to backhaul usage).
[0031] In multi-link operation (MLO) both STA and APs can possess multiple links that can be
simultaneously active. These links may or may not use the same bands/channels.
[0032] MLO allows sending PHY protocol data units (PPDUs) on more than one link between
a STA and an AP. The links may be carried on different channels, which may be in different
frequency bands. Based on the frequency band and/or channel separation and filter performance,
there may be restrictions on the way the PPDUs are sent on each of the links.
[0033] MLO may include a basic transmission mode, an asynchronous transmission mode, and
a synchronous transmission mode.
[0034] In a basic transmission mode, there may be multiple primary links, but a device may
transmit PPDU on one link at a time. The link for transmission may be selected as follows. The
device (such as an AP or a STA) may count down a random back off (RBO) on both links and
select a link that wins the medium for transmission. The other link may be blocked by in-device
interference. In basic transmission mode, aggregation gains may not be achieved.
[0035] In an asynchronous transmission mode, a device may count down the RBO on both links
and perform PPDU transmission independently on each link. The asynchronous transmission
mode may be used when the device can support simultaneous transmission and reception with
bands that have sufficient frequency separation such as separation between the 2.4 GHz band and
the 5 GHz band. The asynchronous transmission mode may provide both latency and aggregation
gains.
[0036] In a synchronous PPDU transmission mode, the device may count down the RBO on
both links. If a first link wins the medium, both links may transmit PPDUs at the same time. The
9
transmission at the same time may minimize in-device interference and may provide both latency
and aggregation gains.
[0037] Multi-AP coordination and MLO are two features directed to improve the performance
of Wi-Fi networks as the Multi-AP coordination is directed toward utilizing (distributed)
coordination between different APs to reduce inter-Basic Service Set (BSS) interference for
improved spectrum utilization in dense deployments, and the MLO supports high data rates and
low latency by leveraging flexible resource utilization offered by the use of multiple links for the
same device.
OVERVIEW
[0038] The present disclosure is directed to phased roaming procedure in which different
context associated with performance of a Non-AP MLD in a Wi-Fi network are transferred from
a current AP MLD to a target AP MLD in a manner that minimizes adverse impact on data
transfer and operation of the Non-AP MLD in the network during the execution of the roaming
process.
[0039] In one aspect, a method includes initiating a roaming procedure for a Non-Access Point
Multi-Link Device (Non-AP MLD) to roam from a current Access Point Multi-Link Device
(current AP MLD) onto a target AP MLD; determining whether a multi-phased roaming
procedure for the Non-AP MLD to roam to the target AP MLD is possible; performing the multiphased roaming procedure when the multi-phased roaming procedure is possible; and performing
a single-phased roaming procedure when the multi-phased roaming procedure is not possible.
[0040] In another aspect, the multi-phased roaming procedure includes a roaming preparation

[0041] In another aspect, the roaming preparation phase procedure includes one or more of

candidate target AP MLDs, wherein the target AP MLD is selected from among the one or more

the Non-AP MLD with one or more candidate target AP MLDs, and reserving one or more
resources on the one or more candidate target AP MLDs for possible roaming of the Non-AP
MLD thereon.

EXAMPLE EMBODIMENTS
[0060] In Wi-Fi 8, support for seamless or smooth roaming capability is a strong consideration
to improve Wi-Fi roaming quality. In particular, to support smooth roaming or mobility in a
campus wide Wi-Fi network, Wi-Fi client devices can create an association with the campusnetwork (also referenced herein as an ESS, an NID, and/or an MDM) instead of creating an
association with an individual AP MLD. The ESS might be represented by a mobility domain or
a global network (e.g., NID). Further, within a single mobility domain, there can be multiple
"sub-mobility domains," where each of the multiple “sub-mobility domains” may map to a single
campus.
[0061] Currently, a Wi-Fi client device creates its association with the ESS network represented
by a (sub)Mobility Domain Multi-Link Device (MLD), instead of associating with a single AP
MLD within the ESS. Such an architecture can enable the Wi-Fi client device to roam seamlessly
13
between AP MLDs without requiring re-association and reestablishment of contexts with each
new AP MLD. Further, because the Wi-Fi client device associates with the Mobility Domain
MLD covering all the AP MLDs of the ESS, such an architecture also reduces roaming time to
realize seamless roaming.
[0062] As part of efforts to support such seamless and smooth roaming (within a given ESS or
otherwise), it is desired to reduce roaming transition time and minimize delays added due to
roaming operations. When roaming to a new target AP MLD, the context for a STA needs to be
transferred/established on the target AP MLD. Some of this context requires reserving resources
on the target AP MLD. If this context transfer needs to be established again by the STA with the
target AP MLD, then doing so adds significant delay and network overhead associated with the
roaming. Hence, it is desired to transfer the context between AP MLDs and reserve resources on
the target AP MLD to achieve fast roaming time.
[0063] However, transferring all the context and reserving resources on target AP MLDs can
add to roaming delays and impact data flow during roaming. Hence, it is desired to define an
approach where data flow is impacted minimally during context transfer for roaming operation.
[0064] Aspects of the present disclosure are directed to a mechanism to minimize roaming
delays added due to context transfer by using phased transfer of context/state information.
[0065] This disclosure provides various embodiments related to context transfers (and resource
reservations) on target AP MLD(s) in one or more phases. In some examples, static context are
transferred during a roaming preparation phase and dynamic context/state is transferred during a
roaming execution phase where the data flow might be impacted. Additionally, enhancements
are disclosed to provide a time-bound completion for roaming operation to avoid over reserving
of resources for a long period of time on potential candidate AP MLDs for roaming.

title: NON-ORIENTED ELECTRICAL STEEL SHEET AND MANUFACTURING METHOD THEREFOR
abstract: A non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to one embodiment of the present invention comprises 1.8-2.8 wt% of silicon (Si), 0.1-0.8 wt% of manganese (Mn), 0.4-1.5 wt% of aluminum (Al), 0.005 wt% or less of sulfur (S), 0.005 wt% or less of titanium (Ti), 0.07 wt% or less of tin (Sn), 0.065 wt% or less of niobium (Nb), 0.076 wt% or less of molybdenum (Mo), and the balance of iron (Fe) and other inevitable elements, and thus iron loss can be reduced.
specification:
The present invention relates to a non-oriented electrical steel sheet and a manufacturing
method for a non-oriented electrical steel sheet.
[BACKGROUND ART]
[0002] In accordance with recent trends in electrification and automation in the manufacturing
industry, interest in industrial electric motor is increasing. An electric motor is a device which
generates a driving force required for machinery using electricity so that an energy efficiency
which allows the electric motor to operate for a longer time using the same amount of energy is a
very important technical factor. The energy efficiency of the electric motor is affected by a
magnetic property and a mechanical property of a non-oriented electrical steel sheet which is used
as an iron core of the electric motor.
[0003] Specifically, the non-oriented electrical steel sheet is a material having a uniform
magnetic property in all direction regardless of a rolling direction so that iron loss needs to be
lowered and a magnetic flux density needs to be increased to improve the energy efficiency.
[0004] The magnetic flux density refers to the number of magnetic field lines induced to a
material under a specific magnetic field and is generally evaluated by a value B50 induced under a
magnetic field of 5000 A/m and uses Tesla (T) as a unit. The iron loss is a loss caused when a
material of the electrical steel sheet is magnetized and refers to a sum of a hysteresis loss, an eddy
current loss, and an anomalous loss.
[0005] In order to improve the iron loss of the electrical steel sheet, an alloying element which
- 3 -
increases a specific resistance, such as silicon (Si), manganese (Mn), and aluminum (Al) is added
or a thickness of the material is reduced to reduce an eddy current loss. However, if a large
amount of elements which increase the specific resistance is added, there may be problems, such
as reduction of the magnetic flux density and a rollability, due to the increased amount of alloying
element. Further, main alloying elements and additive elements are bonded with each other to
form precipitate and a micro precipitate hinders movement of magnetic domains to deteriorate the
magnetic property.
[0006] Accordingly, there is a need for a technology for reducing an iron loss of the non-oriented
electrical steel sheet.

[0045]
[0046] Silicon (Si)
[0047] Silicon (Si) is a major additive element of an electrical steel sheet and reduces the iron
loss by increasing specific resistance of steel. If silicon is insufficiently added, the improvement
effect of the iron loss is insufficient. In the meantime, if silicon is excessively added, a magnetic
flux density is reduced and cold rollability may be degraded due to the increased brittleness.
Accordingly, it is necessary to appropriately control a content of silicon.
[0048] If a content of silicon is less than 1.8 wt%, the above-described effect may not be expected
and if the content of silicon exceeds 2.8 wt%, there may be problems, such as reduced magnetic
flux density and increased brittleness. Accordingly, the non-oriented electrical steel sheet
- 8 -
according to the embodiment of the present invention may include 1.8 to 2.8 wt% of silicon.
[0049]
[0050] Manganese (Mn)
[0051] Similar to silicon (Si), manganese (Mn) is an element which increases the specific
resistance to lower the iron loss, thereby improving the magnetic property. Further, manganese
is also added for the purpose of improving a fraction of the texture having advantageous magnetic
property. Further, manganese is bonded with sulfur (S) in the steel to form sulfide, such as MnS.
[0052] If a content of manganese is less than 0.1 wt%, a minute MnS precipitate is formed to
suppress the growth of crystal grains and if the content of manganese exceeds 0.8 wt%, a coarse
MnS precipitate is formed to reduce the magnetic flux density. Accordingly, the non-oriented
electrical steel sheet according to the embodiment of the present invention may include 0.1 to 0.8
wt% of manganese.
[0053]
[0054] Aluminum (Al)
[0055] Aluminum (Al) is an element which increases the specific resistance, along with silicon
(Si) and manganese (Mn), to reduce the iron loss, and serves as a major additive element of the
electrical steel sheet. Aluminum serves to reduce magnetic anisotropy to reduce the magnetic
deviation.
[0056] If a content of aluminum is less than 0.4 wt%, an increased amount of specific resistance
is not sufficient to increase high frequency iron loss and a minute nitride is formed to increase a
deviation of the magnetic property. In contrast, if the content of aluminum exceeds 1.5 wt%,
nitride is excessively formed to lower the magnetic flux density and cause degradation of a cold
rollability. Accordingly, the non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to the embodiment of
the present invention may include 0.4 to 1.5 wt% of aluminum.
- 9 -
[0057]
[0058] Sulfur (S)
[0059] Sulfur (S) is an impurity element which is inevitably contained during the manufacturing
process. If a large amount of sulfur is added, brittleness is caused. Further, sulfur is bonded
with manganese (Mn) to form MnS precipitate to increase the iron loss. Accordingly, it is
desirable to add sulfur as little as possible. The non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to
the embodiment of the present invention may include 0.005 wt% or less of sulfur.
[0060]
[0061] Titanium (Ti)
[0062] Titanium (Ti) is an element which has a high tendency to form precipitate in the steel and
is bonded with carbon (C) or nitrogen (N) to form precipitate, such as TiC or TiN. The
precipitates may suppress the growth of grains. The more the titanium is added, the higher the
fraction of precipitate and texture which is disadvantageous to magnetization is formed to
deteriorate the magnetic property. Accordingly, it is desirable to add titanium as little as possible
and the non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to the embodiment of the present invention
may include 0.005 wt% or less of titanium.
[0063]
[0064] Tin (Sn)
[0065] Tin (Sn) may suppress oxygen and nitrogen on the surface from permeating into the steel
to deteriorate the iron loss. Tin is a grain boundary segregation element, and if tin is excessively
added exceeding 0.07 wt%, it may hinder grain growth and impair magnetism. Accordingly, it
is necessary to control the content and the non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to the
embodiment of the present invention may include 0.07 wt% or less of tin. Desirably, tin may be
included in an amount of more than 0 wt% and 0.07 wt% or less.
- 10 -
[0066]
[0067] Niobium (Nb)
[0068] Niobium (Nb) is bonded with carbon (C) or nitrogen (N) to form precipitate, such as NbC
in the grain. At this time, the growth of grains and movement of magnetic wall are suppressed
due to the precipitate to impair the iron loss. Accordingly, the non-oriented electrical steel sheet
according to the embodiment of the present invention may include 0.065 wt% or less of niobium.
[0069]
[0070] Molybdenum (Mo)
[0071] Molybdenum (Mo) is a strong carbonitride-forming element. If a content of
molybdenum is excessive, a minute carbide is formed to increase the iron loss and is detrimental
to a magnetic property so that it is desirable not to add molybdenum if possible. Accordingly,
the non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to the embodiment of the present invention may
include 0.076 wt% or less of molybdenum.
[0072]
[0073] The non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to the embodiment of the present
invention may further include 0.005 wt% or less of carbon (C), 0.02 wt% or less of phosphorus
(P), and 0.005 wt% or less of nitrogen (N).
[0074]
[0075] Carbon (C)
[0076] Carbon is bonded with titanium (Ti) or niobium (Nb) to form carbide, such as TiC or NbC,

according to the embodiment of the present invention may include 0.005 wt% or less of carbon.
[0077]

desirable to add phosphorus as little as possible and the non-oriented electrical steel sheet

add nitrogen as little as possible. The non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to the

[0098] With regard to selective growth of Goss grains, according to the coincidence site lattice
boundary (CSL) theory proposed by Harase, et al., it is known that in the non-oriented electrical

The CSL grain boundary refers to a special grain boundary in a low energy state which satisfies a

[00123] In the manufacturing method for a non-oriented electrical steel sheet according to an
embodiment of the present invention, after the first step S1, the second step S2 of forming a hotrolled steel sheet by hot rolling the steel material may be performed. To be more specific, the

[00124] First, the reheating step is performed prior to the hot rolling step to reheat the steel

[00125] At this time, if the reheating temperature is lower than 1100C, the rolling load is

[00126] Accordingly, in the reheating step according to the embodiment of the present invention,

the finishing temperature is lower than 800C, the rolling is performed in a secondary phase area

problem in that the strength is sharply lowered.

title: AN ASSEMBLY OF A ROTOR FOR AN ELECTRICALLY EXCITED SYNCHRONOUS MOTOR (EESM
abstract:
AN ASSEMBLY OF A ROTOR FOR AN ELECTRICALLY EXCITED
SYNCHRONOUS MOTOR (EESM)
An assembly (100) of a rotor for an electrically excited synchronous motor
(EESM) is disclosed. The assembly (100) comprises a rotor core (102)
comprising a plurality of T-shaped poles (104-1, 104-2….n)
circumferentially distributed about the rotor core (102). Each T-shaped pole
includes a first structure (106) extending radially outward and a second
structure (108) connected to the rotor core (102). The second structure (108)
supports a field winding (112) configured to generate primary magnetic
flux upon excitation. A magnet (110) composed of ferrite-based magnetic
material is positioned between adjacent first structures (106) and configured
to provide supplementary magnetic flux. The combined action of the field
winding (112) and the magnet (110) establishes a hybrid excitation
configuration within a common magnetic circuit of the rotor core (102).

TECHNICAL FIELD
[001] The present disclosure relates generally to an electrically excited
synchronous motor (EESM) and more particularly to an assembly of a rotor
having a plurality of T-shaped poles with ferrite-assisted hybrid excitation
configuration.5
BACKGROUND
[002] An electric machines are widely used in industrial, automotive,
traction, renewable energy, and automation applications for converting
electrical energy into mechanical energy. Among various types of electric
machines, synchronous motors are commonly employed due to their ability10
to operate at constant speed under varying load conditions. A synchronous
motor operates based on the interaction between a rotating magnetic field
produced by a stator and a magnetic field generated by a rotor.
[003] synchronous motors may be categorized into a permanent magnet
synchronous motor (PMSMs) and an electrically excited synchronous15
motor (EESMs). In PMSMs, permanent magnets are mounted on or
embedded within the rotor to establish a constant magnetic field. These
permanent magnets are typically composed of a rare-earth magnetic
material such as neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) or samarium cobalt. The
stator windings are energized with alternating current to create a rotating20
magnetic field, which interacts with the rotor magnetic field to produce
torque.
[004] Although PMSMs provide a high torque density and a compact size,
the use of a rare-earth materials presents certain challenges. The Rare-earth
magnets are subject to supply chain volatility, cost fluctuations, and25
potential demagnetization under elevated temperature conditions.
3
Furthermore, the magnetic field in PMSMs is fixed in magnitude, limiting
flexibility in controlling flux levels across wide speed ranges.
[005] Electrically excited synchronous motors (EESMs) provide an
alternative configuration wherein the rotor magnetic field is generated by
field windings supplied with direct current. In such machines, excitation5
current flowing through rotor windings produces the magnetic field
required for synchronous operation. The magnitude of rotor magnetic flux
can be adjusted by controlling the excitation current, thereby enabling field
controllability and extended operating ranges.
[006] Conventional EESMs typically include a solid or a laminated rotor10
core having salient poles around which field windings are wound. Electrical
power is supplied to the rotor windings through a slip rings or a brushless
excitation system. While EESMs eliminate the dependency on permanent
magnets, they often require significant excitation current to achieve
adequate air-gap flux density. The flow of excitation current through rotor15
windings can result in copper losses, thermal loading, and efficiency
considerations. Thermal management of the rotor structure is therefore an
important design aspect.
[007] Various rotor constructions have been proposed in the prior art to
improve magnetic flux concentration and electromagnetic performance.20
Flux-concentrated rotor designs attempt to guide and intensify magnetic
flux in desired regions. Laminated rotor cores are frequently used to reduce
eddy current losses and improve magnetic performance. However,
segmentation and structural variations in rotor architecture may introduce
mechanical complexity, manufacturing challenges, and assembly25
considerations.
[008] Hybrid excitation synchronous machines have also been proposed in
which permanent magnets are combined with electrically excited windings.
In many such configurations, the permanent magnets act as a primary or
4
substantial source of rotor magnetic flux, with excitation windings
providing supplementary flux control. In several known implementations,
rare-earth magnets are utilized to achieve high magnetic strength. These
hybrid machines may improve torque output under certain operating
conditions but can still rely on expensive magnetic materials.5
[009] In addition, the geometric configuration of rotor poles, including
radial extensions, pole shoes, and flux paths, plays a significant role in
determining air-gap flux distribution. The spatial arrangement of rotor
poles around the rotor core affects torque ripple, magnetic saturation, and
electromagnetic interaction with the stator. The positioning of magnetic10
elements relative to rotor poles can further influence flux distribution and
machine characteristics.
[0010] Increasing pole count in synchronous motors may enhance torque
characteristics, but such modifications can complicate rotor manufacturing
and may impact structural rigidity. Rotor cooling and thermal dissipation15
remain significant considerations, particularly in high-power traction and
industrial applications.
[0011] Accordingly, various conventional synchronous motor architectures
have attempted to balance torque performance, controllability, material
cost, and structural configuration. However, existing designs often involve20
trade-offs between magnetic strength, excitation current requirements,
mechanical complexity, and reliance on specific magnetic materials.
SUMMARY
[0012] Embodiments of the present disclosure present technological
improvements as solutions to one or more of the above-mentioned technical25
problems.
[0013] Before the present subject matter relating to an electrically excited
synchronous motor (EESM), it is to be understood that this application is
5
not limited to the particular system described, as there can be multiple
possible embodiments which are not expressly illustrated in the present
disclosure. It is also to be understood that the terminology used in the
description is for the purpose of describing the implementations or versions
or embodiments only and is not intended to limit the scope of the present5
subject matter.
[0014] The present disclosure provides an assembly of a rotor for an
electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM) incorporating a hybrid
excitation configuration using ferrite-based magnetic material. The
assembly comprises a rotor core having a plurality of T-shaped poles10
mounted on and circumferentially distributed about the rotor core. Each T-
shaped pole includes a first structure extending radially outward and a
second structure extending radially inward and connected to the rotor core.
[0015] The second structure of each T-shaped pole carries a field winding
configured to generate primary magnetic flux upon application of15
excitation current. The first structure cooperates with a ferrite-based
magnet positioned between two consecutive first structures of adjacent T-
shaped poles. The ferrite magnet is configured to provide supplementary
magnetic flux in alignment with the magnetic flux generated by the field
winding, thereby establishing a hybrid excitation arrangement within a20
common magnetic circuit.
[0016] In one aspect, the plurality of T-shaped poles are arranged at
substantially equal angular intervals around the rotor core to provide
balanced magnetic distribution. The assembly is free of rare-earth magnetic
materials and utilizes ferrite-based magnets as flux-assisting elements.25
[0017] The hybrid excitation structure enables controlled generation of
magnetic flux through electrical excitation while supplementing the
magnetic circuit through ferrite-assisted flux contribution. The structural
6
configuration of the T-shaped poles facilitates effective magnetic interaction
with a stator in synchronous operation. By combining electrically generated
flux and ferrite-assisted flux within the assembly, the system enhances air-
gap magnetic flux density, supports improved torque generation for a given
rotor size, and reduces excitation current requirements, thereby5
contributing to improved operational efficiency while maintaining field
controllability.

[0018] The foregoing detailed description of embodiments is better
understood when read in conjunction with the appended drawings. For10

[0019] The present disclosure is described in detail with reference to the15

[0020] Figure 1 illustrates an isometric view of an assembly showing a rotor20

[0021] Figure 2 illustrates a cross-sectional view depicting magnetic flux
distribution within the assembly, showing interaction between electrically25
7
generated magnetic flux and magnet-assisted flux across the rotor and air-

described herein.
DETAILED DESCRIPTION
[0024] Some embodiments of this disclosure, illustrating all its features, will15
now be discussed in detail. The words "comprising," "having," "containing,"
and "including," and other forms thereof, are intended to be equivalent in
meaning and be open ended in that an item or items following any one of
these words is not meant to be an exhaustive listing of such item or items
or meant to be limited to only the listed item or items. It must also be noted20
that as used herein and in the appended claims, the singular forms "a," "an,"
and "the" include plural references unless the context clearly dictates
otherwise. Although an electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM),
similar or equivalent to those described herein can be used in the practice
or testing of embodiments of the present disclosure, the exemplary, the25
electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM) is now described.
8
[0025] Various modifications to the embodiments described herein will be
readily apparent to those skilled in the art, and the generic principles
defined herein may be applied to other rotor configurations and
synchronous motor architectures. Although the present disclosure has been
described in the context of an assembly for an electrically excited5
synchronous motor, one of ordinary skill in the art will recognize that the
disclosed structure may be implemented in various electric machine
applications requiring controlled magnetic excitation. Thus, the present
disclosure is not intended to be limited to the embodiments illustrated but
is to be accorded with the widest scope consistent with the principles and10
features described herein.
[0026] In electrically excited synchronous motors, the generation and
control of rotor magnetic flux play a critical role in determining torque
capability, efficiency, and operational stability. Conventional electrically
excited rotor constructions typically rely entirely on field windings to15
establish magnetic flux. In such arrangements, sufficient air-gap flux
density is achieved by supplying higher excitation current to the rotor
windings. However, increasing excitation current may lead to elevated
copper losses, thermal stress within the rotor structure, and increased
cooling requirements. The thermal behaviour of the rotor becomes20
particularly significant in traction and high-power applications where
continuous operation under load is expected.
[0027] Permanent magnet synchronous motors provide an alternative
approach by embedding high-energy permanent magnets within the
rotor. While such machines can produce high torque density, they25
commonly depend on rare-earth magnetic materials. Rare-earth magnets
are associated with cost sensitivity, material availability concerns, and
performance variations under high-temperature conditions.
9
Furthermore, the magnetic field generated by permanent magnets
remains substantially fixed, limiting the extent of field weakening or flux
control at high rotational speeds.
[0028] Hybrid excitation machines have also been explored in the prior
art, combining permanent magnets with field windings. In several5
known implementations, permanent magnets act as the primary flux
source, while excitation windings provide auxiliary control. These
configurations may improve electromagnetic performance under certain
