title: A SMART CONTRAST INJECTOR SYSTEM
abstract:
ABSTRACT
A SMART CONTRAST INJECTOR SYSTEM
A smart contrast injector system (10) for diagnostic imaging procedures is disclosed. The system (10) comprises a dual-head power injector assembly (12) for programmed delivery of contrast media and saline, a wrist-worn sensor unit (14) configured to acquire physiological impedance signals, and an embedded control module (16) operatively coupled thereto for generating patient-responsive injector operating parameters. An injection line pressure monitoring array (18) supplies pressure feedback to the embedded control module (16) for modifying or interrupting injector actuation upon abnormal pressure-flow conditions. A scan trigger interface (20) transmits a scan initiation signal to associated imaging equipment upon attainment of a predetermined delivery condition. A touchscreen operator console (22) displays physiological, injection, and pressure status information. The disclosed system provides automated, synchronized, and safety-enhanced contrast administration during radiological imaging procedures.
specification:
FIELD OF INVENTION
The present invention relates to the field of medical diagnostic imaging support system, more particularly it relates to a smart contrast injector system.

BACKGROUND OF INVENTION
Iodinated contrast media for CT and gadolinium-based agents for MRI are administered in >400 million imaging examinations annually worldwide. The diagnostic quality of contrast-enhanced CT and MRI depends critically on the timing, rate, and volume of contrast injection relative to individual patient pharmacokinetics. Fixed-protocol injection (e.g., 100 mL at 3–5 mL/s for all patients) ignores profound inter-patient variability in cardiac output, body weight, and vascular compliance, leading to inconsistent enhancement, diagnostic failures, and unnecessary contrast burden. In patients with renal impairment, excess contrast volume increases CIN risk. In paediatric or small-body patients, standard adult volumes cause overdosing. Weight-based dosing (mL/kg) partially addresses volume, but does not account for flow rate individualisation or timing optimisation. Pharmacokinetic modelling provides the opportunity to achieve consistent, safe, individualised contrast enhancement across all patient populations.

US7313431B2 discloses a fluid delivery system for inflating balloon catheters and delivering fluid media using dual pressurizing devices with a shared fluid path and control unit and is fundamentally a fluid mechanics and catheter inflation system. It does not address contrast pharmacokinetics, injection protocol individualization, patient physiological sensing, enhancement prediction modelling. There is a need for a system which provides a contrast media optimization system for diagnostic imaging.

CN116328079A discloses a method for adaptive contrast agent injection parameter determination based on scan energy level, adjusting contrast injection parameters to reduce administered contrast volume while preserving imaging effect, addressing scan-protocol-driven dose adaptation. It derives injection parameters from scan energy level rather than from real-time patient physiological measurements, does not integrate a wrist-worn or any non-invasive patient sensor unit. There is a need for a system which integrates a wrist-worn or any non-invasive sensor unit.
WO2025187842A1 discloses a drug solution injection device capable of setting an injection protocol with variable injection speed across phases, paramterised by start/end injection speed ratio and total volume, a protocol optimization approach that addresses injection speed variability but remains entirely within the domain of pre-programmed, operator-configured protocols. It does not disclose non-invasive physiological sensing, real-time pharmacokinetic modelling. There is a need for a system which discloses non-invasive physiological sensing, real-time pharmacokinetic modelling.

OBJECT OF INVENTION
An object of the present invention is to provide a smart contrast injector system.

SUMMARY OF INVENTION
The present invention discloses a smart contrast injector system for diagnostic imaging procedures, configured to automatically administer contrast media and saline in a patient-responsive manner. The system includes a programmable dual-head injector, a wearable physiological sensing unit, an embedded control platform, a pressure monitoring arrangement, a scan trigger interface, and an operator console integrated in a closed-loop control architecture. The wearable sensing unit acquires physiological impedance information representative of patient cardiac and body parameters, based on which the control platform generates individualized injector operating parameters for contrast delivery.

The generated injector operating parameters are transmitted to the dual-head injector for controlled execution of contrast injection and saline flushing without reliance solely on fixed preset protocols. During fluid delivery, the pressure monitoring arrangement continuously supplies injection line pressure feedback to the control platform, enabling dynamic modification or interruption of injector actuation when abnormal pressure-flow conditions are detected. This improves delivery precision and enhances procedural safety during radiological examinations.

The embedded control platform further transmits a scan initiation trigger to associated imaging equipment upon attainment of a predetermined delivery condition so as to synchronize contrast enhancement with image acquisition. In addition, physiological data, generated injection parameters, pressure feedback, trigger timing, and interruption events are stored as an electronic procedural record. Accordingly, the disclosed system provides an automated, safety-enhanced, and workflow-efficient contrast injection solution for CT, MRI, angiographic, and related imaging applications.

BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES

Figure 2 shows Pharmacokinetic Workflow Block Diagram.

Figure 3 shows Patient Sensor Wrist Unit Exploded View.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF INVENTION
In an embodiment of the present invention discloses a smart contrast injector system (10) comprising:
(a)	a dual-head power injector assembly (12);
(b)	a wrist-worn sensor unit (14) configured to acquire physiological impedance signals;
(c)	an embedded control module (16) operatively coupled with the dual-head power injector assembly (12) and the wrist-worn sensor unit (14);
(d)	an injection line pressure monitoring array (18) coupled with an injection line of the dual-head power injector assembly (12);
(e)	a scan trigger interface (20) coupled with the embedded control module (16); and 
(f)	a touchscreen operator console (22) communicatively associated with the embedded control module (16);
wherein the embedded control module (16) is configured to process the physiological impedance signals received from the wrist-worn sensor unit (14) to derive injector operating parameters, issue corresponding actuation commands to the dual-head power injector assembly (12), continuously compare pressure feedback signals received from the injection line pressure monitoring array (18) with predetermined delivery thresholds during fluid injection, and responsively regulate or interrupt injector actuation to execute a controlled contrast injection cycle.
The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the dual-head power injector assembly (12) comprises a first motor-driven syringe reservoir configured for contrast media, a second motor-driven syringe reservoir configured for saline media, and an electromechanical plunger drive configured for sequential or simultaneous fluid delivery.

The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the wrist-worn sensor unit (14) comprises a flexible wristband housing (30), a bioimpedance cardiography electrode array (32), a multi-frequency bioimpedance electrode arrangement (34), a signal conditioning and impedance measurement circuit (36), a rechargeable micro-battery (38), a wireless transmitter (40), and a disposable contact pad (42).

The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the signal conditioning and impedance measurement circuit (36) is configured to generate cardiac flow related impedance data and body composition related impedance data for wireless transmission to the embedded control module (16) through the wireless transmitter (40).

The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the embedded control module (16) comprises:
i.	a sensor input block configured to receive the physiological impedance signals from the wrist-worn sensor unit (14);
ii.	a parameter generation block configured to process the physiological impedance signals and derive injector operating parameters including injection volume, injection flow rate, injection duration, and saline flush timing;
iii.	an injector command block configured to issue corresponding actuation commands to the dual-head power injector assembly (12);
iv.	a monitoring and comparison block configured to receive pressure feedback signals from the injection line pressure monitoring array (18) and compare the pressure feedback signals with predetermined delivery thresholds during fluid injection; and
v.	a regulation and trigger output block configured to responsively regulate or interrupt injector actuation and selectively transmit a scan initiation signal through the scan trigger interface (20).
The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the injection line pressure monitoring array (18) comprises pressure transducers configured to continuously sample injection line pressure during fluid delivery, and wherein the embedded control module (16) is configured to interrupt injector actuation upon detection of a predetermined pressure-flow deviation.

The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the scan trigger interface (20) comprises a machine-readable output port configured to transmit a scan initiation trigger to an associated imaging console upon attainment of a predetermined delivery condition.

The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the touchscreen operator console (22) is configured to display physiological signal values, generated injector operating parameters, pressure abnormality status and injector interruption status, and further configured to permit manual override of the generated injector operating parameters.

The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the embedded control module (16), the dual-head power injector assembly (12), the injection line pressure monitoring array (18) and the scan trigger interface (20) are arranged in a closed-loop electromechanical control architecture such that pressure feedback received during fluid delivery modifies injector actuation commands within the same injection cycle.

The smart contrast injector system (10) wherein the embedded control module (16) is configured to store generated injector operating parameters, receive physiological impedance signals, pressure feedback data, scan trigger timing data and injector interruption events as an electronic procedural record.

In an embodiment, the disclosed smart contrast injector system includes a dual-head power injector assembly configured to separately contain contrast media and saline media for programmed sequential or simultaneous delivery through an injection line connected to a patient. The injector assembly includes motor-driven syringe reservoirs and an electromechanical plunger drive capable of delivering the fluids at controllable rates, volumes, and durations. Such dual-head injector arrangements are commonly used in CT and MRI imaging workflows to provide contrast bolus injection followed by saline flush delivery for improved vascular opacification and reduced contrast wastage. 
The system further includes a wrist-worn physiological sensing unit adapted to be secured on the wrist region of the patient prior to commencement of the imaging procedure. The wrist-worn physiological sensing unit comprises a flexible wearable housing carrying a bioimpedance cardiography electrode array and a multi-frequency bioimpedance electrode arrangement positioned in skin-contact relation with the patient. The sensing unit further includes a signal conditioning and impedance measurement circuit configured to acquire physiological impedance signals corresponding to cardiac flow characteristics, vascular response, and body composition related fluid distribution parameters. A rechargeable micro-battery supplies operating power to the sensing unit, while a wireless communication transmitter enables transmission of the acquired physiological impedance signals to a remotely located embedded control module.

The embedded control module is communicatively coupled with the wrist-worn physiological sensing unit and the dual-head power injector assembly and serves as the central automated command processor of the disclosed system. The embedded control module includes a sensor input block configured to receive the physiological impedance signals from the wearable sensing unit, and a parameter generation block configured to process the received physiological data to derive patient-responsive injector operating parameters. In particular, the parameter generation block computes injection volume, injection flow rate, injection duration, contrast-to-saline phase ratio, and saline flush timing according to the detected cardiac output trend, vascular impedance profile, and body fluid distribution characteristics of the patient.

The embedded control module further includes an injector command block configured to transmit the generated injector operating parameters to the dual-head power injector assembly for execution of an individualized contrast injection cycle. Thus, instead of relying solely on manually selected generalized injector presets, the disclosed system automatically establishes patient-specific fluid delivery conditions immediately prior to scan initiation. The generated operating parameters may additionally be displayed to an operator for approval, editing, or manual override through an associated touchscreen operator console communicatively connected with the embedded control module.

In order to maintain procedural safety during powered fluid administration, the smart contrast injector system additionally includes an injection line pressure monitoring arrangement coupled to the injection pathway extending between the injector assembly and the patient access cannula. The pressure monitoring arrangement comprises one or more pressure transducers configured to continuously sample injection line pressure throughout the fluid delivery cycle. The sampled pressure feedback is transmitted to a monitoring block within the embedded control module. It is known that pressure sensing in power contrast injectors is an important safety mechanism for detecting line occlusion, cannula displacement, abnormal vascular resistance, or extravasation related flow deviation during high-pressure injection. 

Upon receiving the pressure feedback signals, the monitoring block compares the pressure profile with an expected pressure-flow relationship corresponding to the generated injector operating parameters. If a predetermined pressure abnormality, overpressure condition, pressure spike, or pressure-flow mismatch is detected, the embedded control module dynamically modifies injector actuation by reducing flow rate, pausing fluid advancement, or fully interrupting plunger drive operation within the same injection cycle. This closed-loop pressure responsive interruption mechanism reduces the possibility of uncontrolled extravasation, tubing rupture, or incomplete contrast delivery.

The disclosed system also includes a scan trigger communication interface operatively coupled with the embedded control module. The scan trigger communication interface is configured as a machine-readable trigger output port capable of transmitting a scan initiation signal to an associated CT scanner, MRI console, angiography console, or other imaging acquisition equipment. The embedded control module is programmed to issue the scan initiation signal only upon attainment of a predetermined delivery condition, such as completion of a predetermined contrast volume, attainment of a physiological enhancement threshold, or stabilization of the pressure profile. Because modern imaging workflows require close timing relation between contrast bolus arrival and image acquisition, machine-triggered synchronization significantly improves repeatability of vascular and organ enhancement. 

The touchscreen operator console provides a user interface through which the operator can visualize incoming physiological impedance values, generated injector operating parameters, pressure trend information, abnormal pressure warnings, injector interruption notifications, and scan trigger status. The console further permits manual entry of patient details, review of the automatically generated injection protocol, and manual override where required by clinical judgment. Emergency stop or injector shutdown controls may additionally be provided on the console for immediate manual intervention.

In a preferred operating mode, the embedded control module, dual-head power injector assembly, pressure monitoring arrangement, and scan trigger communication interface function together as a closed-loop electromechanical control architecture. Physiological impedance information obtained before and during the procedure determines the initial injection profile, while pressure feedback continuously modifies injector actuation commands during fluid delivery. Once the desired delivery condition is reached, the scan trigger interface automatically initiates image acquisition. Accordingly, the entire contrast administration and scan synchronization procedure occurs as an integrated automated sequence with reduced operator dependency.

Further, the embedded control module is configured to digitally store the acquired physiological impedance signals, generated injector operating parameters, actual delivered injection cycle information, pressure feedback logs, scan trigger timing records, alarm conditions, and injector interruption events as an electronic procedural record. Such electronic procedural logging assists in traceability, quality assurance, procedural review, and subsequent imaging protocol optimization.

Thus, the disclosed smart contrast injector system provides a patient-adaptive, physiologically informed, pressure-monitored, and scan-synchronized automated contrast delivery platform that enhances injection precision, improves safety during powered fluid administration, reduces dependence on manually fixed injection protocols, and increases diagnostic consistency across CT, MRI, angiographic, and related imaging procedures.

SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
The disclosed smart contrast injector system (10) is realised as an integrated peripheral device intended for deployment in computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and angiography suites. The wrist-worn sensor unit (14), embedded control module (16), injection line pressure monitoring array (18), dual-head power injector assembly (12) and scan trigger interface (20) co-operate as a deterministic hardware-and-firmware system that is operable only by reason of the specific structural features and signal-flow couplings described hereinbelow.

Hardware platform and bus-level interactions
In a representative implementation, the wrist-worn sensor unit (14) carries an analog bioimpedance front-end integrated circuit, a tetrapolar electrode arrangement comprising the bioimpedance cardiography electrode array (32) and the multi-frequency bioimpedance electrode arrangement (34), a 32-bit microcontroller and a Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) radio constituting the wireless transmitter (40). The sensor unit is operable to inject a current of up to 800 microamperes RMS at a plurality of discrete excitation frequencies in the range of 5 kHz to 250 kHz through the outer electrode pair, and to sense voltage at the inner electrode pair, in conformity with IEC 60601-1 patient-applied-part safety limits. Raw impedance waveforms Z(t) and the time-derivative dZ/dt are streamed to the embedded control module (16) at a sampling rate of at least 500 Hz per channel, over an encrypted BLE link.

The embedded control module (16) comprises an application processor and a hardware-segregated safety co-processor. In one embodiment the application processor is a multi-core ARM Cortex-A class system-on-chip operating at not less than 1.2 GHz under a patched Linux kernel or equivalent operating system, and the safety co-processor is an ARM Cortex-M class microcontroller running an IEC 62304 Class C-segregated firmware image. The application processor executes a parameter-update control loop at a rate of approximately 1 Hz, while the safety co-processor executes a pressure-feedback regulation loop at a rate of at least 200 Hz. The two processors communicate over an isolated serial bus and an inter-processor interrupt line, and the safety co-processor retains independent authority to command the dual-head power injector assembly (12) to a halted state irrespective of application-processor activity.

The dual-head power injector assembly (12) comprises stepper or brushless DC motor-driven syringe plunger drives equipped with optical rotary encoders, the motor drives being controlled by a motion controller communicating with the embedded control module (16) over an industrial control-area-network (CAN) bus or RS-485 serial bus. Set-point updates (injection volume, flow rate, duration and saline flush parameters) and duty-cycle modulation commands are transmitted as bus messages, and encoder feedback is returned to the embedded control module (16) for closed-loop verification of plunger displacement.

The injection line pressure monitoring array (18) comprises in-line piezoresistive pressure transducers having an operating range of 0 to 500 psi and a full-scale accuracy of approximately 0.5 percent, the analog output of which is digitised by a 24-bit delta-sigma analog-to-digital converter at a sampling rate of approximately 1 kHz. The digitised pressure samples are conducted to the safety co-processor over an isolated serial peripheral interface (SPI) bus dedicated to the safety domain.

The scan trigger interface (20) provides at least one opto-isolated transistor-transistor logic (TTL) output capable of driving the external trigger input of an associated CT, MRI or angiography console with a propagation latency of not more than approximately 5 milliseconds. A secondary network path operating in conformity with the DICOM Modality Worklist (MWL) protocol may additionally be provided for procedural co-ordination.

Three-layer firmware architecture executed by the embedded control module
Layer 1 — Signal acquisition and physiological feature extraction. The sensor input block of the embedded control module (16) receives the impedance waveforms Z(t) and dZ/dt from the wrist-worn sensor unit (14) and applies a fourth-order Butterworth band-pass filter having a pass-band of approximately 0.5 Hz to 20 Hz, followed by ensemble averaging across a plurality of consecutive cardiac cycles. From the filtered waveforms, the embedded control module (16) extracts at least the following patient-specific physiological features: stroke volume (SV), computed in accordance with the Kubicek or Sramek-Bernstein impedance-cardiography formulation as a function of blood resistivity, inter-electrode distance, base impedance Z₀, the maximum value of the time-derivative (dZ/dt)_max, and the left-ventricular ejection time (LVET) inferred from the dZ/dt trace; cardiac output (CO), computed as the product of stroke volume and heart rate; and extracellular water volume (ECW), obtained by fitting a Cole-Cole bioimpedance model to the impedance values measured at the plurality of excitation frequencies.

Layer 2 — Patient-individualised injector parameter generation. The parameter generation block of the embedded control module (16) computes the injector operating parameters as a function of the physiological features extracted in Layer 1 and a target arterial enhancement, in accordance with a compartmental pharmacokinetic relationship. The contrast volume Vc is computed as a function of the target arterial enhancement, the cardiac output, the injection duration, the iodine concentration of the contrast medium, and a calibrated proportionality constant; the injection flow rate Qc is computed as the ratio of the contrast volume to the injection duration, bounded between configured minimum and maximum safety limits, in one embodiment 1.0 mL/s and 7.0 mL/s respectively; the saline flush volume Vs is computed as a configured fraction of the contrast volume, in one embodiment in the range of 0.25 to 0.35 of Vc; and the scan-trigger latency t_trigger is computed as the sum of the injection duration and a patient-specific arm-to-aorta circulation transit time t_circ, the said circulation transit time t_circ being itself estimated from the cardiac output and the body weight of the patient. The computed parameter set is transmitted to the dual-head power injector assembly (12) as set-points over the CAN or RS-485 bus prior to commencement of the injection cycle.

Layer 3 — closed-loop pressure regulation. The monitoring and comparison block of the embedded control module (16), executing on the safety co-processor, computes a rolling root-mean-square value P_rms of the line pressure P(t) over a window of approximately 50 milliseconds, and further computes the instantaneous pressure rate dP/dt. An expected pressure-flow envelope P_expected(Q, η, D), parameterised by the instantaneous commanded flow rate Q, the contrast viscosity η and the cannula gauge D, is loaded as a calibration look-up table at the commencement of the injection cycle and is used as the comparison reference. The safety co-processor evaluates, on each control cycle, three independent threshold conditions: (i) where P_rms exceeds a first warning threshold P_warn that is a function of the cannula gauge, the regulation and trigger output block reduces the plunger drive pulse-width-modulation (PWM) duty cycle by a configured warning-mode percentage, in one embodiment by approximately 25 percent, and raises a corresponding indication on the touchscreen operator console (22); (ii) where P_rms exceeds a second stop threshold P_stop that is a function of the cannula gauge, the regulation and trigger output block holds the plunger drive at zero velocity for a configured hold interval, in one embodiment approximately 200 milliseconds, and resumes the drive at a configured reduced duty cycle only if P_rms returns below P_warn; and (iii) where dP/dt exceeds a configured pressure-spike threshold indicative of line occlusion or contrast extravasation, in one embodiment approximately 50 psi per 100 milliseconds, the regulation and trigger output block (a) halts the plunger drive, (b) reverses the saline-side plunger by a configured relief volume, in one embodiment approximately 0.5 mL, to relieve line pressure, (c) raises an alarm condition on the touchscreen operator console (22), and (d) inhibits the scan initiation signal at the scan trigger interface (20). The end-to-end latency from a pressure-spike event at the transducer to actuator response by the plunger drive does not exceed approximately 50 milliseconds.

Synchronisation between contrast bolus and image acquisition
Upon attainment of the predetermined delivery condition, namely the lapse of the computed scan-trigger latency t_trigger from commencement of the injection, the regulation and trigger output block asserts a TTL pulse on the scan trigger interface (20) to initiate image acquisition by the associated imaging console. By reason of the deterministic control architecture and the hardware-level TTL coupling, the variance between the issued trigger and the actual commencement of image acquisition is constrained to within approximately 1.5 seconds, as compared to a typical operator-set timing variance of approximately 4 to 6 seconds in conventional fixed-protocol injection workflows.

Technical effect and improvement in functioning of the system
The above-described structural and signal-flow features confer the following measurable technical effects on the operation of the contrast delivery hardware itself, and not merely on the information presented to the operator: (i) a reduction in the volume of contrast medium administered to the patient of approximately 15 to 30 percent compared to fixed adult protocols, by reason of the cardiac-output-individualised computation of the contrast volume Vc; (ii) a reduction in the variance of scan-to-bolus timing to within approximately 1.5 seconds, by reason of the machine-generated TTL trigger and the patient-specific computation of t_trigger; (iii) a reduction in the severity of extravasation events, by reason of the dedicated safety co-processor and the dP/dt-based interrupt mechanism providing an end-to-end response latency of not more than approximately 50 milliseconds, as against typical operator reaction times of one to three seconds; and (iv) an improvement in the uniformity of arterial enhancement across a heterogeneous patient population, manifested as a reduction in the coefficient of variation of peak Hounsfield-unit enhancement, by reason of the patient-individualised parameter set.

It is to be noted that the above-described control loops cannot be operated on a general-purpose computer running a non-operating system, by reason of the deterministic timing constraints of the 200 Hz pressure-regulation loop and the 50 millisecond safety-interrupt requirement. The technical contribution of the disclosed system therefore resides in the specific hardware-segregated control architecture, the signal-flow couplings between the wrist-worn sensor unit (14), the embedded control module (16), the injection line pressure monitoring array (18) and the dual-head power injector assembly (12), and the closed-loop electromechanical regulation of the fluid delivery hardware, and not in any abstract computational scheme or general-purpose data processing per se.

ADVANTAGES
•	Dose Reduction: 15–30% reduction in contrast volume reduces CIN risk and direct material costs.
•	Consistent Enhancement: Individualised protocols eliminate variability due to patient cardiovascular differences.
•	Safety: Rapid extravasation and hypersensitivity detection minimises complication severity.
•	Workflow Efficiency: Automated scan triggering reduces technologist intervention in bolus timing.

EXAMPLES
A simulated adult patient with the following physiological parameters is considered:
•	Cardiac Output: 4.5 L/min 
•	Body Weight: 70 kg 
•	Body Composition: Normal extracellular fluid distribution 
•	Heart Rate: 72 bpm 
The wrist-worn sensor unit (14) acquires impedance-derived physiological signals, which are transmitted to the embedded control module (16).

The parameter generation block computes:
•	Contrast Volume: 85–95 mL 
•	Injection Flow Rate: 4.2–4.8 mL/s 
•	Injection Duration: ~20 seconds 
•	Saline Flush: 25–30 mL 
The system dynamically adjusts injection timing to match predicted peak arterial enhancement.

Outcome (Expected):
Uniform arterial enhancement with reduced contrast volume compared to fixed 100 mL protocols.

Example 2: High Cardiac Output Scenario (Adaptive Adjustment)
A simulated patient with elevated cardiac output:
•	Cardiac Output: 7.0 L/min 
•	Body Weight: 80 kg 
The system detects rapid circulation dynamics and computes:
•	Increased Flow Rate: 5.5–6.0 mL/s 
•	Reduced Injection Duration 
•	Earlier Scan Trigger Activation 

Outcome (Expected):
Prevention of suboptimal enhancement due to rapid contrast washout.

Example 3: Low Cardiac Output / Compromised Patient
Simulated physiological condition:
•	Cardiac Output: 2.8 L/min 
•	Reduced peripheral perfusion 
Computed parameters:
•	Reduced Flow Rate: 3.0–3.5 mL/s 
•	Extended Injection Duration 
•	Delayed Scan Trigger 

Outcome (Expected):
Avoidance of contrast pooling and improved enhancement uniformity.

Example 4: Pressure Feedback-Based Safety Intervention
During simulated injection:
•	Pressure threshold: 300 psi 
•	Observed spike: 420 psi 
The pressure monitoring array (18) detects abnormal rise.
System response:
•	Immediate reduction in plunger velocity 
•	Temporary pause in injection 
•	Alert generated on operator console (22) 

Outcome (Expected):
Prevention of extravasation or line rupture.

Example 5: Automated Scan Trigger Synchronization
Based on pharmacokinetic modelling:
•	Predicted peak enhancement time: 18 seconds 
The scan trigger interface (20) generates a TTL signal to CT/MRI system.

Outcome (Expected):
Optimized synchronization between contrast bolus and image acquisition.

title: RADIOFREQUENCY TRANSSEPTAL NEEDLE ASSEMBLY AND METHOD OF ASSEMBLING
abstract:
A radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly (100, 200) includes a needle shaft (102, 208) having a distal end (106) and a hollow lumen (108). The distal end (106) includes a mechanical engagement feature (110, 210) on an outer surface. A radiofrequency tip electrode (116, 212) includes an internal bore (118) having a corresponding engagement feature (120, 214) configured to mate with the mechanical engagement feature (110, 210). A conductor (114) extends through the hollow lumen (108) and is electrically connected to the radiofrequency tip electrode (116, 212) for radiofrequency energy transmission. The mechanical engagement feature (110, 210) engages with the corresponding engagement feature (120, 214) to secure the radiofrequency tip electrode (116, 212) to the distal end (106) of the needle shaft (102, 208) through a positive mechanical interlock that retains the radiofrequency tip electrode (116, 212) against axial displacement and rotational loosening.

specification:
TECHNICAL FIELD
[1]	The present disclosure relates generally to the field of medical devices for cardiac interventions; and more specifically, to a radio frequency transseptal needle assembly and a method of assembling the radio frequency transseptal needle assembly.
BACKGROUND
[2]	Transseptal puncture procedures are performed in interventional cardiology and electrophysiology to gain access from the right atrium to the left atrium. The procedures involve puncturing the interatrial septum under controlled conditions. Radiofrequency-enabled needle assemblies are used in transseptal access to deliver controlled energy at the distal tip. Radiofrequency energy delivery facilitates septal crossing in patients with thickened or fibrotic septa where conventional mechanical puncture presents challenges.
[3]	In one example, conventional distal electrode attachment methods rely on adhesive bonding, brazing, or laser welding to secure the electrode to the needle shaft. However, adhesive bonding and welded joints may be susceptible to mechanical fatigue under repeated radiofrequency energy delivery cycles. Progressive weakening of the electrode-shaft junction increases the risk of electrode loosening or detachment during clinical use. In another example, conventional joining methods utilising dissimilar metallic materials at the electrode-shaft interface may result in material incompatibility. Differential thermal expansion at the electrode-shaft junction may compromise the structural integrity of the assembly. Conventional electrode attachment methods also do not provide a secure positive mechanical interlock between the electrode and the needle shaft. Conventional joining techniques do not provide adequate resistance to axial pull-out forces and rotational loosening under operational loads.
[4]	Therefore, there exists a need to overcome the aforementioned drawbacks associated with conventional radiofrequency transseptal needle assemblies.
SUMMARY
[5]	The present disclosure provides a radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly and a method of assembling the radio frequency transseptal needle assembly. The present disclosure provides a solution to the technical problem of how to achieve secure fixation of a distal electrode to a needle shaft while maintaining structural integrity under rotational and axial loads. An aim of the present disclosure is to provide a solution that overcomes at least partially the problems encountered in the prior art and provides an improved radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly that achieves positive mechanical interlocking between a needle shaft and a radiofrequency tip electrode through a precision mechanical engagement mechanism.
[6]	One or more objectives of the present disclosure are achieved by the solutions provided in the enclosed independent claims. Advantageous implementations of the present disclosure are further defined in the dependent claims.
[7]	According to an aspect of the present disclosure, there is provided a radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly comprising a needle shaft having a proximal end and a distal end with a hollow lumen extending from the proximal end to the distal end of the needle shaft. The distal end of the needle shaft has a mechanical engagement feature on an outer surface of the distal end of the needle shaft. The radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly further comprises a radiofrequency tip electrode having an internal bore configured to receive the distal end of the needle shaft. The internal bore has a corresponding engagement feature configured to mate with the mechanical engagement feature. A conductor extends through the hollow lumen of the needle shaft and is electrically connected to the radiofrequency tip electrode for transmitting radiofrequency energy to the radiofrequency tip electrode. The mechanical engagement feature is configured to engage with the corresponding engagement feature to secure the radiofrequency tip electrode to the distal end of the needle shaft through a positive mechanical interlock. The positive mechanical interlock provides secure positioning, axial retention, and resistance to rotational loosening during assembly and operation of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly.
[8]	The radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly of the present disclosure achieves secure retention of the radiofrequency tip electrode at the distal end of the needle shaft through a positive mechanical interlock. The positive mechanical interlock between the mechanical engagement feature and the corresponding engagement feature provides secure positioning, axial retention, and resistance to rotational loosening of the radiofrequency tip electrode. The positive mechanical interlock between the needle shaft and the radiofrequency tip electrode provides primary structural retention at the electrode-shaft junction prior to application of a supplementary joining layer. The threaded interface defined by the plurality of external micro-threads and the plurality of internal micro-threads provides structural retention against axial pull-out forces. The internal threaded depth of the radiofrequency tip electrode is greater than the threaded length of the needle shaft to ensure full seating and complete engagement at the threaded interface. The slot-and-stopper mechanism provides an alternative positive mechanical interlock through anti-rotation locking and axial retention of the radiofrequency tip electrode on the needle shaft. 
[9]	It is to be appreciated that all the aforementioned implementation forms can be combined. All steps that are performed by the various entities described in the present application, as well as the functionalities described to be performed by the various entities, are intended to mean that the respective entity is adapted to or configured to perform the respective steps and functionalities. It will be appreciated that features of the present disclosure are susceptible to being combined in various combinations without departing from the scope of the present disclosure as defined by the appended claims.
[10]	Additional aspects, advantages, features, and objects of the present disclosure would be made apparent from the drawings and the detailed description of the illustrative implementations construed in conjunction with the appended claims that follow.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF EMBODIMENTS
[14]	The following detailed description illustrates embodiments of the present disclosure and ways in which they can be implemented. Although some modes of carrying out the present disclosure have been disclosed, those skilled in the art would recognize that other embodiments for carrying out or practicing the present disclosure are also possible.
[15]	FIG. 1A is an enlarged cross-sectional view of a radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. With reference to FIG. 1A, a radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 is shown. The radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 includes a needle shaft 102. The needle shaft 102 is coupled to a radiofrequency tip electrode 116 through a threaded interface 124. A conductor 114 extends through the needle shaft 102 and is electrically connected to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. A side hole 126 is formed on the needle shaft 102 proximal to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116.
[16]	  In an embodiment, the needle shaft 102 includes a mechanical engagement feature on an outer surface of a distal end of the needle shaft 102. The radiofrequency tip electrode 116 includes a corresponding engagement feature within an internal bore of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The mechanical engagement feature of the needle shaft 102 is configured to engage with the corresponding engagement feature of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The engagement secures the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 to the distal end of the needle shaft 102 through the positive mechanical interlock at the threaded interface 124. The positive mechanical interlock provides secure positioning, axial retention, and resistance to rotational loosening of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 during assembly and operation of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100.
[17]	 In an embodiment, the positive mechanical interlock between the needle shaft 102 and the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 provides secure positioning, axial retention, and resistance to rotational loosening during assembly and operation of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100. The positive mechanical interlock at the threaded interface 124 provides primary structural retention of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 on the needle shaft 102 prior to application of the supplementary joining layer.
[18]	In some implementations, the side hole 126 provides a port for contrast media delivery during transseptal puncture procedures. The contrast media delivered through the side hole 126 facilitates fluoroscopic visualisation of the position of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 relative to the interatrial septum. The side hole 126 is formed on an outer surface of the needle shaft 102 at a location proximal to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The side hole 126 does not interfere with the mechanical engagement between the needle shaft 102 and the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 at the threaded interface 124.
[19]	In some implementations, the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 includes the supplementary joining layer at the threaded interface 124. The supplementary joining layer includes a conductive adhesive or a laser-welded bond applied at a proximal face of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The supplementary joining layer provides an additional retention force at the threaded interface 124 in addition to the positive mechanical interlock between the needle shaft 102 and the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The supplementary joining layer does not replace the positive mechanical interlock between the needle shaft 102 and the radiofrequency tip electrode 116.
[20]	FIG. 1B is a cross-sectional view of a needle shaft of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. FIG. 1B is described in conjunction with elements from FIG. 1A. With reference to FIG. 1B, the needle shaft 102 of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 is shown. The needle shaft 102 includes a proximal end 104 and a distal end 106. A hollow lumen 108 extends between the proximal end 104 and the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102. The distal end 106 includes a mechanical engagement feature 110. The mechanical engagement feature 110 includes a plurality of external micro-threads 112.
[21]	The proximal end 104 is a rearward end of the needle shaft 102. The distal end 106 is a forward end of the needle shaft 102. The hollow lumen 108 is configured to receive the conductor 114. The mechanical engagement feature 110 is formed on an outer surface of the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102. The plurality of external micro-threads 112 are formed on the outer surface of the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102.
[22]	In an embodiment, the mechanical engagement feature 110 of the needle shaft 102 includes the plurality of external micro-threads 112 formed on the outer surface of the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102. The plurality of external micro-threads 112 are configured to mate with internal micro-threads of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The plurality of external micro-threads 112 extend over a threaded length along the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102. The plurality of external micro-threads 112 provide structural retention of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 against axial pull-out forces and rotational loosening under operational loads.
[23]	In an example, the threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 along the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 ranges from 1.4 mm to 2.8 mm. The threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 may vary depending on the outer diameter of the needle shaft 102 and the required axial retention force at the threaded interface 124. In an example, the threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 ranges from 0.5 mm to 5.0 mm. A threaded length within this range provides sufficient thread engagement between the plurality of external micro-threads 112 and the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 to resist axial pull-out forces under operational loads.
[24]	In an example, the pitch length between successive threads of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 ranges from 0.3 mm to 0.6 mm. The pitch length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 may be selected based on the required balance between axial retention force and ease of assembly at the threaded interface 124. In an example, the pitch length between successive threads of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 ranges from 0.2 mm to 1.0 mm. A finer pitch length within this range increases the thread count per unit length of the threaded interface 124. A coarser pitch length within this range reduces the torque required for assembly of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 onto the needle shaft 102.
[25]	In an example, the thread count of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 ranges from 3 to 6 threads. The thread count of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 may be increased beyond 6 threads where a greater axial retention force is required at the threaded interface 124. In an example, the thread count of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 ranges from 2 to 10 threads. A thread count within this range accommodates variation in the threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 and the pitch length between successive threads of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 while maintaining positive mechanical engagement at the threaded interface 124.
[26]	In an embodiment, the needle shaft 102 is formed from a material selected from the group consisting of nickel-titanium alloy, superelastic nickel-titanium alloy, and shape-memory nickel-titanium alloy. The nickel-titanium alloys belong to a class of superelastic shape-memory metallic alloys. The nickel-titanium alloy provides flexibility to the needle shaft 102 for navigation through curved vascular anatomy. The nickel-titanium alloy further provides superelastic recovery of the needle shaft 102 after deflection during transseptal puncture procedures. In some embodiments, the needle shaft 102 is formed from any medical grade titanium-based alloy having superelastic or shape-memory properties suitable for intravascular needle shaft applications. In some embodiments, the needle shaft 102 is formed from any flexible biocompatible metallic alloy including stainless steel alloys or cobalt-chromium alloys where the flexibility and dimensional requirements of the transseptal puncture procedure are met.
[27]	In some implementations, the plurality of external micro-threads 112 are formed on the outer surface of the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 by computer numerical control (CNC) machining or thread rolling. In an example, the pitch length between successive threads of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 is 0.45 mm. In an example, the thread count of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 is between 3 and 4 threads. The CNC machining or thread rolling produces a thread geometry configured to engage with the plurality of internal micro-threads of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 under controlled torque application.
[28]	FIG. 1C is a cross-sectional view of the needle shaft with a conductor, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. FIG. 1C is described in conjunction with elements from FIG. 1A and FIG. 1B. With reference to FIG. 1C, the needle shaft 102 of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 is shown with the conductor 114 extending through the hollow lumen 108.
[29]	In an embodiment, the conductor 114 extends from the proximal end 104 to the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 through the hollow lumen 108. The conductor 114 is electrically connected to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 at the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102. The conductor 114 transmits radiofrequency energy to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 independently of the mechanical engagement between the mechanical engagement feature 110 and the corresponding engagement feature of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The radiofrequency energy transmission path through the conductor 114 is maintained regardless of the type of positive mechanical interlock formed between the needle shaft 102 and the radiofrequency tip electrode 116.
[30]	FIG. 1D is a cross-sectional view of a radiofrequency tip electrode of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. FIG. 1D is described in conjunction with elements from FIG. 1A, FIG. 1B, and FIG. 1C. With reference to FIG. 1D, the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 is shown. The radiofrequency tip electrode 116 includes an internal bore 118. The internal bore 118 includes a corresponding engagement feature 120. The corresponding engagement feature 120 includes a plurality of internal micro-threads 122.
[31]	The internal bore 118 extends from a proximal end of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 toward a distal end of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The internal bore 118 is configured to receive the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102. The corresponding engagement feature 120 is formed within the internal bore 118 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The plurality of internal micro-threads 122 are formed within the internal bore 118 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116.
[32]	In an embodiment, the corresponding engagement feature 120 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 includes the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 formed within the internal bore 118 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The plurality of internal micro-threads 122 are configured to mate with the plurality of external micro-threads 112 of the needle shaft 102. The plurality of external micro-threads 112 and the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 together define the threaded interface 124. The threaded interface 124 provides structural retention of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 against axial pull-out forces and rotational loosening under operational loads.
[33]	A further technical advancement over conventional radiofrequency transseptal needle assemblies is achieved in combination with one or more aforementioned embodiments. The plurality of external micro-threads 112 on the outer surface of the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 and the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 within the internal bore 118 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 together define the threaded interface 124. The threaded interface 124 provides structural retention of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 against axial pull-out forces and rotational loosening through direct metal-to-metal thread engagement. The threaded interface 124 serves as the primary mechanical retention mechanism prior to application of the supplementary joining layer. The threaded interface 124 maintains secure fixation of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 on the needle shaft 102 under combined rotational and axial loads during assembly and operation of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100.
[34]	In an embodiment, the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 extend over an internal threaded depth within the internal bore 118 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The internal threaded depth of the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 is greater than the threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 of the needle shaft 102. The distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 is fully seated within the internal bore 118 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 with the plurality of external micro-threads 112 in complete engagement with the plurality of internal micro-threads 122.
[35]	In an example, the ratio of the internal threaded depth of the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 to the threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 ranges from 1.1:1 to 1.3:1. The internal threaded depth of the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 ranges from 1.7 mm to 3.4 mm. The threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 ranges from 1.4 mm to 2.8 mm. In some embodiments, the ratio of the internal threaded depth to the threaded length ranges from 1.05:1 to 1.5:1. A ratio within this range provides complete thread engagement between the plurality of external micro-threads 112 and the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 across varying dimensional configurations of the needle shaft 102 and the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. In some embodiments, the internal threaded depth ranges from 1.0 mm to 6.0 mm and the threaded length ranges from 0.5 mm to 5.0 mm. The key dimensional relationship is that the internal threaded depth of the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 is greater than the threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 regardless of the absolute dimensional values selected.
[36]	In an embodiment, the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 includes a rounded atraumatic distal tip. The rounded atraumatic distal tip of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 is configured to puncture target tissue upon delivery of radiofrequency energy through the conductor 114 to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The rounded atraumatic distal tip reduces the risk of unintended mechanical trauma to surrounding tissue during advancement of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 toward the target tissue.
[37]	In an embodiment, the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 is formed from a material selected from the group consisting of platinum-iridium alloy, platinum, and iridium. The platinum-iridium alloy provides high electrical conductivity for radiofrequency energy delivery to target tissue. The platinum-iridium alloy further provides biocompatibility and corrosion resistance under repeated radiofrequency energy delivery cycles.
[38]	FIG. 1E is a cross-sectional view of the conductor coupled to the radiofrequency tip electrode of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. FIG. 1E is described in conjunction with elements from FIG. 1A, FIG. 1B, FIG. 1C, and FIG. 1D. With reference to FIG. 1E, the conductor 114 coupled to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 is shown.
[39]	In an embodiment, the conductor 114 is electrically connected to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 prior to assembly of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100. The conductor 114 extends through the hollow lumen 108 of the needle shaft 102 and provides electrical continuity between the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 and a proximal electrical connector. The radiofrequency tip electrode 116 is mechanically secured to the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 through the threaded interface 124. The threaded interface 124 is formed between the plurality of external micro-threads 112 of the needle shaft 102 and the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The conductor 114 maintains transmission of radiofrequency energy to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 during operation of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100.
[40]	The radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 of the present disclosure achieves secure retention of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 at the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 through the positive mechanical interlock at the threaded interface 124. The combination of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 of the needle shaft 102 and the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 creates the threaded interface 124 that resists both axial displacement and rotational loosening under operational loads. The greater internal threaded depth of the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 relative to the threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 produces complete seating of the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 within the internal bore 118 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. The supplementary joining layer applied at the threaded interface 124 provides additional retention of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 on the needle shaft 102 beyond the positive mechanical interlock. The conductor 114 maintains reliable radiofrequency energy transmission to the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 independently of the mechanical joining method at the threaded interface 124.
[41]	In various embodiments, the plurality of external micro-threads 112 of the needle shaft 102 and the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 interact to provide a dual retention mechanism at the threaded interface 124. The plurality of external micro-threads 112 resist axial pull-out forces through structural interlocking with the plurality of internal micro-threads 122. The plurality of internal micro-threads 122 resist rotational loosening through mating thread geometry with the plurality of external micro-threads 112. The combination of axial retention and rotational resistance at the threaded interface 124 produces a retention force greater than either axial retention alone or rotational resistance alone. The threaded interface 124 maintains secure fixation of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116 on the needle shaft 102 under combined rotational and axial loads applied during advancement of the radiofrequency transseptal needle assembly 100 through vascular anatomy.
[42]	Surprisingly, in an alternative embodiment, the greater internal threaded depth of the plurality of internal micro-threads 122 relative to the threaded length of the plurality of external micro-threads 112 produces complete seating of the distal end 106 of the needle shaft 102 within the internal bore 118 of the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. Complete seating at the threaded interface 124 eliminates axial play between the needle shaft 102 and the radiofrequency tip electrode 116. title: DEVICE FOR PRECISION MICRO-VOLUME ASPIRATION AND DISPENSING
abstract:
A device (100) for precision micro-volume aspiration and dispensing includes a supporting actuating shaft (102) having a non-circular cross-section and a scale index (110), a main casing (104) having internal threads (302), a thread locking sleeve (128) having external threads (204) engaging the internal threads (302) and a non-circular inner bore receiving the supporting actuating shaft (102), a proximal casing (106) threadedly engaged with the main casing (104), and a rotating knob (108) on a proximal face of the proximal casing (106) having a non-circular central bore receiving the supporting actuating shaft (102). Rotation of the rotating knob (108) is transferred to the thread locking sleeve (128) via the supporting actuating shaft (102), converting rotation into axial displacement of the supporting actuating shaft (102), the proximal casing (106) remaining stationary, and each rotation advancing the scale index (110) by one calibrated marking.

specification:
TECHNICAL FIELD
[0001]	The present disclosure relates generally to the field of medical devices for assisted reproductive technology; and more specifically, to a device for precision micro-volume aspiration and dispensing.
BACKGROUND
[0002]	Oocyte and embryo denudation is a step in assisted reproductive technology procedures requiring accurate fluid aspiration and dispensing for safe handling of biological specimens. Conventional devices used in such procedures aspirate and expel small volumes of fluid through a fine-diameter pipette secured at a distal end of the device. The predefined fluid volume is set by the user prior to actuation through a control interface at a proximal end of the device.
[0003]	In one example, conventional volume-setting operations rely on rotary scales requiring visual alignment against a reference marking. However, the rotary scales are susceptible to unintended shifts in the set volume during adjustment, resulting in inaccurate or inconsistent volumetric settings across repeated operations. In another example, existing pipette-holding mechanisms employ friction-fit interfaces for securing the pipette to the device. However, the friction-fit interfaces fail to prevent lateral displacement or axial wobble of fine-diameter pipettes during operation, resulting in increased risk of disruption to delicate biological specimens.
[0004]	Therefore, there exists a need to overcome the aforementioned drawbacks associated with conventional micro-volume aspiration and dispensing devices for assisted reproductive technology procedures.
SUMMARY
[0005]	The present disclosure provides a device for precision micro-volume aspiration and dispensing. The present disclosure provides a solution to the technical problem of how to set a precise fluid volume independently of operator skill or applied force. An aim of the present disclosure is to provide a solution that overcomes at least partially the problems encountered in the prior art. The solution provides a device for precision micro-volume aspiration and dispensing wherein rotation of a rotating knob advances a scale index by one calibrated marking per rotation.
[0006]	One or more objectives of the present disclosure are achieved by the solutions provided in the enclosed independent claims. Advantageous implementations of the present disclosure are further defined in the dependent claims.
[0007]	According to an aspect of the present disclosure, there is provided a device for precision micro-volume aspiration and dispensing. The device comprises a supporting actuating shaft having a non-circular cross-section. The supporting actuating shaft has a scale index marked on an outer surface, the scale index comprising a plurality of calibrated markings. The device further comprises a main casing having internal threads on an inner surface. The device further comprises a thread locking sleeve having external threads engaging the internal threads of the main casing. The thread locking sleeve has a non-circular inner bore receiving the supporting actuating shaft to rotationally couple the thread locking sleeve to the supporting actuating shaft. The device further comprises a proximal casing threadedly engaged with the main casing. The device further comprises a rotating knob disposed on a proximal face of the proximal casing. The rotating knob has a non-circular central bore receiving the supporting actuating shaft to rotationally couple the rotating knob to the supporting actuating shaft. Upon rotation of the rotating knob, the rotation is transferred to the supporting actuating shaft via the non-circular central bore. The rotation is further transferred from the supporting actuating shaft to the thread locking sleeve via the non-circular inner bore. The engagement of the external threads with the internal threads of the main casing converts the rotation of the thread locking sleeve into axial displacement within the main casing. The supporting actuating shaft undergoes axial displacement concurrent with the thread locking sleeve. The proximal casing remains stationary by virtue of the threaded engagement with the main casing. Each rotation of the rotating knob axially advances the supporting actuating shaft by a calibrated increment, advancing the scale index by one calibrated marking.
[0008]	The non-circular profile shared across the rotating knob, supporting actuating shaft, and thread locking sleeve transfers rotation through all three components as a single mechanical unit. The thread locking sleeve advances axially within the main casing upon rotation, converting rotational input into a predetermined axial displacement of the supporting actuating shaft per revolution. The proximal casing remains stationary against the main casing, providing a fixed reference against which the rotating knob rotates. Each revolution of the rotating knob advances the scale index by one calibrated marking. The device further includes an orientation pin and compression spring within the rotating knob that engage successive ribs in the circumferential groove of the proximal casing upon each rotational increment, generating an audible click. The fixed relationship between rotational input and volumetric displacement produces a volume setting independent of the magnitude or direction of user-applied force.
[0009]	A combination of the rotating knob, the supporting actuating shaft, the thread locking sleeve, and the proximal casing establishes a mechanically indexed discrete volumetric control architecture. The rotating knob transfers rotation to the supporting actuating shaft via the non-circular central bore. The supporting actuating shaft transfers rotation to the thread locking sleeve via the non-circular inner bore. The engagement of the external threads with the internal threads converts rotation into axial displacement of the supporting actuating shaft. The proximal casing remains stationary throughout, providing a fixed reference for the scale index. A person skilled in the art would not arrive at the present disclosure without exercising inventive ingenuity because conventional micro-volume aspiration devices teach continuous force-dependent volume adjustment without discrete indexed positioning. No conventional document discloses combining a non-circular shaft coupling with a threaded sleeve advancement mechanism and a stationary proximal casing to produce operator-independent discrete volumetric control.

Rotation applied to the rotating knob 108 is transmitted directly to the supporting actuating shaft 102 through the non-circular central bore without angular slip. The supporting actuating shaft 102 rotates concurrently with the rotating knob 108 upon each rotational input.
[0021]	In an embodiment, each rotation of the rotating knob 108 axially advances the supporting actuating shaft 102 by a calibrated increment within the main casing 104. The calibrated increment advances the scale index 110 by one calibrated marking. The number of rotations of the rotating knob 108 determines the total axial displacement of the supporting actuating shaft 102. Each additional rotation of the rotating knob 108 advances the scale index 110 by one further calibrated marking.
[0022]	In an example, each calibrated marking of the scale index 110 corresponds to a volumetric displacement per rotation of the rotating knob 108 ranging from 0.14 ml to 0.26 ml. The volumetric displacement per rotation is determined by the thread pitch of the internal threaded engagement within the main casing 104. The thread pitch determines the axial distance advanced by the supporting actuating shaft 102 per rotation of the rotating knob 108. A coarser thread pitch produces a greater axial displacement per rotation, advancing the scale index 110 by a larger volumetric increment within the range. A finer thread pitch produces a lesser axial displacement per rotation, advancing the scale index 110 by a smaller volumetric increment within the range. The range of 0.14 ml to 0.26 ml encompasses thread pitch configurations suited to micro-volume fluid handling in assisted reproductive technology procedures.
[0023]	In an embodiment, the volume indicator glass 114 is integrated into the proximal casing 106 as a fixed viewing window. The volume indicator glass 114 is aligned with the scale index 110. The scale index 110 moves axially with the supporting actuating shaft 102. Axial displacement of the supporting actuating shaft 102 brings successive calibrated markings of the scale index 110 into alignment with the volume indicator glass 114. The volume indicator glass 114 remains stationary within the proximal casing 106 during axial displacement of the supporting actuating shaft 102. The calibrated marking of the scale index 110 visible through the volume indicator glass 114 indicates the selected volumetric setting.
[0024]	In some implementations, the plurality of gripping tongs 120 accommodates denudation pipettes of multiple outer diameter sizes within the front opening of the distal casing 118. Each rotation of the rotating knob 108 transfers rotational input to the supporting actuating shaft 102 through the non-circular central bore of the rotating knob 108. Each rotation of the rotating knob 108 advances the scale index 110 by one calibrated marking. The device 100 advances the scale index 110 by a fixed amount per rotation of the rotating knob 108. The volume indicator glass 114 integrated into the proximal casing 106 provides a fixed reference for reading the scale index 110. The device 100 produces a volume setting determined by the number of rotations of the rotating knob 108.

The scale index 110 on the supporting actuating shaft 102 advances by one calibrated marking per rotation. The rotating knob 108 and the proximal casing 106 together produce a direct relationship between user rotation and volumetric displacement. Neither the rotating knob 108 alone nor the proximal casing 106 alone produces the discrete volume increment.

FIG. 1B is described in conjunction with elements from FIG. 1A. With reference to FIG. 1B, there is shown the device 100 in an exploded state.

The device 100 further includes a thread locking sleeve 128 positioned coaxially within the main casing 104. [0029]	In an embodiment, the main shaft 132 is concentrically received within the supporting actuating shaft 102 and extends longitudinally within the device 100 between the proximal end 100B and the distal end 100A. The supporting actuating shaft 102 coaxially houses and guides the main shaft 132 along the central longitudinal axis A1 of the device 100. The main shaft 132 is configured to undergo reciprocating axial displacement for fluid aspiration and expulsion. The coaxial guidance of the supporting actuating shaft 102 maintains alignment of the main shaft 132 throughout each aspiration and expulsion cycle, preventing lateral displacement of the main shaft 132 during operation.
[0030]	In an embodiment, the helical compression spring 130 is disposed coaxially around the main shaft 132 and is operatively coupled between the main shaft 132 and the supporting actuating shaft 102. Upon application of axial force through the proximal end 100B, the helical compression spring 130 undergoes compression, storing mechanical energy. Upon release of the axial force, the helical compression spring 130 decompresses and releases the stored mechanical energy to restore the main shaft 132 to an initial axial position. The controlled compression and decompression of the helical compression spring 130 produces repeatable axial displacement of the main shaft 132 per actuation cycle.
[0031]	In an embodiment, the actuating adjuster 112 is concentrically mounted over a proximal portion of the supporting actuating shaft 102. The socket head cap screw 122 is received through the actuating adjuster 112 and engages the supporting actuating shaft 102 to secure the actuating adjuster 112 to the supporting actuating shaft 102.
