title: Self-Sustaining Evaporative Cooling Curtain System with Automatic Water Recirculation
abstract: The present invention relates to a low-energy evaporative cooling curtain for reducing the temperature of air entering a building through a window. The system comprises a window-mountable frame, a water reservoir, a honeycomb evaporative cooling pad, and a water delivery arrangement configured to distribute water uniformly over the cooling pad. As air passes through the wetted honeycomb pad, evaporation of water absorbs heat from the incoming air, thereby reducing its temperature before entering the room. The system is configured to operate using natural airflow and/or a conventional ceiling fan, without requiring a dedicated blower or compressor. In an embodiment, the system may further comprise a solar power source, water pump, temperature and humidity sensors, controller, and rechargeable battery for automated water circulation and monitoring. The evaporative cooling curtain provides a compact, economical, and energy-efficient cooling solution suitable for residential and other buildings, particularly in hot and dry climatic conditions.
specification:
1)Field of the Invention: - This invention relates to low‑energy cooling systems for buildings, and more particularly to an evaporative cooling curtain that can be mounted on standard residential windows. The curtain uses a honeycomb cooling pad and a simple water delivery system to cool incoming air through evaporation. It is designed to work passively with natural airflow or together with a common ceiling fan to reduce room temperature without using a separate blower or compressor. The invention is especially suited for homes in hot climates, such as in India, where people need a cheaper and more energy‑efficient alternative to air conditioners.

2)Background of Innovation: - 
Preamble to the Description
The increasing frequency of extreme summer temperatures, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions such as India, has significantly increased the demand for affordable and energy-efficient indoor cooling solutions. During peak summer months, ambient temperatures commonly range between 40°C and 45°C, causing severe thermal discomfort, reduced productivity, and adverse health effects, especially in residential buildings occupied by low- and middle-income families. Conventional air-conditioning systems are widely used for indoor cooling; however, their adoption is limited by their high initial purchase cost, typically exceeding ₹30,000, and substantial electricity consumption, generally ranging from 1 to 2 kWh per hour. Continuous operation of such systems can result in monthly electricity expenses of ₹5,000–₹10,000 or more, making them economically impractical for a large segment of the population. Furthermore, the increased use of air conditioners contributes to higher peak electricity demand and greater greenhouse gas emissions due to indirect energy consumption.
The electronic circuit is powered by a 10W solar panel that charges a 3.7V 2000mAh Li-ion battery through an MPPT charge controller, providing continuous operation for 10-12 hours daily even during cloudy weather. An ESP32 microcontroller serves as the central brain, continuously monitoring room temperature and humidity via a DHT22 sensor and water reservoir level using an ultrasonic HC-SR04 sensor. When room temperature exceeds 38°C and humidity remains below 70%, the ESP32 activates a 5V DC water pump through a relay module, delivering precisely 50ml/min water flow to keep the 50mm thick honeycomb cooling pad optimally saturated for maximum evaporative efficiency. Four status LEDs indicate system operation (green: normal, yellow: low water, red: high humidity, blue: solar charging), while a buzzer provides audible alerts for low water levels. The system connects WiFi to a mobile app allowing users to monitor real-time temperature drop (typically 10-12°C), water consumption, battery status, and receive automatic notifications for reservoir refilling. During nighttime, the circuit switches to battery power and enters low-power sleep mode, waking every 30 minutes to check conditions. An integrated light sensor ensures the water pump only operates during daylight hours when solar power is available, maximizing energy efficiency and eliminating electricity bills while delivering consistent room cooling through synergy with existing ceiling fans.


3)Summary of the Invention
The present invention relates to a solar-powered intelligent evaporative cooling curtain system for providing energy-efficient and eco-friendly indoor cooling. The system comprises a 50 mm honeycomb evaporative cooling pad, a 5-litre water reservoir, a low-power DC water pump, an ESP32 microcontroller, and temperature and humidity sensors for automatic water circulation. Powered by a solar panel and battery, the system is mounted on a standard 4 ft × 4 ft window and cools incoming air through evaporative cooling. The cooled air is circulated using existing ceiling fans or natural ventilation, eliminating the need for dedicated blowers. The system also supports Wi-Fi-based monitoring and control through a mobile application, providing a compact, low-cost, and sustainable alternative to conventional air-conditioning and evaporative cooling systems.

4) Prior Art Search: -
	Patent application US5775580A describes an evaporative cooling system designed to cool air by passing it through a wetted evaporative medium. The invention improves conventional evaporative cooling by incorporating a controlled water distribution system that maintains uniform wetting of the evaporative pad, thereby improving cooling efficiency while minimizing water wastage. The patent is primarily intended for ducted or enclosed air-handling systems rather than standalone residential window-mounted units.
	US7014174B2, assigned to Adobe Air Inc. (later associated with Champion Cooler Corporation), presents an improved evaporative cooling system with a focus on durability, corrosion resistance, and simplified manufacturing. Unlike earlier patents that primarily concentrated on cooling performance, this invention addresses the structural design of the evaporative cooler housing, making it easier to manufacture, assemble, transport, and maintain while preserving cooling efficiency. US7014174B2 represents an important advancement in the manufacturing and structural engineering of evaporative coolers by introducing corrosion-resistant, clinched metal housing construction and modular assembly. However, its focus is on improving the physical design of conventional evaporative coolers rather than introducing smart, renewable-energy-powered cooling solutions. This leaves opportunities for innovations such as solar-powered, IoT-enabled, window-mounted evaporative cooling curtains with intelligent water management and ceiling-fan-assisted airflow, which target energy-efficient residential cooling in a different application domain.
	CN201731589U proposes an evaporative heat reclaiming device that recovers waste heat from industrial processes by using water as the primary heat-transfer medium. The invention aims to improve energy utilization by capturing thermal energy that would otherwise be lost and reusing it for heating or process applications. Unlike conventional evaporative coolers intended for human thermal comfort, this utility model focuses on industrial heat recovery and energy conservation. CN201731589U contributes to the field of industrial thermal management by introducing an evaporative heat reclaiming device that uses water as an efficient heat-transfer medium for waste heat recovery. Its objective is to improve industrial energy efficiency rather than provide indoor cooling. Consequently, it differs substantially from your proposed solar-powered, IoT-enabled, honeycomb evaporative cooling curtain, which is intended as a window-mounted residential cooling solution operating with ceiling-fan-assisted airflow and intelligent environmental control. While both technologies involve evaporative heat transfer and water circulation, their applications, system architecture, and intended functions are fundamentally different.

5) Brief Description of Drawing: -
Figure 1: Front perspective view of the evaporative cooling curtain mounted on a 4 ft × 4 ft window, showing the solar panel (100), aluminium frame (101), honeycomb pad (102), water reservoir (103), water level indicator (104), mounting clips (105), frame height (106), side channel (107), drain plug (108), and frame width (109).

Figure 2: Electronic circuit diagram of the evaporative cooling curtain, showing the solar power input (200), MC4 connector (201), MPPT solar charge controller (202), fuse (203), 5V DC-DC buck converter (204), sensor unit (205), ESP32 microcontroller (206), relay module (207), water pump (208), lithium-ion battery (209), user interface (210), wiring legend (211), power flow (212), and system specifications (213).

6)Detailed Description of the Preferred Embodiment

 Figure 1 Referring to Figure 1, the evaporative cooling curtain comprises a solar panel (100), rated at 12V, mounted at the top of the assembly to power the electronic system. The curtain frame (101) is constructed from corrosion-resistant, lightweight aluminium and provides structural support for the assembly. A honeycomb cooling pad (102), 50 mm thick, is positioned within the frame and provides high water retention and evaporation efficiency. A water reservoir (103), of 5-litre capacity, is positioned at the base of the frame and stores and supplies water to the pad. A water level indicator (104) is fitted to the reservoir to allow the user to visually check the remaining water level.
Four mounting clips (105) are provided along the sides of the frame for quick and secure installation on a window frame, without the need for tools. The frame has an overall height (106) of 4 ft (1220 mm). A side channel (107) runs along the frame and distributes water evenly over the honeycomb pad (102). A drain plug (108) is provided at the base of the reservoir for easy cleaning and maintenance. The frame has an overall width (109) of 4 ft (1220 mm), matching standard window dimensions.
Referring to Figure 2, the electronic circuit of the system is powered by a solar panel (200), rated at 18V/40W, connected through an MC4 connector (201) to an MPPT solar charge controller (202). The MPPT controller (202) regulates the charging of an 11.1V, 2200 mAh lithium-ion battery (209), in a 3S configuration, and supplies power, through a 5A fuse (203), to a 5V DC-DC buck converter (204), which regulates the supply to the control electronics at 5V, 2A.
An ESP32 microcontroller (206) forms the central control unit of the system. It receives power at its VIN pin from the buck converter (204) and is connected to a DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor (205), which monitors ambient conditions. The ESP32 (206) is further connected to a 5V relay module (207), which switches a 12V DC water pump (208) on and off, based on the sensor readings, so as to control delivery of water to the honeycomb pad (102). An optional user interface (210), comprising an OLED display, push buttons, and a status LED, may be connected to the ESP32 (206) for local monitoring and control.
The wiring of the circuit follows a defined colour-coded legend (211), in which red indicates a positive connection, black a negative connection, green a signal connection, and yellow a data connection. The overall power flow (212) of the system proceeds from the solar panel (200), through the MPPT solar charge controller (202), to the lithium-ion battery (209), then through the 5V DC-DC buck converter (204), to the ESP32 microcontroller and its associated system loads (206), including the water pump, sensor, and user interface.
The system specifications (213) of the preferred embodiment are as follows: a solar panel rated at 18V/40W; a battery rated at 11.1V lithium-ion in a 3S configuration; an MPPT charger with a maximum output of 12.6V; a buck converter with an output of 5V/2A; a water pump rated at 12V DC, delivering a typical flow rate of 50 ml per minute; a controller in the form of an ESP32 development module; and a sensor in the form of a DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor.

6.1 Working Procedure of Evaporative Cooling Curtain System:
 In use, the solar panel (200) generates electrical power during daylight hours. This power is regulated by the MPPT solar charge controller (202), which charges the lithium-ion battery (209) while simultaneously supplying the system through the 5V DC-DC buck converter (204). The ESP32 microcontroller (206) continuously monitors the ambient temperature and humidity through the DHT22 sensor (205). When the sensed temperature exceeds a predefined threshold and the humidity remains within an acceptable range, the ESP32 (206) energises the relay module (207), which activates the water pump (208). The pump draws water from the reservoir (103) and delivers it, through the side channel (107), evenly across the honeycomb pad (102), keeping it saturated. As air passes through the wetted pad (102), whether through natural airflow or with the assistance of a ceiling fan, it is cooled through evaporation before entering the room.
Once the sensed conditions no longer call for further water delivery, the ESP32 (206) de-energises the relay module (207), switching off the pump (208), so as to conserve water and battery power. The water level indicator (104) allows the user to check the remaining water in the reservoir (103) at a glance, and the reservoir may be drained and cleaned through the drain plug (108) as part of routine maintenance. Where fitted, the optional user interface (210) allows the user to view system status locally and adjust operating settings.

7) Object of the Invention:
1.	To provide an evaporative cooling curtain that operates on solar power at zero electricity cost, suitable for standard 4 ft × 4 ft residential windows in India.
2.	To automatically maintain optimal saturation of the honeycomb pad through an ESP32-controlled water delivery system, based on real-time temperature and humidity readings.
3.	To achieve a room cooling of 10°C to 12°C through use with a common ceiling fan, without requiring a dedicated blower system.
4.	To enable remote monitoring of cooling performance, water level, and solar charging status through a Wi-Fi-based mobile application, with maintenance alerts.
5.	To provide a curtain that can be installed without tools, using a clip-on mounting system, with a replaceable pad giving a working life of more than five years.
6.	To provide a low-cost, low-maintenance cooling solution as an alternative to air conditioners for households in hot climates.
8) Obviousness
 The present invention makes use of components that are individually well known, such as honeycomb pads, solar panels, and ESP32 microcontrollers, which are commonly used in evaporative coolers and IoT-based projects. The use of solar power together with a water pump for pad saturation follows established principles of evaporative cooling, and WiFi-based monitoring reflects standard smart-home functionality. Considered individually, each component would appear to be a routine and predictable choice for residential cooling.

9)Non-obviousness
1. Although honeycomb pads, solar power, and window curtains are individually known, they have not previously been combined into a single window-mounted curtain that operates passively with a ceiling fan under smart solar control.
2. Conventional evaporative coolers require bulky housing and dedicated fans. The present curtain eliminates both requirements by making use of an existing ceiling fan, which is not a straightforward substitution given the difference in airflow characteristics between a dedicated blower and indirect fan circulation.

10)Novelty
1. A curtain-form evaporative cooling device: no known prior art discloses a honeycomb pad configured specifically as a hanging curtain for a window, as opposed to a fixed cooler or casing.
2. Integration with ceiling fan airflow: no known existing system has been designed specifically to operate with a room ceiling fan, as opposed to a dedicated blower.
11) Industrial Applications: - 
	The invention is applicable to residential cooling and is particularly suited to urban households seeking an affordable, low-maintenance alternative to air conditioning. Its compact and low-cost design also makes it suitable for student hostels and paying-guest accommodation, as well as small offices and shops requiring low-cost cooling for limited spaces.
	In an enlarged, modular form, the curtain design may also be used in warehouses and factories, as a replacement for conventional industrial evaporative coolers, and in greenhouses and poultry farms, where curtain-style panels are simpler to install than rigid cooling walls. The system may also provide humidification and cooling for worker comfort in textile and garment manufacturing units.
	The invention may further be offered as a complementary product by ceiling fan manufacturers, solar equipment suppliers, and real estate developers, and has potential application in other regions with hot, dry climates, including parts of the Middle East, Africa, and South Asia.

title: AN ENERGY EFFICIENT FURNACE
abstract:
The present invention is related to an energy efficient furnace, this high energy-efficient
metal melting or smelting furnace comprising an upper zone (110), a middle zone (109), and
a lower zone (108). The upper zone (110) has a top opening (101) for charging metal or metal
ore and fuel, and is lined with a refractory wall lining (102) supported by a supporting brick
construction (103). The middle zone (109) separates the upper zone (110) from the lower
zone (108) and is provided with a hole (104) permitting passage of flue gas and molten metal.
A space for flue gas suction (105) withdraws flue gas from the lower zone (108), creating a
low-pressure region to promote efficient combustion. The lower zone (108) has a hole for
molten metal (106) and a hole for slag (107), and may house a crucible (201) accessible
through a door (202), the crucible having a hole for removing molten metal (203) and a hole
for removing slag (204).

The furnace is constructed in three main sections or zones, as illustrated in

The lower zone of the furnace is provided with a flue gas extraction system
connected to a heat exchanger. The flue gas extraction system, which may include a
vacuum pump, ejector, eductor, or any equivalent device, continuously withdraws flue
10 gas from the lower zone while simultaneously drawing fresh atmospheric air into the
heat exchanger. Heat contained in the flue gas is transferred to the incoming air,

zone of the furnace to preheat the metal or metal ore and improve the overall thermal
efficiency. The cooled flue gas is subsequently directed to a flue gas treatment
15 system, where greenhouse gases and other pollutants are reduced or treated before
discharge to ensure compliance with applicable environmental regulations.
During start-up, the furnace is charged with combustible fuel, such as
charcoal, coke, raw coal, or any other suitable fuel. The fuel is ignited from the upper

title: SMART SOCIETAL OPTIMIZATION-DRIVEN DEEP CONVOLUTIONAL NEURAL NETWORK FOR EPILEPTIC SEIZURE PREDICTION
abstract:
ABSTRACT
The present disclosure relates to artificial intelligence-based healthcare systems, particularly to an intelligent epileptic seizure prediction framework employing a Smart Societal Optimization (SSO) algorithm integrated with a Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN). Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals are acquired and subjected to preprocessing including filtering, normalization, segmentation, and artifact removal. The processed signals are supplied to a deep convolutional neural network for hierarchical feature extraction. Smart Societal Optimization is used to optimize selected model hyperparameters during training to improve prediction performance. The trained model classifies EEG segments into pre-ictal, ictal, or inter-ictal states and enables early warning generation for caregivers or patients. The framework is intended for real-time seizure monitoring applications and may be implemented on cloud, edge, or wearable computing platforms.
specification:
FIELD OF THE DISCLOSURE
The disclosure relates to machine learning, biomedical signal processing, deep learning, and intelligent healthcare systems.
More particularly, the disclosure relates to AI-assisted prediction of epileptic seizures using optimized convolutional neural network architectures.

BACKGROUND
Epilepsy affects millions of individuals worldwide. Prediction of seizures before their onset can improve patient safety and enable timely medical intervention.
Traditional EEG analysis relies on handcrafted features and classical machine learning classifiers, which may have limited ability to model complex nonlinear temporal patterns. Deep learning approaches have improved predictive performance by learning hierarchical representations directly from EEG data. However, selecting appropriate hyperparameters remains computationally challenging.
Optimization algorithms have therefore been investigated to automate parameter tuning and improve predictive accuracy.

OBJECTIVES
The objectives include:
●	developing an intelligent seizure prediction framework;
●	integrating optimization with deep neural networks;
●	improving prediction accuracy while reducing false alarms;
●	supporting real-time deployment;
●	enabling wearable healthcare monitoring;
●	reducing computational complexity during model optimization.

SUMMARY
The proposed framework includes:
1.	EEG acquisition
2.	Signal preprocessing
3.	Deep CNN feature extraction
4.	Smart Societal Optimization-based hyperparameter tuning
5.	Multi-class seizure prediction
6.	Early warning generation
The optimization module searches the hyperparameter space while the CNN extracts discriminative spatial-temporal EEG representations.

BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES
Figure 1
Overall system architecture illustrating EEG acquisition, preprocessing, deep CNN, optimization engine, prediction module, and alert generation.
Figure 2
Flowchart of the Smart Societal Optimization algorithm including initialization, social interaction, cooperation, learning, evaluation, and iterative updating.
Figure 3
Deep CNN architecture showing convolutional layers, pooling layers, batch normalization, dense layers, dropout, and Softmax classifier.
Figure 4
Real-time deployment architecture using wearable EEG device, edge processor, cloud server, mobile application, and caregiver notification.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
Step 1: EEG Acquisition
EEG signals are continuously collected using wearable or clinical EEG systems.

Step 2: Preprocessing
The preprocessing stage includes
●	band-pass filtering
●	notch filtering
●	artifact removal
●	normalization
●	segmentation
●	window generation

Step 3: Feature Learning
Each EEG segment is supplied to a deep CNN comprising multiple convolutional blocks.
Each block consists of
●	convolution
●	ReLU activation
●	batch normalization
●	max pooling
The final feature maps are flattened and supplied to fully connected layers.

Step 4: Smart Societal Optimization
The optimization module tunes selected CNN hyperparameters such as:
●	learning rate
●	batch size
●	dropout rate
●	number of filters
●	kernel size
●	optimizer selection
Candidate solutions are evaluated using a fitness function based on validation performance.

Step 5: Classification
The optimized CNN predicts EEG states including
●	Pre-Ictal
●	Ictal
●	Inter-Ictal
Softmax output probabilities determine the predicted class.

Step 6: Alert Generation
When a pre-ictal condition exceeds a configurable confidence threshold, an alert may be transmitted to:
●	patient
●	caregiver
●	clinician
using mobile, cloud, or edge computing platforms.

ADVANTAGES
●	Improved prediction accuracy
●	Reduced false alarm rate
●	Automated parameter optimization
●	Real-time monitoring capability
●	Suitable for wearable healthcare
●	Scalable cloud deployment
●	Adaptive learning capability

APPLICATIONS
●	Wearable epilepsy monitoring
●	Hospital intensive care monitoring
●	Telemedicine
●	Smart healthcare systems
●	Edge AI medical devices
●	Remote patient monitoring

DRAWING

 ,
claims:
CLAIMS
Claim 1
A computer-implemented epileptic seizure prediction system comprising an EEG acquisition module, a preprocessing module, a convolutional neural network configured to classify EEG segments, and an optimization module that adjusts one or more training hyperparameters of the neural network using a population-based search strategy, wherein the system outputs a seizure prediction state.
Claim 2
The system of claim 1, wherein the preprocessing module performs one or more of filtering, artifact reduction, normalization, segmentation, or windowing of EEG signals.
Claim 3
The system of claim 1, wherein the convolutional neural network comprises a plurality of convolutional layers, activation layers, pooling layers, and one or more fully connected layers configured to classify EEG data into seizure-related states.
Claim 4
The system of claim 1, wherein the optimization module evaluates candidate hyperparameter configurations using a fitness metric derived from model performance on validation data.
Claim 5
The system of claim 1, further comprising an alert module configured to generate a notification when the predicted probability of a pre-seizure state exceeds a predetermined threshold.
Claim 6
The system of claim 1, wherein the seizure prediction system is deployable on one or more of a wearable device, an edge computing platform, a cloud computing platform, or a mobile application.

title: “DESIGN OF AN FSM FREE LOW POWER SUCCESSIVE APPROXIMATION REGISTER (SAR) LOGIC USING CAPTURE AND HOLD OPERATION WITH CLOCK GATING FOR SAR ADCS”
abstract:
DESIGN OF AN FSM FREE LOW POWER SUCCESSIVE APPROXIMATION REGISTER (SAR) LOGIC USING CAPTURE AND HOLD OPERATION WITH CLOK GATING FOR SAR ADCS
Abstract
An FSM-free, low-power Successive Approximation Register (SAR) logic architecture for Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs) utilizes a capture-and-hold operation with data-dependent localized clock gating. The architecture comprises a modular bit-slice arrangement where each bit stage includes a modified SAR register and an event-driven SAR control block. The SAR register integrates an XOR-NAND gating circuit that monitors data transitions between the current bit and an upcoming bit, disabling the clock during stable periods to enforce a sleep mode. The control block eliminates conventional FSMs, decoders, and multiplexers, implementing instead a two-way transmission gate latch structure controlled directly by the transition edge of the upcoming bit line. Upon transition, the latch captures the comparator output and electrically isolates the bit-slice, suppressing subsequent switching noise and minimizing dynamic power dissipation. The architecture reduces the per-bit transistor count to 68, achieving a 700 ps conversion speed and 1.56 mW average power. 
(FIG. 1)
specification:
DESIGN OF AN FSM FREE LOW POWER SUCCESSIVE APPROXIMATION REGISTER (SAR) LOGIC USING CAPTURE AND HOLD OPERATION WITH CLOK GATING FOR SAR ADCS

Technical field
The present disclosure relates generally to the technical domain of mixed-signal integrated circuit design, electronic data converters, and low-power digital control architectures. More particularly, the present invention relates to a high-speed, power-optimized Successive Approximation Register (SAR) logic circuit architecture deployed within Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs). The architecture specifically utilizes an event-driven, finite state machine (FSM)-free control methodology combined with a localized, data-dependent clock gating network. This structural arrangement minimizes dynamic switching energy, reduces transistor count, suppresses internal switching noise, and enhances the overall power-delay product, rendering the invention highly applicable to ultra-low-power biomedical systems, implantable cardiac pacemakers, Internet of Things (IoT) edge devices, and scalable high-performance signal acquisition instruments. 
Background of the Invention
Successive Approximation Register (SAR) Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs) have emerged as a preferred architecture for medium-to-high-resolution applications characterized by moderate sampling rates. In a typical SAR ADC topology, a binary search algorithm is executed over a plurality of successive clock cycles to resolve an analog input voltage into its nearest digital equivalent representation. The foundational building blocks of such a system routinely comprise an input sampling switch, a dynamic comparator, a capacitive digital-to-analog converter (CDAC) network, and a digital SAR control block. The digital SAR control block operates as the logic core of the converter, continually interpreting the binary decisions generated by the dynamic comparator to sequentially manipulate the bit-line switches of the CDAC network, thereby iteratively converging the reference voltage toward the sampled input voltage. 
Despite the intrinsic energy efficiency associated with the mostly digital architecture of SAR topologies, conventional implementations suffer from severe performance bottlenecks dictated by the structural overhead of the SAR control logic. Traditional synchronous SAR control architectures rely heavily on a centralized Finite State Machine (FSM) governed by a globally distributed, continuously running master clock. This FSM-driven sequence typically incorporates structural elements such as ring counters, multi-bit shift registers, 3x8 or 2:4 decoders, and multi-input multiplexers to sequentially guide each bit position through three rigid, repeating macro-states, specifically a shifting mode, a data load mode, and a memorization mode. For an N-bit conversion resolution, conventional topographies often require 2N or more power-intensive D-flip-flops (DFFs) and an extensive quantity of combinational gates, which can frequently exceed 296 transistors per individual bit-slice. 
The primary deficiency of this conventional synchronous control arrangement stems from the global clock tree and the continuous state-switching activity. Because the global clock signal is delivered uniformly across all digital blocks regardless of their instantaneous functional relevance, the internal nodes, logic gates, and memory elements toggle continuously throughout the entire conversion cycle. This constant redundant switching dissipates a massive amount of dynamic power (\frac12 C V^2 f), which frequently renders the control logic a hidden power bottleneck, restricting the viability of the entire ADC in strict, energy-constrained micro-systems such as implantable medical devices or battery-operated real-time IoT nodes. Furthermore, the considerable hardware density yields a large silicon area overhead, while the massive influx of concurrent digital transitions introduces high switching noise, causing parasitic substrate coupling that directly degrades the spectral purity and linearity of the analog-to-digital interface. 
Alternative contemporary solutions have attempted to exploit fully asynchronous or self-timed control loops to eliminate the global clock grid. While these asynchronous approaches do avoid global clock tree distribution losses, they inherently introduce a severe hardware penalty in the form of complex event-driven handshaking networks, local done-detectors, delay-line calibrations, and metastability suppression filters. This intricate coordination logic frequently consumes nearly 30% of the total ADC power budget, introducing substantial design complexity and susceptibility to process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variations. Consequently, there exists a critical, unfulfilled need in the state of the art for a robust, structurally simplified synchronous SAR control logic that circumvents the power penalties of traditional synchronous FSMs and the structural complexities of asynchronous multi-phase sequencing networks. 
Objects of the Invention
The principal objective of the present invention is to provide a highly optimized, FSM-free synchronous SAR control logic architecture that substantively overcomes the structural deficiencies, area overheads, and high dynamic power consumption characteristics of the prior art. 
Another objective of the present invention is to introduce a localized, data-dependent clock gating mechanism within the SAR shift register that calculates real-time signal transitions using an integrated XOR-NAND topology, thereby automatically forcing idle bit slices into an ultra-low-power sleep mode without introducing latency or disrupting the binary search path. 
Yet another objective of the present invention is to completely eliminate complex, high-gate-count components such as state registers, decoders, and multiplexers from the bit-level control logic, substituting them with an event-driven, two-way transmission gate latch structure synchronized to the transition edge of an upcoming bit slice. 
Still another objective of the present invention is to minimize the total transistor count per bit position from approximately 296 transistors down to 68 transistors, effectively reducing the silicon area, optimizing layout density, and suppressing localized digital switching noise to substantially improve the overall signal-to-noise and distortion ratio (SNDR) and linearity of the SAR ADC. 
A final objective of the present invention is to achieve sub-nanosecond conversion cycle latency alongside milliwatt-range power dissipation, rendering the scalable architecture highly compatible with monotonic switching schemes and ideally optimized for inclusion within high-density biomedical implants, pacemaker microcircuits, and low-power IoT electronics. 
Summary of the Invention
The present invention addresses these objectives by disclosing an FSM-free, low-power successive approximation register (SAR) logic architecture that operates on a capture-and-hold principle tightly coupled with data-dependent localized clock gating. The architecture completely re-engineers the digital core of a SAR ADC by segmenting the control loop into a highly optimized, dual-block configuration per bit-slice: a modified power-efficient SAR shift register and an ultra-lean, event-driven SAR control logic block. By replacing multi-state synchronous state machines and combinational decoders with a decentralized, transition-triggered latch structure, the present invention isolates internal node switching to single functional events per bit position, thereby minimizing dynamic power dissipation and hardware area. 
According to a primary aspect of the present invention, the power-efficient SAR register comprises a cascaded chain of D-flip-flops that function as a shift register initialized by an external conversion start signal. To mitigate global clock distribution losses, a data-dependent clock gating network is integrated locally within each flip-flop stage. This clock gating network comprises an exclusive-OR (XOR) logic gate coupled to a NAND logic gate. The XOR gate continuously monitors and computes the logical difference between the current input of the respective flip-flop and the output of the immediately upcoming bit position. When these two digital values are identical, the XOR output settles to a logic low state, effectively disabling the propagation of the system clock pulse through the NAND gate and forcing the respective flip-flop into a zero-power sleep mode. Conversely, when a valid data transition occurs between the current input and the upcoming bit output, the XOR output transitions to a logic high state, instantly gating the system clock through to the flip-flop to allow normal binary search propagation. 
According to another aspect of the present invention, the SAR control logic block completely discards traditional FSM decoders and multiplexers, implementing instead an ultra-lean two-way latch structure configured to execute a distinct capture-and-hold operation. Each control logic block uses the digital transition of the immediately upcoming bit position as its primary latching and isolation trigger. When the upcoming bit position is at a logic low state, a transmission gate situated at the input of the bit slice remains conductive, allowing the instantaneous output of the main comparator to propagate through a buffer stage composed of series-connected inverters. However, at the precise instance when the upcoming bit position undergoes a positive digital transition, the input transmission gate is deactivated and an internal feedback transmission gate loop is enabled. This structural change instantly captures and locks the comparator's output corresponding to that specific bit position into a localized static latch, while simultaneously establishing total electrical isolation for that specific bit-slice. Once isolated, no subsequent switching or voltage transitions can occur within that bit position's control buffer, even if the main comparator toggles during later bit cycles, ensuring that the control logic acts as a single-event-per-bit system that consumes near-zero standby power during the remainder of the conversion cycle.

Detailed Description 
The structural configuration and operational methodology of the FSM-free low-power Successive Approximation Register (SAR) logic using a capture-and-hold operation with clock gating will now be described in detail with reference to preferred embodiments and functional circuit arrangements. The complete architecture is designed to interface seamlessly within a multi-bit SAR Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) system, which typically includes a differential or single-ended capacitive digital-to-analog converter (CDAC) network, a high-speed dynamic comparator, and integrated bootstrap sampling switches. 
The overall macro-architecture of the complete SAR logic is organized as a modular, bit-slice configuration, where an N-bit resolution ADC incorporates N uniquely assigned stages cascaded sequentially from the most significant bit (MSB) position down to the least significant bit (LSB) position. Each independent bit-slice is structurally identical and comprises a modified SAR register block and a novel SAR control logic block. Rather than depending on a centralized, multi-state digital controller, the proposed architecture distributes the control burden locally across the bit-slices by utilizing the interconnecting digital data lines as event triggers. This arrangement allows the entire system to run synchronously with a global clock signal while behaving internally as an event-driven, single-transition topology. 
The power-efficient SAR register block within each bit-slice is implemented utilizing a single D-flip-flop structurally modified to incorporate a dedicated data-dependent clock gating circuit. Instead of routing the primary system clock directly to the clock pin of the D-flip-flop, a localized, gated clock signal is synthesized on-chip within each bit slice. The data-dependent clock gating circuitry consists of a two-input exclusive-OR (XOR) gate whose output terminal is connected directly to a first input terminal of a two-input NAND gate. The second input terminal of the NAND gate is coupled directly to the master system clock distribution line. The two inputs of the local XOR gate are tied to the immediate data input line (S_n) of that specific flip-flop stage and to the data output line (S_n-1) of the immediately succeeding, upcoming bit position, respectively. 
The operation of this localized clock gating circuit directly suppresses unnecessary dynamic power dissipation by monitoring data stability. During periods when the binary search algorithm is processing alternative regions of the CDAC or when the localized data remains unchanged, the data input line (S_n) and the upcoming bit output line (S_n-1) maintain identical logical states. Consequently, the output of the XOR gate settles to a solid logic low level (GND or 0), which forces the output of the NAND gate to remain constantly at a static logic high level (VDD or 1) regardless of the continuous high-frequency toggling of the master system clock. This action eliminates all clock edge propagation into the internal parasitic capacitances of that specific D-flip-flop, keeping the stage in an ultra-low-power sleep mode. Conversely, when a valid binary search data shift propagates down the register chain, a temporary mismatch occurs between S_n and S_n-1, causing the XOR gate output to transition to a logic high level. This transition enables the NAND gate, allowing a localized clock pulse to propagate directly to the D-flip-flop, ensuring normal data shifting performance without introducing setup or hold-time violations. 
The detailed schematic composition of the proposed FSM-free SAR control logic block per individual bit-slice avoids complex combinational decoders or multi-transistor multiplexers. Each control block slice comprises a multi-stage transmission gate ring latch configuration driven directly by the upcoming bit line signal (S_n-1) and its logical complement (\overlineS_n-1). A first input transmission gate is positioned at the primary input terminal of the control block to receive the raw output signal from the dynamic comparator. This input transmission gate is formed by a parallel combination of an NMOS transistor and a PMOS transistor, wherein the gate terminal of the NMOS transistor is driven by the complement signal \overlineS_n-1 and the gate terminal of the PMOS transistor is driven by the true upcoming bit line signal S_n-1. The output of this first input transmission gate is routed through a stabilizing buffer stage comprising two CMOS inverters connected in series, which subsequently drives the main output node (Q_n) of the control block via an additional pair of drive inverters to interface with the switch controls of the CDAC network. 
Crucially, the control logic block incorporates a second internal loop transmission gate and a third isolation transmission gate to execute the distinct capture-and-hold operation. The second transmission gate is arranged in a cross-coupled feedback loop with an internal inverter stage to form a static regenerative latch. The gate controls of this feedback transmission gate are inverted relative to the first input transmission gate, meaning its NMOS gate terminal is tied to S_n-1 and its PMOS gate terminal is tied to \overlineS_n-1. A third transmission gate is positioned along the comparator input path to provide dynamic isolation. 
The technical execution of the capture-and-hold sequence proceeds through distinct phases governed by the voltage transitions of S_n-1. When the upcoming bit line S_n-1 is at a logic low state (GND), the first input transmission gate is highly conductive, allowing the real-time evaluation voltage from the comparator to pass freely through the series inverters to initialize the current bit output Q_n. During this phase, the secondary feedback transmission gate remains completely non-conductive, preventing internal latch contention. At the exact instance when the upcoming bit line S_n-1 experiences a positive-going transition from logic low to logic high, the first input transmission gate turns off, blocking the comparator input path. Simultaneously, the secondary feedback transmission gate turns on, engaging the internal inverter feedback loop. This captures the comparator output value corresponding to that precise decision edge and locks it securely into the static latch. 
Once this capture event terminates, the entire bit-slice is electrically isolated from both the comparator output and the master clock distribution network. Even if the main comparator continues to toggle at a high frequency during subsequent clock cycles to resolve lower-order bits, the structural combination of the deactivated input transmission gate and the static latch prevents any voltage fluctuations or dynamic charging currents from penetrating the isolated bit-slice. The circuit components within the isolated slice remain in a static, non-switching state, reducing the dynamic current consumption (I_SAR) to near-zero levels. 
This event-driven behavior transforms the conversion operation into a single-event-per-bit system. The entire multi-mode functionality of conventional state machines is compressed into the natural, transition-triggered sequencing of the transmission gates. In terms of hardware implementation costs, a conventional SAR control block requires an implementation budget of approximately 276 transistors per bit position due to the incorporation of 4:1 multiplexers, 2:4 decoders, and multi-input OR gates. The proposed control logic block achieves an identical functional bit-resolution using only 48 transistors total for the dual-control structure (24 transistors per individual single block). Combined with the 20 transistors allocated for the standard D-flip-flop of the SAR register, the entire per-bit transistor consumption drops from 296 transistors down to 68 transistors. For a 12-bit SAR ADC implementation, this structural optimization provides a substantial reduction in total digital transistor count from 816 down to 355 transistors. 
The high-speed capabilities and electrical efficiency of the present invention have been validated through transient simulations conducted within a Cadence design environment. The simulated timing waveforms demonstrate that the entire binary search sequence for a 12-bit configuration completes within a total latency of only 0.7 ns (~700 ps). Specifically, the precise time delay measured from the positive transition edge of the upcoming bit signal S_n-1 to the corresponding stable settling response of the output Q_n is approximately 724 ps, proving that the architecture provides ultra-high-speed data conversion matching or exceeding conventional asynchronous designs. Furthermore, current waveform profiling demonstrates that the dynamic current consumption of the complete SAR block drops to near-zero levels immediately following each localized capture event, yielding an average power dissipation of only 1.56 mW for a 12-bit conversion block. The architecture also minimizes localized substrate switching noise, which directly enhances the linearity, total harmonic distortion (THD), and spurious-free dynamic range (SFDR) of the associated SAR ADC without necessitating complex analog calibration networks. 
Advantages of the Invention
The FSM-free low-power SAR logic architecture disclosed herein provides several distinct techno-legal, functional, and commercial advantages over conventional data converter control circuits, including:
•	Substantial Reduction in Dynamic Power Dissipation: By implementing localized, transition-driven XOR-NAND clock gating, the present invention eliminates unnecessary clock distribution losses across idle or stable register segments, constraining digital power consumption strictly to active node transitions and lowering average power to 1.56 mW for a 12-bit system. 
•	Near-Zero Standby Power States: The utilization of the unique capture-and-hold transmission gate architecture ensures that each individual bit-slice is completely electrically isolated immediately following its single conversion decision event, suppressing redundant switching and yielding near-zero power usage during stable input conditions. 
•	Ultra-High-Speed Operational Velocity: The elimination of complex FSM processing states, multi-level decoders, and multiplexer propagation delays allows the binary search sequence to execute with a sub-nanosecond conversion latency of approximately 700 ps, facilitating high-speed data acquisition. 
•	Extensive Silicon Area Optimization: Compressing the control circuit layout from 296 transistors down to 68 transistors per bit position yields an approximate 77% reduction in total component density, drastically shrinking the required silicon die area and lowering manufacturing costs for large-scale integrated circuit production. 
•	Suppression of Localized Switching Noise: Minimizing the total number of active digital gates and limiting concurrent clock edge transitions significantly reduces internal switching noise, preventing parasitic substrate noise coupling into adjacent high-precision analog blocks and naturally enhancing the overall spectral linearity and SNR of the ADC. 
•	Enhanced Architectural Scalability and Reliability: The decentralized, modular bit-slice configuration operates without requiring centralized FSM logic controllers or intricate asynchronous handshake delay matching, permitting the architecture to scale seamlessly to higher bit resolutions (N > 12) or lower supply voltages without risking timing hazards or metastability. 
•	Full Compatibility with Monotonic Switching Topologies: The deterministic, edge-triggered latch synchronization guarantees precise compatibility with energy-efficient monotonic CDAC switching configurations, making the invention highly suitable for critical low-power applications such as implantable cardiac pacemakers, wearable health monitors, and remote IoT edge nodes.

title: SYSTEM FOR SECURE EMBEDDED DEVICE IDENTIFICATION USING HARDWARE FINGERPRINT SIGNAL EXTRACTION
abstract: A system for secure identification of an embedded device is disclosed. A challenge and excitation module causes a hardware resource of the embedded device to perform a defined operating activity, and a signal acquisition module acquires one or more hardware-originated response signals temporally associated with the activity. The response signals are conditioned, aligned and converted into stable device-discriminative features. Features from one or more physical signal domains are fused into a composite hardware fingerprint, while a quality evaluator determines whether the acquisition is sufficiently reliable for identity determination. The fingerprint is quantized and protected using error-tolerant information and a one-way transformation or helper-data arrangement, thereby reducing dependence on retention of raw signal traces or a clonable stored identifier. An identity decision module compares a newly derived fingerprint with protected reference fingerprint information and generates a device identity or trust output when fingerprint similarity and acquisition-quality criteria are jointly satisfied. Accompanied Drawing [FIGS. 1-2].
specification:
The present invention relates generally to embedded-system security and device authentication. More particularly, the invention relates to a system for identifying and authenticating an embedded device by extracting a reproducible hardware fingerprint from intrinsic physical signal responses of electronic components and interconnects of the device, without requiring a permanently stored conventional device identifier as the sole basis of identity.
[002] The invention further relates to acquisition, conditioning, feature extraction, fusion, protection, comparison and trust determination techniques for deriving a device-specific fingerprint from one or more measurable hardware-originated signals generated under a controlled operating challenge.
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
[003] Embedded devices are increasingly deployed in industrial control, transportation, energy, healthcare equipment, consumer electronics, communication infrastructure and networked sensing environments. Such devices frequently require reliable identification before firmware is provisioned, a communication session is established, privileged functionality is enabled, or a remote service accepts data originating from the device.
[004] Conventional identification mechanisms commonly rely on serial numbers, programmed identifiers, cryptographic keys, certificates or other digital credentials stored in non-volatile memory. Although such mechanisms are useful, a stored identifier can become a target for extraction, duplication, substitution, cloning or unauthorized transfer, particularly when an adversary obtains physical access to the embedded device.
[005] Hardware-based identification techniques have therefore been proposed in which manufacturing variations are used as a source of device uniqueness. However, practical deployment can be affected by temperature, supply variation, ageing, electromagnetic interference, clock drift, measurement noise, component replacement and changes in operating state. A raw physical response may consequently be insufficiently stable for dependable field identification.
[006] Certain known approaches depend upon a dedicated physical unclonable function circuit or a specially fabricated security element. Such additions can increase bill-of-material cost, consume silicon area, require redesign of an existing product, or be unavailable in legacy embedded devices. There remains a need for an identification architecture capable of using naturally occurring signal characteristics of already-present hardware resources.
[007] A further technical problem is that a single measured parameter may not provide adequate entropy and stability simultaneously. For example, oscillator frequency can be distinctive yet temperature-sensitive, while a transient current response may contain rich device information but can vary with load. Reliance on one measurement domain can therefore increase false rejection or false acceptance under changing environmental conditions.
[008] Another difficulty arises from the security of the fingerprint itself. If a stable fingerprint is stored or transmitted in an exposed form, interception may permit replay or correlation of a device across systems. A useful embedded-device identification solution should therefore protect the extracted fingerprint and preferably avoid retention of unnecessary raw analogue traces.
[009] There is also a requirement to distinguish intrinsic device variation from temporary disturbances and malicious manipulation. Signal acquisition should be synchronized with a defined challenge or operating event, and the extracted characteristics should be assessed for quality, consistency and cross-domain agreement before an identity decision is generated.
[010] Existing authentication arrangements may additionally require a network connection or a central server for every decision. In safety-critical or resource-constrained deployments, local verification is desirable so that a device can establish an identity or trust state even when connectivity is intermittent, while still supporting remote enrollment and verification when available.
[011] Accordingly, there exists a need for a secure embedded-device identification system that derives a repeatable and device-specific hardware fingerprint from intrinsic signal responses, compensates for operating and environmental variation, combines features from one or more signal domains, protects the resulting fingerprint, and produces an authentication decision without depending exclusively on a clonable stored identifier.
[012] The present invention addresses the foregoing technical requirements by providing a challenge-synchronized signal extraction architecture in which selected hardware-originated signals are sampled, normalized, converted into stable discriminative features, fused into a protected fingerprint representation and compared with an enrolled reference subject to quality and tolerance criteria.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
[013] An object of the present invention is to provide a system for secure identification of an embedded device using intrinsic hardware signal characteristics generated by manufacturing tolerances and device-specific physical behavior.
[014] Another object of the invention is to obtain the device identity from signals available from functional hardware resources of the embedded device, thereby reducing dependence on a dedicated identity circuit or on a permanently stored plain-text identifier.
[015] In one aspect, the system comprises a challenge and excitation module configured to place the embedded device or a selected hardware resource into a defined operating condition, a signal acquisition module configured to acquire one or more hardware-originated response signals, a conditioning module configured to normalize and suppress disturbances in the acquired signals, and a feature extraction engine configured to derive a plurality of device-discriminative features.
[016] The hardware-originated response signals may include, individually or in combination, power-supply transient characteristics, clock or oscillator timing characteristics, start-up timing, voltage response, current response, analogue conversion residuals, memory-access timing, communication-edge timing, thermal response, or other measurable physical responses arising from tolerances of the device hardware.
[017] A fingerprint fusion engine binds features obtained from different sampling windows and/or signal domains into a composite fingerprint representation. A quality evaluator determines whether the acquired response satisfies predetermined stability and integrity criteria, thereby preventing a low-quality or manipulated acquisition from being accepted merely because selected features fall within a comparison tolerance.
[018] The composite fingerprint is transformed into a protected representation using quantization, error-tolerant encoding and a one-way cryptographic transformation or helper-data arrangement, such that the system can compare a newly derived fingerprint with an enrolled reference without requiring long-term retention of the complete raw signal trace.
[019] An identity decision module compares the protected fingerprint or a reconstruction derived therefrom with reference fingerprint information stored locally or remotely and generates a device identity or trust output when a required similarity condition and quality condition are jointly satisfied.
[020] The disclosed architecture improves robustness by synchronizing acquisition to a challenge event, compensating for measured environmental or operating parameters, selecting stable features, and optionally requiring agreement between features derived from different physical signal domains.
[021] The invention is applicable to newly manufactured as well as legacy embedded devices, and may be implemented by firmware, programmable logic, a security controller, an external verifier, or a combination thereof, without limiting the invention to any particular processor architecture or communication protocol.
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS
[022] The accompanying drawings illustrate exemplary embodiments of the invention and, together with the following description, explain the principles and operation of the secure embedded-device identification system. The drawings are schematic and are not necessarily drawn to scale.
[023] FIG. 1 illustrates a functional block diagram of a system for secure embedded-device identification using hardware fingerprint signal extraction, including a challenge and excitation module, signal acquisition module, conditioning module, feature extraction engine, fingerprint fusion engine, secure reference store and identity decision module.
[024] FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary signal-processing flow for generating a protected device fingerprint from challenge-synchronized multi-domain hardware responses, including sampling, normalization, event alignment, feature extraction, feature binding, quality scoring, quantization and protected fingerprint generation.
DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION
[025] Referring to FIG. 1, a secure identification system 100 is arranged to identify an embedded device 110 from measurable physical responses of hardware already forming part of, or electrically associated with, the embedded device 110. The embedded device 110 may comprise a microcontroller-based product, processor board, sensor node, control unit, communication module, programmable logic device, system-on-chip assembly or another electronic apparatus having one or more hardware resources that exhibit repeatable device-specific physical variation.
[026] A challenge and excitation module 120 causes a selected hardware resource to enter a predetermined state or execute a predetermined activity. The challenge may comprise a controlled processor workload, a defined memory-access sequence, a switching pattern applied to an input/output resource, an oscillator enable event, a power-domain transition, an analogue conversion sequence, or a communication transmission pattern. The challenge establishes a reproducible temporal reference for measurement and need not reveal or encode the device identity.
[027] A signal acquisition module 130 acquires at least one response signal produced during or following the challenge. The acquisition may be internal to the embedded device 110 or may be performed by a verifier electrically coupled to the device. In an exemplary embodiment, the module 130 samples two or more physically different response domains so that identity is not dependent upon a single parameter.
[028] A first response domain may comprise a supply-current or supply-voltage transient associated with the controlled activity. Manufacturing variations in transistor characteristics, interconnect resistance, decoupling behavior and switching paths can produce small but repeatable differences in transient shape, settling behavior, spectral energy and event timing. A second response domain may comprise clock-related timing, oscillator frequency, duty-cycle asymmetry, edge displacement or phase behavior associated with the same or a synchronized challenge interval.
[029] Additional response domains may be obtained from start-up latency, memory read or write timing, peripheral response timing, analogue-to-digital conversion residual patterns, sensor-interface settling, thermal rise characteristics or communication edge timing. The particular signals are selected according to the hardware resources available in the target embedded device and according to their measured repeatability and discriminatory contribution.
[030] The conditioning module 140 receives the sampled response and performs one or more of offset removal, gain normalization, resampling, filtering, outlier suppression, baseline correction, drift compensation and environmental compensation. Environmental parameters such as supply voltage and temperature may be measured contemporaneously and used to normalize the response or to select an applicable reference model.
[031] As illustrated in FIG. 2, controlled challenge 210 is followed by multi-domain sampling 220. Normalization and noise rejection 230 reduce measurement variability that is not attributable to persistent device characteristics. Windowing and event alignment 240 align the sampled data relative to a challenge marker, detected transition or correlation peak so that corresponding physical events are compared across enrollment and verification acquisitions.
[032] A feature extraction engine 150 derives a feature vector from the conditioned response. Temporal features may include rise time, fall time, settling time, time-to-threshold, local extrema, integrated energy, derivative characteristics and event-to-event timing. Spectral features may include selected frequency-bin energy, harmonic ratios, spectral centroid or band-energy relationships. Statistical features may include variance, skewness, correlation coefficients and distributions calculated over repeated challenge instances.
[033] The feature extraction engine 150 preferably does not treat every measurable feature as equally useful. During enrollment, repeated acquisitions are used to determine intra-device stability of candidate features. Features exhibiting excessive variation are discarded or assigned reduced weight, while features providing stable separation from corresponding features of other devices are retained or assigned increased weight.
[034] Cross-domain feature binding 260 combines features that arise from different physical phenomena but correspond to the same challenge. In one embodiment, a temporal relationship between a power transient feature and a clock timing feature is included in the composite representation. Such binding makes substitution or replay of an isolated signal trace less effective because a valid identity requires mutually consistent responses across the selected domains.
[035] A quality and stability evaluator 270 calculates a quality score for each acquisition. The quality score may be based on signal-to-noise ratio, challenge alignment confidence, number of valid samples, environmental range, consistency across repeated challenge cycles, and cross-domain temporal agreement. A verification attempt is rejected or repeated when the quality score is below a threshold, independently of the apparent fingerprint similarity.
[036] The fingerprint fusion engine 160 receives the selected features and forms a composite fingerprint. Feature values may be normalized to enrollment-derived ranges and quantized into symbols or bits. To accommodate bounded physical variation, the system may apply tolerance bands, reliability masks, error-correcting information or secure helper data. The helper data is selected so that it assists reconstruction or comparison of a stable fingerprint while not directly constituting the device identity.
[037] In an exemplary protected-fingerprint process 290, the stable quantized representation is supplied to a one-way cryptographic function, optionally together with a verifier nonce, deployment-specific salt or context value. The resulting protected fingerprint may be retained as reference information in secure reference store 170. Raw analogue traces may be discarded after enrollment or after extraction of the required features, thereby reducing exposure of detailed physical response information.
[038] During enrollment, the challenge is repeated a plurality of times under one or more permissible operating conditions. The system determines a reference feature center, feature tolerance, feature reliability indication and/or protected reference representation. Enrollment may be accepted only when the acquired responses satisfy a minimum repeatability criterion, thereby avoiding creation of an unstable reference.
[039] During verification, the same class of challenge is applied and a fresh response is acquired. The newly extracted feature vector is compensated using current operating parameters and is compared with the enrolled information. A similarity value may be determined from weighted feature distances, bit agreement after error tolerance, successful reconstruction of a protected value, or a combination thereof.
[040] The identity decision and trust output module 180 generates a positive identity determination only when at least a fingerprint-matching criterion and an acquisition-quality criterion are satisfied. In an embodiment employing multiple signal domains, the module 180 additionally requires a minimum domain-consistency criterion. The output may comprise a binary authenticated/not-authenticated state, a device identity associated with the matched reference, or a trust token usable by another embedded or network function.
[041] To resist replay, a challenge may be selected from a set of operating challenges or may incorporate a variable challenge parameter. Different challenges can cause different hardware activity while preserving a device-specific relationship among extracted features. The reference store 170 may accordingly retain challenge-indexed fingerprint information or parameters defining an expected response region.
[042] To resist deliberate signal injection, the acquisition module 130 may obtain physically separated measurements, such as an internal timing measurement and an externally observed supply response, and the decision module 180 may test temporal coherence between them. A forged signal introduced at one measurement point is thereby less likely to satisfy the expected cross-domain relationship.
[043] The system may perform local authentication within the embedded device when sufficient trusted execution and secure storage are available. Alternatively, the embedded device may expose challenge-controlled measurements or extracted features to an external verifier. A hybrid implementation may perform raw-signal processing locally and transmit only a protected fingerprint or verification result.
[044] In resource-constrained implementations, feature extraction may be implemented using integer arithmetic, fixed-point digital filters, lookup tables and a reduced set of high-reliability features. In higher-performance implementations, statistical classifiers may be used to determine feature weighting or expected response regions, provided that the final identity decision remains based on physical hardware-originated response characteristics.
[045] The disclosed system does not require that a particular signal type be present in every embodiment. The technical principle is the derivation of a repeatable identity from intrinsic, challenge-synchronized physical signal characteristics, followed by stability-aware feature processing and protected comparison. Accordingly, substitutions among measurable hardware response domains fall within the scope of the invention.
[046] In an illustrative implementation, a microcontroller is commanded to execute a fixed arithmetic and memory-access sequence while the verifier samples supply current and a timer captures clock-edge intervals. The current trace is aligned to a trigger edge, normalized for supply level, and reduced to selected transient and spectral features. The clock intervals are reduced to frequency and short-term timing features. Features failing a stability mask are excluded, and the remaining features are fused and quantized.
[047] The quantized representation is processed with error-tolerant helper information and a one-way transformation to generate a protected reference during enrollment. At verification, a newly acquired representation is reconstructed within allowed tolerances and tested against the protected reference. The device is accepted only if reconstruction or similarity succeeds and the contemporaneous quality score remains above the required threshold.
[048] The combination of challenge synchronization, multi-domain physical response acquisition, stability-based feature selection, cross-domain binding, quality gating and protected reference comparison provides a technical effect of improved resistance to identifier cloning and improved reliability under ordinary operating variation, while permitting use with embedded hardware that may not include a dedicated hardware identity primitive.
[049] The foregoing embodiments are illustrative and not restrictive. Various modifications in the challenge source, signal domains, sampling circuitry, feature definitions, protection mechanism and comparison technique may be made by a person skilled in the art without departing from the scope of the invention as defined by the claims.
