specification:
Smart Sensorized Pen for Adaptive Handwriting Rehabilitation
Field of the Invention
The present invention relates generally to the field of assistive rehabilitation devices and, more particularly, to an intelligent handwriting assistance system employing embedded motion sensing, adaptive signal processing, and haptic feedback for improving handwriting quality and motor coordination. More specifically, the invention pertains to a smart writing pen configured to monitor handwriting dynamics in real time, detect abnormal writing behaviour, and provide personalized tactile guidance for handwriting rehabilitation of individuals suffering from handwriting impairments including dysgraphia, dyspraxia, dyslexia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and other neurodevelopmental or motor coordination disorders. The invention further relates to embedded systems, wearable rehabilitation technologies, motion tracking systems, human-machine interaction, and personalized educational assistive devices.
Background of the Invention
Handwriting continues to remain one of the most fundamental communication skills despite the widespread adoption of digital devices. The ability to write legibly requires synchronized functioning of fine motor muscles, visual perception, cognitive planning, finger dexterity, grip control, wrist movement, and continuous hand-eye coordination. Children affected by neurological or developmental disorders such as dysgraphia, dyspraxia, dyslexia, autism spectrum disorders, and ADHD frequently experience significant challenges in acquiring proper handwriting skills. Such individuals often exhibit inconsistent stroke formation, unstable pen movement, irregular writing pressure, poor letter spacing, improper grip posture, and reduced writing confidence. Conventional rehabilitation techniques generally rely upon repeated manual supervision by teachers, therapists, or caregivers, making the rehabilitation process labour-intensive, subjective, and difficult to personalize.
Existing handwriting improvement tools primarily consist of specially designed grips, ergonomic writing instruments, tracing sheets, occupational therapy exercises, or digital tablets. While these solutions provide some assistance, they do not continuously monitor handwriting movements nor do they actively guide the user during writing activities. Most commercially available digital pens are designed primarily for handwriting digitization, note recording, or writing capture rather than therapeutic rehabilitation. Consequently, users receive little or no immediate indication regarding incorrect writing behaviour, resulting in delayed correction and slower motor learning.
Among the existing literature, the publication entitled "Teaching and Rehabilitation of Handwriting for Children in the Digital Age: Issues and Challenges" by N. Bonneton-Botté et al. (2023) discusses the application of digital technologies and artificial intelligence for handwriting rehabilitation. However, the publication mainly focuses on educational frameworks and rehabilitation methodologies without providing an embedded smart writing instrument capable of performing real-time handwriting motion analysis together with individualized adaptive tactile correction during the writing process. Likewise, previously reported smart pen technologies have primarily concentrated on handwriting assessment or dysgraphia diagnosis rather than providing an integrated closed-loop rehabilitation mechanism that continuously senses handwriting movement and actively assists the user during writing.
Accordingly, there exists a need for a compact, portable, intelligent assistive writing device capable of continuously acquiring handwriting motion parameters, analysing writing quality in real time, learning individual writing characteristics, and providing instantaneous corrective guidance without requiring continuous therapist intervention. Such a system should be suitable for repeated daily rehabilitation, adaptable to different users, inexpensive to manufacture, and capable of promoting gradual improvement in handwriting quality and motor coordination while maintaining ease of use in educational and rehabilitation environments.
Summary of the Invention
The present invention provides a smart assistive writing pen configured to facilitate handwriting rehabilitation through continuous motion sensing, adaptive handwriting analysis, and real-time haptic guidance. The writing instrument incorporates an embedded processing unit, one or more inertial motion sensors, grip sensing elements, memory, wireless communication circuitry, rechargeable power management circuitry, and a vibration-based feedback mechanism integrated within a compact pen housing. During handwriting activities, the embedded sensing system continuously captures dynamic writing parameters including pen orientation, acceleration, angular velocity, stroke trajectory, writing stability, writing rhythm, grip behaviour, and motion consistency. The acquired sensor information is processed by embedded firmware to generate quantitative handwriting behaviour metrics representing the user's motor coordination and writing performance.
The embedded controller evaluates the measured handwriting characteristics against adaptive reference models generated from the individual user's previous writing sessions. Whenever unstable strokes, irregular motion trajectories, abnormal writing speed, inconsistent orientation, or improper writing behaviour are detected, the haptic actuator immediately generates vibration cues that guide the user toward correcting the writing movement while the writing activity is still in progress. Consequently, the user receives instantaneous corrective assistance instead of post-writing evaluation, thereby enabling rapid motor learning and reinforcing proper handwriting habits through repetitive guided practice.
The invention further maintains personalized user profiles that continuously evolve based on historical handwriting behaviour. The adaptive calibration mechanism automatically modifies correction thresholds, feedback sensitivity, and rehabilitation parameters according to improvements observed during successive writing sessions, thereby providing individualized rehabilitation rather than applying identical correction criteria to every user. The system may additionally store rehabilitation data locally or transmit performance information wirelessly to an external application for long-term monitoring by parents, therapists, or educators.
In one embodiment, the invention integrates an inertial measurement unit, force-sensitive grip sensor, haptic driver, rechargeable battery, wireless communication module, and embedded microcontroller within a lightweight writing instrument suitable for daily educational use. The architecture enables portability while minimizing power consumption and preserving conventional writing ergonomics. The invention thereby combines sensing, intelligent analysis, personalized rehabilitation, and corrective tactile interaction into a single integrated assistive writing device.
Adaptive Rehabilitation Progress Prediction Engine. This engine analyses long-term handwriting improvement trends using historical motion signatures and dynamically predicts the user's expected rehabilitation progression. Based on the predicted learning trajectory, the controller proactively adjusts vibration intensity, correction timing, stroke sensitivity thresholds, and rehabilitation difficulty levels before deterioration in handwriting performance occurs. Unlike conventional systems that merely react to detected writing errors, the predictive adaptation mechanism continuously optimizes rehabilitation parameters according to anticipated motor learning behaviour, thereby reducing user frustration, preventing over-correction, and improving long-term rehabilitation efficiency. This predictive adaptive rehabilitation capability provides a significant technical advancement over existing handwriting assistance systems by transforming the device from a reactive corrective instrument into an intelligent personalized rehabilitation companion.
Accordingly, the disclosed invention provides an integrated, intelligent, portable, and adaptive handwriting rehabilitation platform capable of improving handwriting consistency, writing confidence, fine motor coordination, and long-term learning outcomes for users experiencing handwriting-related disabilities. The invention is particularly suitable for deployment in schools, rehabilitation centres, occupational therapy clinics, hospitals, special education institutions, and home-based therapeutic environments while maintaining a compact architecture suitable for everyday use.
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS
The invention is illustrated in the accompanying drawing(s), throughout which like reference numerals indicate corresponding parts in the various figures in accordance with Indian patent drafting practice.
FIG. 1 illustrates a schematic block diagram of a smart assistive writing pen system (100) incorporating a motion sensing unit (102), a grip force sensor (104), an embedded microcontroller (106), an adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108), a user profile memory (110), a haptic driver (112), a vibration actuator (114), a wireless communication module (116), and a rechargeable power management unit (118) configured to provide adaptive handwriting rehabilitation.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION 
The present invention relates to a smart assistive writing pen system (100) configured to facilitate handwriting rehabilitation and motor skill enhancement through continuous motion sensing, adaptive handwriting analysis, personalized corrective feedback, and embedded intelligent processing. More particularly, the invention provides an integrated electronic writing instrument capable of continuously monitoring handwriting behaviour during normal writing operations and generating instantaneous tactile feedback whenever abnormal handwriting movement, unstable stroke formation, inconsistent grip behaviour, or improper writing posture is detected. The invention has been specifically designed for assisting children and individuals experiencing handwriting impairment associated with dysgraphia, dyspraxia, dyslexia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), developmental coordination disorder, neurological rehabilitation, stroke recovery, and other motor coordination deficiencies. Unlike conventional writing instruments that merely function as passive tools, the disclosed smart writing pen actively observes writing dynamics, analyses writing behaviour, and guides the user toward improved handwriting performance through adaptive rehabilitation.
Referring to FIG. 1, the smart assistive writing pen system generally comprises a writing pen assembly (100) including a motion sensing unit (102), a grip force sensor (104), an embedded microcontroller (106), an adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108), a user profile memory (110), a haptic driver (112), a vibration actuator (114), a wireless communication module (116), and a rechargeable power management unit (118). These hardware modules operate cooperatively to acquire handwriting information, analyse movement characteristics, identify writing abnormalities, generate corrective feedback, and progressively improve handwriting performance through adaptive learning.
The outer housing of the smart writing pen (100) is preferably manufactured using lightweight engineering polymer, reinforced polycarbonate, ABS material, composite polymer, aluminium alloy, or any equivalent durable material suitable for repeated educational and rehabilitation usage. The housing is ergonomically designed to resemble a conventional writing pen so that users can comfortably hold and operate the device without requiring specialized training. The internal cavity accommodates all electronic hardware modules while maintaining balanced weight distribution for natural writing movement. The housing further includes provisions for charging, firmware updating, wireless communication, indicator lighting, and cartridge replacement without affecting normal writing ergonomics.
The motion sensing unit (102) constitutes one of the principal sensing elements of the invention. In one preferred embodiment, the motion sensing unit comprises a nine-axis inertial measurement unit including a three-axis accelerometer, three-axis gyroscope, and three-axis magnetometer integrated within a compact sensor package. The motion sensing unit continuously acquires multidimensional handwriting movement data including linear acceleration, angular velocity, rotational orientation, stroke trajectory, writing inclination, pen tilt, dynamic movement acceleration, and writing rhythm. During writing, the sensor captures several hundred measurements per second, thereby allowing accurate reconstruction of handwriting motion with high temporal resolution. Such continuous sensing enables the system to distinguish between stable writing behaviour and irregular writing movement associated with handwriting disorders.
The grip force sensor (104) is positioned within the gripping region of the writing pen where the user's fingers naturally contact the pen body. The grip force sensor may comprise a force-sensitive resistor, capacitive pressure sensor, piezoelectric sensor, resistive pressure element, strain gauge, or any equivalent pressure measuring device capable of continuously detecting gripping force applied by the user during handwriting. Excessive gripping pressure often indicates muscular stress, fatigue, anxiety, or poor motor coordination, whereas insufficient gripping force may reduce writing stability and result in irregular stroke formation. Accordingly, the grip force sensor continuously monitors gripping behaviour and generates electrical signals corresponding to real-time pressure variations, enabling the system to evaluate writing comfort and motor control simultaneously with handwriting movement.
The outputs generated by the motion sensing unit (102) and grip force sensor (104) are transmitted to the embedded microcontroller (106), which functions as the central processing unit of the smart writing pen. The embedded microcontroller preferably comprises a low-power high-performance processor such as an ARM Cortex-M series processor, Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 system-on-chip, ESP32 processor, STM32 microcontroller, or any equivalent embedded controller capable of executing sensor fusion algorithms, adaptive learning software, communication protocols, and feedback generation processes. The microcontroller receives raw sensor signals from both sensing modules and performs signal conditioning including amplification, analogue-to-digital conversion, filtering, synchronization, timestamp generation, calibration compensation, coordinate transformation, and sensor fusion before forwarding the processed information for handwriting analysis.
To improve measurement reliability, the embedded microcontroller executes multiple digital signal processing algorithms for eliminating environmental disturbances and sensor noise. In one embodiment, low-pass filtering removes high-frequency vibration introduced by accidental hand tremor, while complementary filtering combines accelerometer and gyroscope outputs to estimate accurate pen orientation. Kalman filtering may additionally be employed to minimize cumulative sensor drift and improve handwriting trajectory reconstruction. Consequently, the processed handwriting information accurately represents the actual writing movement performed by the user while eliminating erroneous sensor fluctuations.
The processed handwriting information generated by the embedded microcontroller (106) is subsequently supplied to the adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108). The adaptive handwriting analysis engine represents the intelligent decision-making component responsible for evaluating handwriting quality. The handwriting analysis engine may be implemented through embedded firmware, artificial intelligence algorithms, machine learning models, statistical handwriting evaluation techniques, rule-based classifiers, or combinations thereof. The analysis engine continuously evaluates multiple handwriting characteristics including stroke smoothness, writing velocity, stroke continuity, acceleration consistency, pen orientation stability, writing rhythm, motion variability, stroke interruption frequency, writing hesitation, directional deviation, grip consistency, and overall handwriting coordination.
Unlike conventional rehabilitation devices that compare writing against a predefined fixed reference, the adaptive handwriting analysis engine develops individualized handwriting profiles for every user. During initial calibration sessions, baseline handwriting characteristics are recorded while the user performs ordinary writing exercises including alphabets, numbers, geometric figures, sentences, and freehand writing. These baseline measurements establish personalized writing thresholds that reflect the user's natural motor capability rather than idealized handwriting standards. Consequently, subsequent handwriting analysis compares current handwriting behaviour against individualized baseline characteristics, thereby significantly improving rehabilitation effectiveness for users possessing different levels of motor impairment.
Whenever the adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108) detects deviations exceeding predetermined adaptive thresholds, corrective intervention is initiated immediately. Examples of such deviations include excessive writing tremor, abrupt stroke interruption, inconsistent acceleration, excessive grip pressure, unstable writing orientation, prolonged hesitation, irregular writing rhythm, or uncontrolled pen movement. Rather than waiting until the writing exercise has been completed, the invention performs continuous online evaluation so that corrective guidance is delivered while the handwriting activity remains in progress. Such immediate intervention significantly accelerates motor learning by enabling the user to recognize incorrect writing behaviour at the exact moment the abnormal movement occurs.
To further enhance rehabilitation accuracy, the invention continuously updates its adaptive thresholds according to the user's observed improvement over multiple writing sessions. Consequently, rehabilitation difficulty gradually increases as handwriting performance improves, thereby preventing both under-training and over-correction. This adaptive learning capability allows the invention to remain effective throughout different stages of rehabilitation, beginning from severely impaired handwriting and progressively advancing toward normal handwriting performance without requiring manual recalibration by therapists.
Continuing with FIG. 1, the handwriting analysis engine (108) communicates continuously with the user profile memory (110), which serves as a long-term storage module for maintaining personalized rehabilitation information. The user profile memory may comprise non-volatile flash memory, EEPROM, embedded storage, removable memory, cloud-based storage, or combinations thereof. The memory stores individual calibration parameters, handwriting history, grip characteristics, rehabilitation progression records, sensor calibration coefficients, writing performance indices, adaptive threshold values, and firmware configuration settings. Unlike conventional handwriting devices that erase writing information after every session, the disclosed invention continuously accumulates rehabilitation history, thereby enabling longitudinal analysis of handwriting improvement. The stored historical information allows the embedded controller to determine whether the user has improved, deteriorated, or maintained handwriting quality over extended periods of usage.
The adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108) retrieves historical handwriting records from the user profile memory (110) before initiating every rehabilitation session. By comparing present handwriting behaviour with previous writing sessions, the controller establishes a dynamic rehabilitation model that continuously adjusts corrective thresholds according to the user's motor learning capability. Consequently, users showing rapid improvement receive more stringent correction criteria, whereas users requiring slower rehabilitation receive comparatively relaxed feedback thresholds. This personalized adaptation minimizes unnecessary corrective feedback while ensuring that the rehabilitation process remains challenging enough to stimulate gradual motor improvement. The adaptive learning architecture therefore prevents excessive vibration alerts that could otherwise discourage young users while simultaneously avoiding insufficient correction that may reduce therapeutic effectiveness.
Following handwriting evaluation, the adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108) transmits corrective instructions to the haptic driver (112). The haptic driver is responsible for generating precisely controlled vibration signals corresponding to the detected handwriting abnormality. In one preferred embodiment, the haptic driver comprises a dedicated vibration control integrated circuit capable of regulating vibration frequency, amplitude, pulse duration, waveform characteristics, and repetition intervals. The driver may control either a linear resonant actuator, eccentric rotating mass motor, piezoelectric actuator, or equivalent tactile feedback mechanism capable of producing comfortable and distinguishable vibration patterns. Different handwriting abnormalities may correspond to different vibration signatures. For example, a brief low-intensity vibration may indicate slight writing instability, whereas repeated high-frequency vibration pulses may indicate excessive grip pressure or abrupt stroke interruption requiring immediate correction.
The vibration actuator (114) converts the electrical signals generated by the haptic driver (112) into tactile mechanical feedback that is immediately perceived by the user through the fingers holding the writing pen. Since tactile sensation is delivered directly through the hand without interrupting visual attention, the user can continue writing naturally while simultaneously receiving corrective guidance. This approach eliminates the need for continuously observing computer displays, visual indicators, or external rehabilitation equipment. The vibration actuator is positioned within the pen body at a location that efficiently transfers vibration energy to the user's fingers while minimizing discomfort and preserving normal writing ergonomics. Consequently, corrective guidance becomes intuitive, immediate, and unobtrusive.
The wireless communication module (116) enables bidirectional communication between the smart writing pen (100) and external computing devices including smartphones, tablet computers, laptops, desktop computers, rehabilitation workstations, educational servers, or cloud-based rehabilitation platforms. The wireless communication module preferably supports Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), Wi-Fi, Near Field Communication (NFC), ZigBee, or equivalent short-range communication technologies depending upon application requirements. Through this communication interface, handwriting performance data, rehabilitation progress reports, firmware updates, personalized writing exercises, and therapist recommendations may be exchanged between the writing pen and external software applications.
In one embodiment, parents or occupational therapists install a dedicated rehabilitation application on a mobile device. After completion of each writing session, the writing pen automatically transmits rehabilitation statistics including average writing stability, stroke consistency, grip pressure variation, handwriting smoothness, vibration correction frequency, session duration, and rehabilitation improvement scores. The application graphically illustrates progress over weeks or months, allowing therapists to evaluate treatment effectiveness without manually observing every writing exercise. Furthermore, firmware updates containing improved handwriting analysis algorithms may be wirelessly downloaded into the embedded microcontroller (106), thereby extending the operational capabilities of the writing pen without requiring hardware modification.
The rechargeable power management unit (118) supplies electrical energy to every electronic module integrated within the writing pen. The power management unit preferably comprises a rechargeable lithium-polymer battery, battery protection circuitry, charging controller, voltage regulation circuitry, fuel gauge integrated circuit, charging connector, over-current protection, over-voltage protection, thermal protection, and power monitoring circuitry. A USB Type-C charging interface may be incorporated to facilitate convenient battery charging using commonly available chargers. The power management circuitry continuously monitors battery voltage, charging current, discharge current, battery temperature, and remaining energy capacity. Whenever battery charge becomes critically low, the microcontroller generates warning indications through vibration patterns, LED indicators, or wireless notifications before automatically entering low-power operation to maximize remaining operating duration.
To extend battery life, the embedded firmware intelligently controls power consumption of individual hardware modules. For example, the motion sensing unit (102) may operate at reduced sampling frequency during inactivity, while the wireless communication module (116) remains in sleep mode until data transmission becomes necessary. Similarly, the haptic driver (112) and vibration actuator (114) are activated only when corrective feedback is required. Such intelligent power management significantly increases operational duration while maintaining high rehabilitation performance.
The smart writing pen may additionally include visual status indicators such as RGB light-emitting diodes for indicating charging status, Bluetooth pairing, battery condition, calibration completion, and rehabilitation mode selection. A multifunction button may be provided for power control, profile selection, calibration initiation, firmware reset, and wireless pairing. These auxiliary functions improve usability without interfering with ordinary handwriting activities.
During operation, the invention functions as an intelligent closed-loop rehabilitation system. Initially, the user powers ON the writing pen and selects an individual rehabilitation profile stored within the user profile memory (110). The embedded microcontroller (106) automatically performs sensor calibration by determining reference orientation, grip characteristics, and environmental compensation parameters. Once calibration is completed, the user begins ordinary handwriting on conventional paper using standard writing exercises such as alphabets, words, numerical figures, or drawing patterns.
As writing progresses, the motion sensing unit (102) continuously captures handwriting movement, while the grip force sensor (104) simultaneously records gripping behaviour. The embedded microcontroller (106) synchronizes, filters, and processes these measurements before supplying the resulting handwriting information to the adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108). The analysis engine compares real-time handwriting behaviour against personalized baseline characteristics stored within the user profile memory (110). Whenever handwriting remains stable, the system permits uninterrupted writing without generating unnecessary corrective signals. However, if unstable writing movement, irregular stroke trajectory, excessive pen tilt, abnormal acceleration, inconsistent rhythm, or excessive gripping pressure is detected, the haptic driver (112) immediately activates the vibration actuator (114), producing tactile guidance that encourages the user to modify writing behaviour.
A practical real-life working example may be considered for better understanding of the invention. Consider a ten-year-old child diagnosed with dysgraphia who experiences difficulty maintaining uniform handwriting during classroom activities. Before commencing rehabilitation, the therapist performs an initial calibration session using the smart writing pen (100). During this session, the child's natural handwriting movement, grip pressure, writing speed, and stroke stability are recorded and stored within the user profile memory (110). Thereafter, the child performs daily handwriting exercises at home using ordinary notebooks.
During one writing exercise, the child unintentionally applies excessive grip pressure while writing the alphabet "M". The grip force sensor (104) immediately detects the abnormal pressure increase, while the motion sensing unit (102) simultaneously identifies irregular stroke acceleration caused by muscular stiffness. These measurements are processed by the embedded microcontroller (106), which forwards the information to the adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108). Since the detected values exceed the personalized threshold stored for that child, the haptic driver (112) instantly activates the vibration actuator (114), producing two short vibration pulses. Without looking away from the notebook, the child naturally relaxes finger pressure and slows the writing movement. The subsequent strokes become smoother and more stable, resulting in improved handwriting quality. At the conclusion of the writing session, the rehabilitation data is wirelessly transmitted through the wireless communication module (116) to the therapist's mobile application, where weekly improvement reports demonstrate gradual enhancement in handwriting consistency, motor coordination, and writing confidence.
In another embodiment, the adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108) incorporates a predictive rehabilitation model that analyses long-term handwriting trends and anticipates future motor performance. Rather than merely reacting to detected handwriting errors, the predictive engine estimates the probability of future writing instability based upon accumulated rehabilitation history stored within the user profile memory (110). Accordingly, the controller proactively modifies vibration intensity, correction sensitivity, rehabilitation difficulty, and adaptive thresholds before deterioration in handwriting quality becomes evident. This predictive adaptation represents a significant technical advancement because rehabilitation continuously evolves according to anticipated user capability rather than solely responding to immediate handwriting errors.
Accordingly, the disclosed smart assistive writing pen (100) integrates advanced motion sensing, intelligent embedded processing, adaptive handwriting evaluation, personalized rehabilitation, tactile corrective guidance, wireless communication, and intelligent power management within a compact writing instrument capable of significantly improving handwriting quality, motor coordination, rehabilitation efficiency, and user confidence while remaining suitable for continuous educational and therapeutic applications.

Advantages of the Invention
1.	The disclosed smart assistive writing pen (100) provides real-time adaptive tactile feedback during handwriting, thereby enabling immediate correction of handwriting errors and significantly improving handwriting consistency, stroke stability, and motor coordination.
2.	The integration of the motion sensing unit (102), grip force sensor (104), adaptive handwriting analysis engine (108), and user profile memory (110) enables personalized rehabilitation by dynamically adjusting corrective feedback according to the individual user's handwriting behaviour and rehabilitation progress.
3.	The compact portable architecture incorporating the embedded microcontroller (106), wireless communication module (116), and rechargeable power management unit (118) allows continuous handwriting rehabilitation in classrooms, rehabilitation centres, hospitals, and home environments without requiring constant therapist supervision.
4.	The invention continuously records handwriting performance and rehabilitation history, allowing objective long-term assessment of handwriting improvement while supporting remote monitoring and individualized therapy through wireless communication.

title: A SYSTEM AND A METHOD FOR SENSOR-FUSION GESTURE-TO-LANGUAGE TRANSLATION AND SPEECH GENERATION COMMUNICATION
abstract:
Disclosed is a system (100) for sensor-fusion based gesture-to-language translation of physical gestures into target-language text and synthesized speech. The system (100) comprises a multimodal sensor array (102), an embedded processing unit (104), a preprocessing module (106), a temporal segmentation module (108), a gesture recognition module (110), a neural machine translation module (112), a text-to-speech module (114), an output interface (116), and a personalization module (118). The multimodal sensor array (102) captures finger-bend, inertial, and image information. The temporal segmentation module (108) identifies gesture onset and offset during continuous signing. The gesture recognition module (110) performs multimodal sensor fusion to generate linguistic tokens and resolve gesture ambiguities. The neural machine translation module (112) converts the linguistic tokens into target-language text, while the text-to-speech module (114) generates synthesized speech. The personalization module (118) provides few-shot user adaptation, enabling continuous, adaptive, privacy-preserving, and substantially on-device gesture translation with reduced external computing dependence.
Fig. 1 is the reference figure.
specification:
TECHNICAL FIELD OF THE INVENTION 
The present invention generally relates to a human–computer interaction and assistive communication system, and more particularly relates to a system and a method of sensor-fusion based gesture recognition and translation of physical hand and body gestures into target-language text and synthesized speech, in accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure.
BACKGROUND 
Gesture-based human–computer interaction is increasingly used for assistive communication, particularly for users communicating through hand gestures or sign language. However, accurately recognizing continuous physical gestures and converting them into meaningful language and speech remains technically challenging.
Existing touchscreen-based systems generally use gestures as commands for manipulating or translating displayed text rather than recognizing the linguistic meaning of physical gestures. Wearable systems using IMU, flex, or similar sensors may capture hand movement or finger bending but can have difficulty distinguishing gestures with similar characteristics. Vision-based systems may additionally be affected by occlusion, lighting conditions, and field-of-view limitations.
Conventional systems also commonly focus on isolated gestures and may not effectively perform real-time temporal segmentation of continuous signing, including transitional movements between successive gestures. Further, recognition, translation, and speech generation are often implemented as separate stages, requiring additional computing resources or external systems.
Recognition accuracy may also vary between users due to differences in hand characteristics, signing speed, movement patterns, and individual signing styles. Systems relying on generalized training data may therefore provide limited user-specific adaptation. Cloud-based processing can further introduce latency, network dependency, and privacy concerns associated with transmission of gesture or image data.
Accordingly, there remains a need for an integrated, low-latency, privacy-preserving gesture-to-language system capable of multimodal gesture recognition, continuous gesture segmentation, user-specific adaptation, language translation, and corresponding speech generation without excessive dependence on external computing infrastructure.
SUMMARY 
In an aspect of the present disclosure, a sensor-fusion based gesture-to-language translation system for translating physical gestures of a user into target-language text and synthesized speech is provided. The system comprises a multimodal sensor array, an embedded processing unit, a preprocessing module, a temporal segmentation module, a gesture recognition module, a neural machine translation module, a text-to-speech module, an output interface, and a personalization module. The system continuously captures gesture-related information including finger-bend, inertial, and image information, preprocesses the captured information, identifies gesture onset and gesture offset from continuous user motion, and recognizes respective gesture segments. Multimodal sensor fusion is performed to resolve ambiguities between gestures having similar hand-motion characteristics or finger configurations. The recognized gestures are converted into linguistic tokens, translated into target-language text, and further converted into synthesized speech substantially on-device. The personalization module performs few-shot user adaptation and confusion-pair correction to provide continuous, adaptive, and privacy-preserving gesture-to-language communication. 
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the multimodal sensor array comprises a wrist-mounted camera having a field of view directed toward the fingers of the user, and image features obtained from the wrist-mounted camera are fused with finger-bend information and inertial information to distinguish gestures having visually or kinematically similar finger articulations. 
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the temporal segmentation module detects gesture onset and gesture offset during continuous signing using probabilistic change-point detection or a neural boundary-detection model and processes overlapping temporal windows to accommodate coarticulation between successive gestures. 
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the gesture recognition module employs a temporal convolutional neural network or a Transformer encoder in association with a connectionist temporal classification decoder or a sequence-to-sequence decoder and generates glosses, word tokens, or phrase-level linguistic tokens corresponding to the identified gesture segments. 
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the neural machine translation module performs on-device neural machine translation of the recognized linguistic tokens into target-language text with phrase-level reordering and morphological processing, while the text-to-speech module employs a low-footprint neural text-to-speech model configured to generate synthesized speech with an end-to-audio latency of less than five hundred milliseconds following completion of the gesture. 
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the personalization module performs few-shot adaptation using user-specific calibration gestures, identifies gesture pairs repeatedly confused during gesture recognition, generates an active-learning prompt requesting selection between candidate gestures, and updates user-specific model parameters based on the received response. 
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the system further comprises a communication interface comprising Bluetooth Low Energy, Wi-Fi, or a combination thereof, and the communication interface selectively offloads language translation to a companion application when a vocabulary size or translation workload exceeds a processing threshold of the embedded processing unit while maintaining gesture recognition locally within the system. 
In some aspects of the present disclosure, the multimodal sensor array comprises textile-integrated conductive-yarn flex sensors embedded within a wearable glove and an inertial measurement unit mounted on the wearable glove or a wrist portion thereof, thereby enabling capture of finger bending, hand orientation, and hand movement during continuous gesture performance. 
In some aspects of the present disclosure, gesture recognition is performed locally by default, while encrypted transmission is employed when external or cloud-assisted processing is selectively used for large-vocabulary neural machine translation or text-to-speech updates, thereby reducing exposure of user gesture data. 
In an aspect of the present disclosure, a method for sensor-fusion based gesture recognition and translation of physical gestures into target-language text and synthesized speech is provided. The method comprises continuously capturing gesture-related information, acquiring multichannel gesture data, preprocessing the multichannel gesture data, segmenting continuous user motion into respective gesture segments, recognizing the gesture segments, generating linguistic tokens, translating the linguistic tokens into target-language text, generating synthesized speech, and outputting the translated text or synthesized speech. The method further performs online temporal segmentation using gesture onset and gesture offset detection, multimodal sensor fusion of finger-bend, inertial, and image information, substantially on-device neural machine translation and speech synthesis, few-shot user personalization, optional selective offloading of translation, and repeated processing of successive gestures.
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS
Fig. 1 illustrates a block diagram of a system for sensor-fusion based gesture recognition and translation of physical gestures into target-language text and synthesized speech, in accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure; and
Fig. 2 illustrates a flow chart of a method (200) for sensor-fusion based gesture recognition and translation of physical gestures into target-language text and synthesized speech, in accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure.
DETAILED DESCRIPTION 
The present invention relates to a wearable or handheld gesture-to-language translation device configured to recognize physical hand and body gestures and convert the recognized gestures into text and synthesized speech in one or more target languages. The device is directed particularly toward human–computer interaction and assistive communication applications, including communication support for users relying on sign language or gesture-based expression. 
The invention employs a multimodal sensor array comprising at least finger-bend sensing and inertial sensing, with optional electromyography sensing and vision-based sensing, to continuously capture hand pose, finger articulation, motion, and associated gesture information. The captured multichannel sensor information is processed by an embedded processor that performs preprocessing, temporal segmentation, and gesture recognition to identify meaningful gesture segments from continuous user motion. 
The recognized gesture segments are converted into linguistic tokens, such as glosses, words, or phrases, and thereafter translated into target-language text using a neural machine translation model. The translated text is presented through a text-output interface and is further converted into synthesized speech using a text-to-speech model, thereby providing an end-to-end gesture-to-language communication pipeline. 
The invention further supports continuous gesture segmentation, multimodal sensor fusion for resolving ambiguities between similar gestures, user-specific adaptation, and substantially on-device processing for low-latency and privacy-preserving operation. In particular, fusion of inertial, finger-bend, and optional vision information improves gesture disambiguation, while few-shot personalization enables adaptation to individual signing styles and commonly confused gesture pairs.
Disclosed is a system for sensor-fusion based gesture recognition and translation of physical hand and body gestures into target-language text and synthesized speech (hereinafter referred to and denoted as “the system 100”), in accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure.
The system (100) includes a multimodal sensor array (102), an embedded processing unit (104), a preprocessing module (106), a temporal segmentation module (108), a gesture recognition module (110), a neural machine translation module (112), a text-to-speech module (114), an output interface (116), a personalization module (118), and a communication interface (120). These components collectively capture continuous gesture information, process and segment the sensor data, recognize the gesture sequence, translate the recognized linguistic tokens into target-language text, generate synthesized speech, and provide user-adaptive operation.
The multimodal sensor array (102) is configured to capture continuous gesture-related information corresponding to movement, posture, orientation, and articulation of the user's hand and fingers. The multimodal sensor array (102) comprises finger-bend sensors and an inertial measurement unit and may further comprise electromyography electrodes and a wrist-mounted or hand-oriented camera. In an embodiment, the finger-bend sensors comprise resistive or optical flex sensors positioned along respective fingers and the thumb, while the inertial measurement unit comprises a six-axis or nine-axis inertial sensor configured to measure acceleration, angular motion, and hand orientation. The optional electromyography electrodes may be positioned proximate to forearm flexor and extensor muscles to obtain muscle-activity information. The optional camera may be positioned at the wrist to capture finger articulation and hand configuration. The multimodal sensor array (102) thereby generates multichannel sensor information representative of the physical gesture performed by the user. 
The embedded processing unit (104) is operatively coupled to the multimodal sensor array (102) and is configured to receive and process the multichannel sensor information generated by the multimodal sensor array (102). The embedded processing unit (104) may comprise an ARM Cortex-M4 or Cortex-M7 system-on-chip, an ESP32-class microcontroller, an STM32-class processor, or another embedded processing platform capable of executing real-time acquisition, preprocessing, and neural inference operations. The embedded processing unit (104) may include internal or external memory and may optionally include a neural processing unit for accelerating machine-learning inference. The embedded processing unit (104) further interfaces with the power supply, local storage, wireless communication hardware, and the output hardware of the system (100), thereby providing the computational platform for executing the gesture-to-language translation pipeline. 
The preprocessing module (106) is executable by the embedded processing unit (104) and is configured to preprocess the multichannel sensor information received from the multimodal sensor array (102). The preprocessing module (106) performs one or more operations including sensor calibration, gravity compensation, drift correction, per-channel normalization, and sliding-window feature extraction. The preprocessing module (106) may determine statistical features including mean, variance, and spectral energy while retaining selected raw temporal sequences for subsequent processing. For flex-sensor information, the preprocessing module (106) may determine a normalized bend ratio; for inertial information, the preprocessing module (106) may perform orientation fusion and gravity compensation; for electromyography information, the preprocessing module (106) may determine an envelope value; and for image information, the preprocessing module (106) may extract hand keypoints. The preprocessing module (106) thereby produces normalized and concatenated gesture features suitable for temporal segmentation and gesture recognition. 
The temporal segmentation module (108) is operatively associated with the preprocessing module (106) and is configured to identify temporal boundaries of individual gestures within continuous movement of the user. The temporal segmentation module (108) detects the onset and the offset of respective gestures during continuous signing and thereby separates continuous sensor streams into gesture segments. In an embodiment, the temporal segmentation module (108) employs probabilistic change-point detection or a neural boundary-detection model, including a one-dimensional convolutional neural network boundary classifier. The temporal segmentation module (108) may process overlapping time windows to accommodate coarticulation occurring between successive gestures and generates gesture-segment timing information for subsequent gesture recognition. 
The gesture recognition module (110) is operatively coupled to the temporal segmentation module (108) and is configured to recognize the gesture represented by each identified gesture segment. The gesture recognition module (110) may employ a trained neural architecture comprising a temporal convolutional neural network, a Transformer encoder, connectionist temporal classification decoding, sequence-to-sequence decoding, or combinations thereof. The gesture recognition module (110) receives features corresponding to the segmented gesture and generates one or more linguistic units comprising glosses, words, or token sequences corresponding to the recognized gesture. Where multiple sensing modalities are available, the gesture recognition module (110) performs multimodal sensor fusion between information obtained from the finger-bend sensors, the inertial measurement unit, and the optional camera or electromyography electrodes. The multimodal fusion facilitates disambiguation between gestures having similar motion characteristics or finger configurations. 
The neural machine translation module (112) is operatively coupled to the gesture recognition module (110) and is configured to translate the linguistic units generated by the gesture recognition module (110) into text corresponding to a selected target language. The neural machine translation module (112) maps the recognized glosses, words, or token sequences into the target-language text while supporting phrase-level reordering and morphological transformation. In an embodiment, the neural machine translation module (112) comprises a Transformer-based neural machine translation model executed locally by the embedded processing unit (104). Alternatively, translation may be selectively performed using a paired companion application when the translation requirement exceeds the processing or vocabulary capacity of the embedded device. 
The text-to-speech module (114) is operatively coupled to the neural machine translation module (112) and is configured to convert the target-language text generated by the neural machine translation module (112) into synthesized speech. The text-to-speech module (114) may comprise a low-footprint neural text-to-speech model configured for embedded execution and may support prosody control and a configurable voice. The text-to-speech module (114) generates an audio stream corresponding to the translated target-language text and supplies the audio stream to the output interface (116). The disclosed implementation targets low-latency generation of synthesized speech following completion of the detected gesture. 
The output interface (116) is operatively coupled to the neural machine translation module (112) and the text-to-speech module (114) and is configured to provide the translated language output to the user or another person. The output interface (116) may comprise a display configured to present the target-language text and an audio transducer configured to reproduce the synthesized speech. In an embodiment, the display comprises an OLED or LCD display, while the audio transducer comprises an onboard speaker or an audio output jack coupled through an audio interface. The output interface (116) may further communicate the translated text or synthesized speech through a companion application. 
The personalization module (118) is operatively associated with the gesture recognition module (110), the neural machine translation module (112), and the embedded processing unit (104) and is configured to adapt operation of the system (100) according to gesture characteristics of an individual user. The personalization module (118) performs few-shot adaptation using user-specific calibration gestures and may identify frequently confused gesture pairs. The personalization module (118) may generate active-learning prompts requesting the user to distinguish between candidate gestures and thereafter update user-specific model parameters based on the received response. The personalization module (118) may further maintain a user-specific lexicon or pronunciation information locally. Accordingly, the personalization module (118) enables progressive adaptation of gesture recognition and language generation according to individual signing styles and user-specific variations. 
The communication interface (120) is communicatively coupled to the embedded processing unit (104) and is configured to establish communication between the system (100) and the companion application or an external computing device. The communication interface (120) may comprise Bluetooth Low Energy, Wi-Fi, or combinations thereof. The communication interface (120) enables transfer of translated information, configuration information, vocabulary information, or model-related information between the system (100) and the companion application. In an embodiment in which the vocabulary size or translation workload exceeds the processing capacity of the embedded processing unit (104), the communication interface (120) enables selective offloading of the translation operation while maintaining gesture recognition locally. When external or cloud-assisted processing is employed, the disclosed architecture may use encrypted transmission, while inference is performed locally by default to preserve privacy and reduce communication dependency. 
In operation, the multimodal sensor array (102) initially captures continuous gesture-related information corresponding to movement, orientation, posture, and finger articulation of the user. The multimodal sensor array (102) obtains the gesture-related information from the finger-bend sensors and the inertial measurement unit and, where provided, from the electromyography electrodes and the wrist-mounted camera. The captured signals collectively form multichannel gesture data representative of the physical hand gesture or continuous signing performed by the user.
The embedded processing unit (104) receives the multichannel gesture data from the multimodal sensor array (102) and continuously executes the gesture-to-language processing pipeline. The embedded processing unit (104) acquires the sensor signals in real time and provides the processing resources for preprocessing, temporal segmentation, gesture recognition, language translation, and speech generation.
The preprocessing module (106) receives the multichannel gesture data through the embedded processing unit (104) and conditions the captured signals for subsequent analysis. The preprocessing module (106) performs sensor calibration, gravity compensation, drift correction, per-channel normalization, and sliding-window processing. The preprocessing module (106) may further determine the bend ratio from the finger-bend sensor signals, determine orientation information from the inertial measurement unit signals, determine the electromyography envelope from the electromyography signals, and extract hand keypoints from the camera images. The preprocessing module (106) thereby generates normalized gesture features corresponding to the continuously captured user motion.
The temporal segmentation module (108) receives the normalized gesture features from the preprocessing module (106) and identifies boundaries between successive gestures in the continuous gesture stream. The temporal segmentation module (108) detects the onset and the offset of each gesture using the probabilistic change-point technique or the neural boundary-detection technique. The temporal segmentation module (108) further handles coarticulation occurring between successive gestures by analysing overlapping temporal windows and generates respective gesture segments for subsequent recognition.
The gesture recognition module (110) receives the gesture segments from the temporal segmentation module (108) and determines the linguistic meaning associated with each gesture segment. The gesture recognition module (110) processes the gesture features using the trained neural model, including the temporal convolutional neural network, the Transformer encoder, the connectionist temporal classification decoder, the sequence-to-sequence decoder, or combinations thereof. The gesture recognition module (110) consequently generates the sequence of linguistic tokens, such as glosses, words, or phrases, corresponding to the performed gestures.
Where information from multiple sensing modalities is available, the gesture recognition module (110) performs multimodal sensor fusion using the finger-bend information, the inertial information, and, where available, the camera information or the electromyography information. The multimodal sensor fusion enables the gesture recognition module (110) to distinguish between gestures having similar motion patterns or hand configurations. In the vision-assisted embodiment, the camera information may be weighted to improve disambiguation of finger-shape variations.
The neural machine translation module (112) receives the sequence of linguistic tokens from the gesture recognition module (110) and translates the recognized linguistic content into the selected target language. The neural machine translation module (112) processes the token sequence through the neural machine translation model and generates corresponding target-language text while accommodating phrase-level reordering and morphological differences between the source representation and the target language.
The text-to-speech module (114) receives the target-language text from the neural machine translation module (112) and converts the target-language text into synthesized speech. The text-to-speech module (114) executes the low-footprint neural text-to-speech model and generates the audio stream corresponding to the translated text. The disclosed processing pipeline is configured to provide low-latency speech generation following completion of the gesture.
The output interface (116) receives the target-language text from the neural machine translation module (112) and the synthesized speech from the text-to-speech module (114). The output interface (116) presents the translated text through the display and reproduces the synthesized speech through the speaker or the audio output interface. Accordingly, the physical gesture performed by the user is converted into both readable target-language text and audible target-language speech.
The personalization module (118) operates in association with the gesture recognition process to adapt the system (100) to the individual user's signing characteristics. The personalization module (118) receives user-specific calibration gestures and performs few-shot adaptation of the recognition model. When the gesture recognition module (110) repeatedly identifies confusion between similar gesture pairs, the personalization module (118) may generate the active-learning prompt requesting the user to select the intended gesture. Based on the received user response, the personalization module (118) updates the user-specific parameters or the locally stored user lexicon, thereby progressively improving recognition accuracy for the particular user.
The communication interface (120), when required, establishes communication between the embedded processing unit (104) and the companion application or the external computing device. The communication interface (120) may communicate translated text, configuration information, vocabulary information, or model-related information through Bluetooth Low Energy or Wi-Fi. When the vocabulary size or the translation workload exceeds the local processing capability, the communication interface (120) may selectively transfer the translation operation to the companion application while the gesture recognition operation remains local. Where external assistance is employed, the transmitted information may be encrypted, while local inference remains the default operating mode.
Thus, during continuous operation, the system (100) sequentially performs gesture sensing through the multimodal sensor array (102), signal conditioning through the preprocessing module (106), gesture-boundary identification through the temporal segmentation module (108), gesture interpretation through the gesture recognition module (110), target-language generation through the neural machine translation module (112), speech generation through the text-to-speech module (114), and presentation of the translated information through the output interface (116). The personalization module (118) continuously supports user-specific adaptation, while the communication interface (120) provides optional external connectivity. The processing sequence is repeatedly executed as new gestures are performed, thereby providing continuous, low-latency gesture-to-text and gesture-to-speech translation.
Fig. 2 illustrates the method (200) for sensor-fusion based gesture recognition and translation of physical gestures into target-language text and synthesized speech, in accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure. The method (200) enables continuous acquisition of gesture information, identification of individual gestures from continuous user motion, multimodal recognition of the identified gestures, translation of the recognized gestures into the target language, generation of synthesized speech, and user-specific personalization.
At step 202, the method (200) comprises capturing, by the multimodal sensor array (102), continuous gesture-related information corresponding to hand movement, hand orientation, and finger articulation of the user. The multimodal sensor array (102) continuously observes the physical gestures performed by the user and generates gesture-related information comprising at least finger-bend information, inertial information, and image information. Accordingly, different characteristics of the performed gesture are captured through multiple sensing modalities rather than relying upon a single source of gesture information.
At step 204, the method (200) comprises acquiring, by the embedded processing unit (104), multichannel gesture data generated from the continuous gesture-related information captured by the multimodal sensor array (102). The embedded processing unit (104) receives the finger-bend information, the inertial information, and the image information and makes the multichannel gesture data available for further processing. The continuous acquisition enables the system (100) to process successive physical gestures without requiring individual gestures to be separately provided by the user.
At step 206, the method (200) comprises preprocessing, by the preprocessing module (106), the acquired multichannel gesture data. The preprocessing module (106) performs at least sensor calibration, normalization, compensation of sensor variations, and generation of normalized gesture features. The preprocessing operation conditions information received from the different sensing modalities into the normalized gesture features suitable for subsequent temporal analysis and gesture recognition.
At step 208, the method (200) comprises segmenting, by the temporal segmentation module (108), the normalized gesture features generated by the preprocessing module (106). The temporal segmentation module (108) detects the gesture onset and the gesture offset within the continuous user motion and identifies respective gesture segments from the continuous gesture stream. The temporal segmentation module (108) performs online temporal segmentation during continuous signing and processes overlapping temporal windows to accommodate coarticulation between successive gestures. Accordingly, individual meaningful gesture segments are identified from continuously changing hand and finger movements without requiring pre-segmented gesture inputs.
At step 210, the method (200) comprises recognizing, by the gesture recognition module (110), the respective gesture segments identified by the temporal segmentation module (108). The gesture recognition module (110) processes the gesture segments using the trained neural model and generates the sequence of linguistic tokens corresponding to the recognized physical gestures.
During the recognizing at step 210, the gesture recognition module (110) performs multimodal sensor fusion of the finger-bend information, the inertial information, and the image information. The information obtained through the different sensing modalities is jointly processed to resolve ambiguity between gestures having similar hand-motion characteristics or finger configurations. Accordingly, the image information representative of finger articulation is considered in combination with the finger-bend information and the inertial information representative of movement and orientation.
Further, during the recognizing at step 210, the gesture recognition module (110) generates the sequence of linguistic tokens using the temporal neural architecture comprising at least one of the convolutional neural network, the Transformer encoder, the connectionist temporal classification decoder, and the sequence-to-sequence decoder. The sequence of linguistic tokens provides the machine-readable linguistic representation of the gestures identified from the continuous gesture stream.
At step 212, the method (200) comprises translating, by the neural machine translation module (112), the sequence of linguistic tokens generated by the gesture recognition module (110) into the target-language text. The neural machine translation module (112) receives the recognized linguistic tokens and processes the linguistic tokens through the neural machine translation model to produce corresponding text in the selected target language. Accordingly, the physical gestures are transformed from the recognized linguistic representation into readable language content.
At step 214, the method (200) comprises generating, by the text-to-speech module (114), synthesized speech corresponding to the target-language text generated by the neural machine translation module (112). The text-to-speech module (114) processes the target-language text using the neural text-to-speech model and produces the synthesized speech representing the translated linguistic content.
The translating at step 212 and the generating at step 214 form part of the end-to-end gesture-to-language processing pipeline executed substantially on the embedded processing unit (104). Thus, the sequence of linguistic tokens obtained from gesture recognition is converted into the target-language text through neural machine translation, and the resulting target-language text is subsequently converted into the synthesized speech without requiring independent manual intervention between the processing stages.
At step 216, the method (200) comprises outputting, through the output interface (116), at least one of the target-language text and the synthesized speech. The output interface (116) thereby communicates the linguistic meaning represented by the user's physical gestures in the selected target language in textual form, audible form, or both textual and audible forms.
At step 218, the method (200) comprises personalizing, by the personalization module (118), the gesture recognition according to characteristics of the individual user. The personalization module (118) performs few-shot adaptation using user-specific calibration gestures. The personalization module (118) further identifies confused gesture pairs when the gesture recognition module (110) encounters gestures having similar characteristics and generates the active-learning prompt for resolving the confused gesture pairs.
The personalization module (118) uses the user-specific calibration information and the response to the active-learning prompt to adapt subsequent gesture-recognition operation to the individual user's manner of performing gestures. Accordingly, the recognition process may progressively accommodate variations associated with the user's signing style and reduce repeated confusion between similar gestures.
At step 220, the method (200) comprises optionally communicating, through the communication interface (120), with the companion application. The communication interface (120) may selectively offload the translation operation to the companion application when the vocabulary size or the translation workload exceeds the processing capability of the embedded processing unit (104). During such selective offloading, the gesture recognition operation is maintained locally, thereby allowing the gesture-capture and gesture-recognition portions of the processing pipeline to continue at the system (100).
At step 222, the method (200) comprises repeating the capturing, acquiring, preprocessing, segmenting, recognizing, translating, generating, outputting, and personalizing operations for successive gestures performed by the user. The multimodal sensor array (102) continues to capture the gesture-related information, and the respective processing modules repeatedly process the incoming gesture stream to provide continuous gesture-to-language translation.
Accordingly, the method (200) integrates continuous temporal segmentation, multimodal sensor fusion, on-device gesture recognition, neural machine translation, synthesized speech generation, and user-specific personalization within the continuous processing pipeline. The method (200) thereby converts continuously performed physical gestures into the target-language text and the synthesized speech while adapting the gesture-recognition process to the individual user and reducing dependence upon external computing infrastructure.
